This is the first time gender is named in the play, and it is named by a woman as a boundary.

annotations.quote: Not framed by nature to contend with men.
annotations.note: The participle is dual again (l. 62): 'the two of us, not ones to fight against men'. Ismene states as a fact of nature the very thing Creon will keep repeating as a fear: that he must not be beaten by a woman, that while he lives no woman shall rule ([[s5]], [[s7]]). The play lets a woman say it first, gently, before a man says it with guards behind him.

annotations.quote: Remember this too that the stronger rules;
annotations.note: Read this carefully, because Ismene never says Creon is right. Her two reasons are that they are women and that they are ruled by people with more force. It is an argument from power only, and she follows it to its end: one must obey 'in this and in things more painful still'.

annotations.quote: Therefore I plead compulsion and entreat
annotations.note: She asks pardon of those under the earth, because, she says, she is being forced (ll. 65-66). So she concedes the main point. The dead have a claim, the claim is being denied, and she needs forgiveness for her part in denying it. The sisters do not disagree about what is right. They disagree about whether right can be done, and Antigone will treat that as no difference at all.

annotations.quote: To overstep in aught the golden mean.
annotations.note: Storr brings in the 'golden mean' and a rhyme to round the speech off. The Greek is blunter: περισσὰ πράσσειν (l. 68, _perissa prassein_), 'to do what is beyond the measure, to act out of one's place', has no νοῦν (_noun_, 'sense') in it. _Perissos_ means excessive, over and above, and Creon will use the same adjective with contempt at the end of [[s7]], calling reverence for the dead 'labour to excess'. Ismene means it kindly, but it is his word.

annotations.quote: I urge no more; nay, wert thou willing still,
annotations.note: A change of ground in two lines. Thirty lines ago she was asking; now she says that even if Ismene changed her mind she would not have her. The speed is the characterisation. Is it fair? Ismene has just asked the dead for pardon and has not said a word against the burial. But Antigone means it, and she keeps to it: when Ismene tries to share the guilt in [[s5]], she is refused in the same terms.

annotations.quote: Go thine own way; myself will bury him.
annotations.note: In the Greek the verb is held over to the start of the next line and stands alone: θάψω (l. 72, _thapso_), 'I will bury him', with an emphatic 'I' before it. The pair is finished. From this point every verb she uses for the deed is first person singular, and the dual she shared with Ismene at ll. 3 and 21 is gone.

annotations.quote: How sweet to die in such employ, to rest,—
annotations.note: Not 'sweet'. The word is καλόν (l. 72, _kalon_), 'fine, noble, beautiful', the adjective of the heroic code, and what is _kalon_ is θανεῖν, 'to die', doing this. Storr has turned a claim about honour into a feeling. Notice how early it comes: she has not yet touched the body and death is already the settled price. The phrase will be repeated to close her part in the scene at l. 97.

annotations.quote: Sister and brother linked in love’s embrace—
annotations.note: Storr elaborates. The Greek line is φίλη at one end and φίλου at the other with the verb κείσομαι between (l. 73): 'dear, I shall lie with him, with one who is dear'. 'Sister and brother' and 'embrace' are his. But he is responding to something real, because _keisomai_ is the verb for lying in a grave and also for lying beside a lover, and she uses it again three lines on. The strand that ends with her going to the tomb as to a bridal chamber in [[s9]] begins here.

annotations.quote: A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth,
annotations.note: The famous oxymoron: ὅσια (l. 74, _hosia_, 'holy things') followed by a participle (_panourgesasa_) from the word for a rogue, someone who will do anything. 'Having committed a holy crime', or 'having piously played the villain'. She knows it is a crime; she never pretends the law does not exist, only that something outranks it. Creon will use the noun from the same root for plain criminality in [[s3]]. 'Banned awhile on earth' is Storr's bridge to the next thought and is not in the Greek.

annotations.quote: But by the dead commended; and with them
annotations.note: Her reason is almost arithmetic: the time during which she must please those below (l. 75) is longer than the time she must please those here, because there she will lie for ever. This is her first justification, and it is about loyalty and duration, not law. It is a reckoning of advantage, though the word for gain, _kerdos_, is nowhere in this scene. Creon will assume in [[s3]] that gain is the only motive anyone could have for touching the body, and in [[s5]] she takes the word from him: to die before her time, she says, she counts as gain. The sum she does here is what she will mean by it.

annotations.quote: Scorn, if thou wilt, the eternal laws of Heaven.
annotations.note: Storr has borrowed 'eternal laws' from the great speech in [[s5]]; nothing so developed is here. The Greek says 'hold in dishonour what the gods hold in honour' (l. 77), with two _time_-words set against each other. It is the first time she claims the gods for her side, and she does it in a parting shot, by throwing at Ismene the verb she used of Creon at l. 22. Ismene is being moved into Creon's column.

annotations.quote: I scorn them not, but to defy the State
annotations.note: βίᾳ πολιτῶν (l. 79), 'in violence to the citizens'. Citizens, not Creon. And ἀμήχανος (_amechanos_), 'without resource, unable': she says she is by nature incapable of it. Remember the phrase. In the disputed lines of her last speech in [[s9]] Antigone herself says she acted 'in defiance of the citizens', in exactly these words. If that passage is genuine, she ends by accepting Ismene's description of what she did.

annotations.quote: To lap my dearest brother in the grave.
annotations.note: φιλτάτῳ (l. 81, _philtatoi_), the superlative of _philos_: 'dearest', most her own. The verb beside it means to heap up a mound, so she is still thinking of a proper tomb, more than she will be able to do. Storr's 'alone' in the line before has no word behind it in the Greek, though it is true enough to the sense.

annotations.quote: O waste no fears on me; look to thyself.
annotations.note: Literally 'set your own lot straight' (l. 83), with a verb built on _orthos_, 'upright'. Straightness is about to become Creon's favourite idea; his first speech in [[s3]] is full of a city set upright and a ship kept on an even keel. Here it is a sneer between sisters, and Ismene will give the word back in the last line of the scene.

annotations.quote: But keep it close and secret, as will I.
annotations.note: After 'in secret' the Greek adds 'and I likewise with you' (l. 85). That phrase is the 'with' Antigone asked for at l. 41, returned in the only form Ismene can manage. She will not share the work, but she will share the silence. It is an offer of complicity, and I think it is meant as a real gift.

annotations.quote: O tell it, sister; I shall hate thee more
annotations.note: ἐχθίων (l. 86, _echthion_), the comparative of _echthros_: 'you will be more of an enemy'. Storr's 'hate' makes it an emotion; the Greek is closer to a status. Ismene is being reclassified, in the same pair of terms Antigone opened with at l. 10. The 'own sibling' of line 1 is now measured on the scale of enemies.

annotations.quote: If thou proclaim it not to all the town.
annotations.note: κηρύξῃς (l. 87, _keryxeis_), 'proclaim as a herald', the verb behind Creon's κήρυγμα at l. 8. She wants her act published in the same way as his edict. This is what complicates any reading of her as a private mourner: secrecy would save her life and she treats the suggestion as an insult. And yet the first burial is done unseen, before the guards are awake. The deed and the declaration are not quite the same person.

annotations.quote: Thou hast a fiery soul for numbing work.
annotations.note: The Greek is a neat antithesis that 'numbing' blurs: θερμὴν ... καρδίαν over ψυχροῖσι (l. 88), 'a hot heart over cold things'. Cold things are chilling deeds, and also, plainly, the dead. It is the most exact thing anyone says about her in the scene. Her warmth is all directed at what is cold.

annotations.quote: If thou succeed; but thou art doomed to fail.
annotations.note: Storr leaves out the most interesting word. Ismene says ἀμηχάνων ἐρᾷς (l. 90): 'you are in love with the impossible'. The verb is from _eros_. Desire enters the play here, long before Haemon is mentioned, and its object is something that cannot be had. When the Chorus sing to Eros in [[s8]], the one who drives even the just mind off course, it is worth remembering that Ismene diagnosed it in her sister first.

annotations.quote: When strength shall fail me, yes, but not before.
annotations.note: She concedes the point about impossibility and makes it irrelevant. Her standard is effort, not result: she will stop when she physically cannot go on. It is a soldier's answer.

annotations.quote: But, if the venture’s hopeless, why essay?
annotations.note: θηρᾶν (l. 92, _theran_), 'to hunt': one should not hunt the impossible in the first place. This is the third use of the same root in fourteen lines (ll. 79, 90, 92), and it is Ismene's word for both herself and the task. Set it beside [[s4|the ode on man]], which praises the creature who is never without resource and who hunts and snares everything that lives. Ismene's vocabulary of helplessness is the ode's vocabulary turned inside out.

annotations.quote: Sister, forbear, or I shall hate thee soon,
annotations.note: Two more forms of _echthros_ in two lines: ἐχθαρεῖ (l. 93), 'you will be hated', and ἐχθρὰ (l. 94), 'an enemy' to the dead man, and justly. The verb with it is προσκείσει, 'you will lie beside', the same root as the κείσομαι of l. 73: Antigone will lie with him as one of his own, Ismene as his enemy. This is where I part from the reading that makes Antigone simply the voice of love. Her line in [[s5]], that she was born to join in loving and not in hating, is true of her towards the dead. Towards the living her division into friend and enemy is as hard as Creon's.

annotations.quote: Say I am mad and give my madness rein
annotations.note: 'Mad' overstates it. Her word is δυσβουλίαν (l. 95, _dysboulian_), 'bad counsel, poor judgement': 'leave me and the folly that is mine'. She takes Ismene's charge and wears it ironically. Good and bad counsel are words the play keeps for its ending: Teiresias calls good counsel the best possession in [[s11]], and the same noun she uses here is on Creon's lips, of himself, over his son's body in [[s13]].

annotations.quote: To wreck itself; the worst that can befall
annotations.note: What she will suffer is τὸ δεινὸν τοῦτο (l. 96), 'this terrible thing'. δεινὸν (_deinon_) is the word that opens [[s4|the ode on man]]: many things are _deina_, formidable, strange, terrible, and nothing more so than a human being. Its first use in the play is hers, about the consequence she is walking towards with her eyes open. Storr's 'the worst that can befall' flattens a word the audience is about to hear sung.

annotations.quote: Is but to die an honorable death.
annotations.note: καλῶς θανεῖν (l. 97), 'to die nobly', closing the ring opened at l. 72. These are her last words before she goes to do it, and they are about the manner of her death, not about her brother. A tutor would ask whether she gets what she asks for. A noose in a sealed cave is not obviously a noble death, and her own lament in [[s9]] suggests that by then she is not sure.

annotations.quote: Have thine own way then; ’tis a mad endeavor,
annotations.note: Her word is _anous_ (l. 99), 'without sense', the negative of the _nous_ Ismene appealed to at l. 68. She does not take it back. Storr marks the end of the scene with a rhyming couplet, as he often does; the Greek has no rhyme, only an antithesis balanced across the line.

annotations.quote: Yet to thy lovers thou art dear as ever.
annotations.note: 'Lovers' means simply her own people. The Greek is τοῖς φίλοις and then ὀρθῶς φίλη (l. 99): 'to your own, truly one of their own'. It can be taken two ways, 'truly dear to those who love you' or 'a true friend to those you love', and I think Ismene means both. She gives the last word on _philos_, and quietly includes herself among the _philoi_ just after being called an enemy. It goes unanswered. Storr's 'Exeunt' hides the staging: Antigone leaves by the side passage toward the plain and Ismene goes back into the house, by different ways.

links.why: Ismene comes back and tries to claim a share in the deed she refuses here, and Antigone's reply is harder than anything in this scene.
'How sweet to die' meets the actual walk to the tomb, and it does not sound sweet any more.
Creon delivers in public, with his reasons, the edict the sisters have only heard by rumour.

s2.essay:
After the sisters' whispering in the dark, the old men of Thebes walk on and greet the sun. It is a real pleasure of the play's construction: private night, then public morning. The elders have just lived through a siege, and their song is the relief of people who expected to be dead or enslaved by now. The enemy army becomes one great white eagle screaming over the walls, and Zeus knocks it out of the sky.

What I notice is where Polyneices sits in this picture. For the elders he is the cause of the eagle, the man whose 'claim' brought a foreign host to burn their towers. They are not thinking of him as anyone's brother. When the brothers do appear, they get four lines at the end of a stanza and the tone goes quiet: one mother, one father, each killed by the other. Then straight back to victory.

And they want to forget. 'Memories of war blot out' is the truest line in the ode, and the play will not let them. The thing they most want to stop thinking about is lying unburied outside the walls and will be the only subject of the day.

Two practical notes on this printing. 'Great Area' is Ares, and 'festal should' is surely 'festal shout'; the text has a few slips like these. And notice that they call on Bacchus to lead the dance. They do it once more, in [[s12]], and both times bad news is already on its way.

annotations.quote: Sunbeam, of all that ever dawn upon
annotations.note: 'Ray of the sun' are the first words of the Chorus, fifteen old men of Thebes filing into the dancing-floor as the sisters leave it. Everything changes at once: dark to light, two voices to many, secrecy to public song, 'I' to 'we'. The elders know nothing of what we have just heard. They do not know of the edict, and they have no idea that the celebration they are beginning has already been undone.

annotations.quote: Our seven-gated Thebes the brightest ray,
annotations.note: The light is κάλλιστον (l. 100, _kalliston_), 'the most beautiful' ever to shine on Thebes. That is the superlative of the word Antigone has just used twice for her own death (ll. 72, 97). For her the beautiful thing is to die doing this; for the elders it is the morning on which the city is still standing. ἑπταπύλῳ ('seven-gated') starts a count of sevens that runs through the song (ll. 118, 141) and keeps the old story of the Seven against Thebes in the audience's mind.

annotations.quote: O eye of golden day,
annotations.note: More exactly 'eyelid': ἁμέρας βλέφαρον (l. 103, _hameras blepharon_). The day is opening its eye, which is a better picture of dawn than a staring 'eye'. And the day is χρυσέας, 'golden'. Remember the gold; it comes back at l. 130 on the other side, as the clanging gold of the enemy's pride.

annotations.quote: How fair thy light o’er Dirce’s fountain shone,
annotations.note: Dirce is the stream on the west side of Thebes, and with Ismenus on the east it stands for the city's own ground. Local water is how a Greek chorus says 'home'. Antigone will call on the same springs as witnesses when she is led away in [[s9]], so the landmark that opens the song of victory returns in the lament of the victory's casualty.

annotations.quote: Far quicker than they came, the Argive force;
annotations.note: The Greek is one long sentence in which the sunbeam itself drives the enemy off, as a rider would, 'with a sharper bridle': χαλινῷ (l. 107, _chalinoi_). And the enemy is singular. The whole army is 'the man from Argos', φῶτα (l. 106), a fugitive running headlong. Storr turns this into a plural 'force' and loses the oddity of an army imagined as a single body, which prepares the eagle that follows.

annotations.quote: The argent shields, the host with scutcheons white.
annotations.note: λεύκασπιν (l. 106, _leukaspin_), 'white-shielded'. The name Argos sounds like the Greek word for 'bright, white', and Storr's 'argent' is a clever way of keeping the play on words. The white shield then becomes the white wing of the eagle, 'of white snow', a few lines on (l. 114). The elders' picture of the enemy is all glare.

annotations.quote: To vindicate fell Polyneices’ claim.
annotations.note: 'Fell', cruel or deadly, is Storr's addition. What the Greek has is a pun on the name: Πολυνείκους (l. 110), 'Much-strife', roused by νεικέων (l. 111, _neikeon_, 'quarrels'). And the quarrels are ἀμφιλόγων (_amphilogon_), 'disputed, with something said on both sides'. In the legend the brothers were to share the throne and Eteocles kept it. So in the very song that celebrates his defeat, the elders' own adjective admits the traitor had a case.

annotations.quote: Like to an eagle swooping low,
annotations.note: The eagle comes screaming shrill, and this part is chanted in marching anapaests, a different rhythm from the sung stanzas, which Storr's layout does not show. The eagle is Zeus's own bird, yet Zeus will strike this one down. With the serpent of l. 125 it makes the omen from the Iliad, eagle against snake, in which the snake wins. And notice the birds. In the prologue birds were to feed on Polyneices (l. 29); here his army is the bird of prey. The punishment has been fitted to the image.

annotations.quote: His spearmen raven at our seven gates.
annotations.note: The eagle stands over the roofs ἀμφιχανὼν (l. 117, _amphichanon_), 'gaping all round' with spears for a beak, at the ἑπτάπυλον στόμα (l. 118), the 'seven-gated mouth' of the city. One mouth gapes at another. Storr's 'raven', to prey greedily, keeps the appetite but drops the mouths.

annotations.quote: But ere a torch our crown of towers could burn,
annotations.note: στεφάνωμα πύργων (l. 120), 'the garland of towers', the city wall seen as a wreath on a head. Storr's 'torch' is in Greek the god's name: 'pine-fed Hephaestus', Ἥφαιστον (l. 121), put for fire itself. Fire is the weapon the attackers brought and, a few lines on, the weapon Zeus uses on them.

annotations.quote: Ere they had tasted of our blood, they turn
annotations.note: γένυσιν (l. 120, _genysin_), 'jaws': before its jaws were filled with αἱμάτων, 'our blood'. The besieger is a carrion-eater. Creon takes this image straight into his decree in [[s3]], where Polyneices is the man who came to feed on kindred blood. The edict then answers the image exactly, by making him the thing that is fed on. I think the ode shows us where Creon's idea of a fitting penalty comes from: the city was already thinking in these pictures.

annotations.quote: Forced by the Dragon; in their rear
annotations.note: The Dragon, the serpent, is Thebes itself (l. 125). The city's first men sprang from the dragon's teeth that Cadmus sowed, so the Thebans are the serpent's brood, and the eagle has met its natural enemy. The Greek of this line is knotted and its exact construction disputed, but the sense is that the serpent was too hard an adversary to master. The dragon was sacred to Ares, whose din is heard in the same line and who appears in person at l. 139.

annotations.quote: For Zeus who hates the braggart’s boast
annotations.note: This is the theology of the song, and it is the play's ending stated in advance. Zeus ὑπερεχθαίρει (l. 128, _hyperechthairei_, 'hates beyond measure') the γλώσσης κόμπους (l. 127), 'boasts of a big tongue'. The Chorus's last words in [[s13]] say that the great words of the over-proud are paid for with great blows. They sing it here about an invader. They will say it there about Creon. Mark also the string of _hyper_-compounds in these lines (ll. 113, 128, 130): going over, hating over, arms carried too high.

annotations.quote: Beheld that gold-bespangled host;
annotations.note: χρυσοῦ καναχῆς (l. 130), 'of clanging gold', with ὑπεροπλίαις, 'in the arrogance of their arms'; the text is uncertain here but those words are clear enough. Storr drops the image just before it, that they came on 'in a great stream', ῥεύματι (l. 129). This is the second gold in the song. The first was the eyelid of day. One is the gods' light and the other is men's display, and Zeus looks at the second and throws fire.

annotations.quote: As at the goal the paean they upraise,
annotations.note: Storr's 'they' is wrong in an interesting way. The Greek turns singular: Zeus hurls fire at one man who was already at the top, starting to shout νίκην (l. 133, _niken_, 'victory'). This is Capaneus, who swore to burn Thebes whether Zeus willed it or not, and the ode never names him. His position on the wall is called βαλβίδων (l. 131, _balbidon_), the line on a race-course, so he is a runner struck down as he breasts the tape. The elders tell it as an athletic event with a divine referee.

annotations.quote: To earthy from earth rebounding, down he crashed;
annotations.note: 'To earthy' is a slip in this printing of Storr; read 'to earth'. The Greek has the earth hitting back, ἀντιτύπᾳ (l. 134, _antitypai_, 'that returns the blow'), and the rare participle τανταλωθεὶς (_tantalotheis_), 'swung through the air', in which a Greek ear probably heard the name of Tantalus, another man who presumed on the gods. The second pair of stanzas begins here, with the fall.

annotations.quote: The fire-brand from his impious hand was dashed,
annotations.note: In the Greek he is 'the fire-bearer' (l. 135), and that is all. 'Impious' is Storr's comment. The Greek does not need to say it: the man carrying fire against Thebes is answered by the god's fire, and the title he bears is the title of his punishment.

annotations.quote: As like a Bacchic reveler on he came,
annotations.note: βακχεύων (l. 136, _bakcheuon_), 'raving like a bacchant', in a mad onrush. Look where the word falls. Bacchus is the god of Thebes, his mother was Theban, and at the end of this same song the elders ask him to lead their dance (l. 154). Yet the first Bacchic thing in the play is the frenzy of the city's attacker. The god's madness is on both sides of the wall, and that is a warning about the god they are about to call on again in [[s12]].

annotations.quote: Outbreathing hate and flame,
annotations.note: 'With the blasts of most hateful winds': ἐχθίστων ἀνέμων (l. 137). ἐχθίστων (_echthiston_) is the superlative of _echthros_, and we have just heard Antigone use the comparative of her own sister (l. 86). For the elders the word is easy. The enemy is the man outside the gates with a torch. The prologue has already shown us someone for whom the line between own and enemy runs through the family and through the city.

annotations.quote: Here, there, great Area like a war-horse wheeled;
annotations.note: 'Area' is a misprint for Ares: μέγας Ἄρης (l. 139). 'War-horse' is vague where the Greek is exact. Ares is δεξιόσειρος (l. 140, _dexioseiros_), the right-hand trace-horse of a four-horse chariot team, the strong one on the outside that does the work on the turn. An Athenian audience knew chariot-racing well. The god of war is the horse that brings the team round, and the enemy's line turns with him.

annotations.quote: Seven captains at our seven gates
annotations.note: Seven captains at seven gates, posted 'equals against equals' (ll. 141-142). This is the matched catalogue of Aeschylus's Seven against Thebes compressed into two lines, and the audience would supply the rest. 'Equals against equals' is the phrase to hold: it applies to six pairs as a boast and to the seventh as a horror.

annotations.quote: Trophy for Zeus who turns the fight;
annotations.note: Ζηνὶ τροπαίῳ (l. 143), Zeus 'of the rout'. A trophy, _tropaion_, is by origin the monument set up at the spot where the enemy turned, _trope_, and ran. Storr's 'who turns the fight' gets the etymology. The six defeated captains leave their bronze to the god. The seventh pair leave nothing to anybody.

annotations.quote: Save two alone, that ill-starred pair
annotations.note: τοῖν στυγεροῖν (l. 144, _toin stygeroin_), in the dual again: 'the two abhorred ones'. Storr's 'ill-starred' is softer than the Greek, which means hateful, abominable. The important thing is that it covers both of them. Before Creon has said a word, the elders do not distinguish patriot from traitor; the brothers are one pair with one adjective. It is the edict in the next scene that divides them, and Antigone's whole case is that they should not be divided.

annotations.quote: One mother to one father bare,
annotations.note: 'Of one father and one mother' (ll. 144-145). In [[s5]] Antigone answers Creon's 'was the other not also your brother?' with almost these words: of one mother and the same father. The Chorus has made her argument for her before she appears, without noticing. In this house, too, 'one father and one mother' is never an innocent phrase.

annotations.quote: Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
annotations.note: 'Drave' is the old past tense of drive. The Greek ends on κοινοῦ θανάτου (l. 147), 'a common death' in which both have their share: _koinon_ once more, the first word of the play (l. 1) and Ismene's word for the brothers' doom (l. 57). Their spears are δικρατεῖς (l. 146), 'both victorious', each one killing its man. And this is all the victory song has to say about the event that made Creon king and that drives the whole play: a few lines, then on to the dancing.

annotations.quote: Now Victory to Thebes returns again
annotations.note: Victory in person, 'great of name', has come to Thebes 'of the many chariots' (ll. 148-149), answering the city's joy with her own. The stanza opens in Greek with a brisk 'but enough', turning away from the brothers. The turn is too quick, and I think we are meant to feel that it is.

annotations.quote: Memories of war blot out.
annotations.note: In the line before, 'should' is a misprint for 'shout'. The elders propose θέσθαι λησμοσύναν (l. 151, _lesmosynan_), 'to make a forgetting' of the war just over. That is the wish the play refuses. There is a body on the plain that cannot be forgotten, a ruler who will not let it be forgotten, and a girl who will not forget it either. Of the three parties the Chorus is the one that would like to move on, and that tells us a good deal about how it will behave under pressure.

annotations.quote: Dance and sing the live night long.
annotations.note: 'With all-night dances', at every temple of the gods (ll. 152-153). 'Live night' is Storr's 'livelong'. None of it happens. By the time this day ends the altars they mean to visit are fouled with scraps of the unburied corpse, as Teiresias reports in [[s11]], and the house they serve has three more dead in it.

annotations.quote: Bacchus, shaker of the ground!
annotations.note: Βάκχιος (l. 154) is to lead the dance, and he is ἐλελίχθων (l. 153, _elelichthon_), 'earth-shaker', the one whose dancers make the ground of Thebes tremble. This is the first of two invocations. The second is the desperate hymn of [[s12]], when the elders beg him to come with healing foot to a city sick with pollution. Having heard his name used for Capaneus's frenzy forty lines ago, we should not assume his coming is always gentle.

annotations.quote: Lo! Creon our new lord draws near,
annotations.note: The anapaests return to announce an entrance. The elders call him βασιλεὺς χώρας (l. 155), 'king of the land', where Antigone called him only the general (l. 8). But they say 'new' twice in two lines: νεοχμὸς (l. 156, _neochmos_) and νεαραῖσι (l. 157), a new ruler by new turns of fortune. _Neochmos_ can carry a hint of the novel and untried. He is introduced as a novelty before he opens his mouth.

annotations.quote: Crowned by this strange chance, our king.
annotations.note: A cool way to announce a monarch. Creon holds the throne because both heirs died yesterday, and everything he does in [[s3]] is done by a man one day into the job and anxious to look equal to it. Storr's 'strange chance' leaves out one thing: in Greek the chances are the gods' (l. 157), 'fortunes sent by the gods'. The elders see heaven's hand in his accession. That is a title he can lose in the same way.

annotations.quote: What, I marvel, pondering?
annotations.note: Literally 'what plan is he rowing': μῆτιν ἐρέσσων (l. 158, _metin eresson_), plying a scheme as one plies an oar. Storr's 'pondering' drops the boat. It matters because Creon's first words in [[s3]] are about the city as a ship that the gods have righted after a storm, and the ship of state is his master image. The elders' metaphor hands him his opening.

annotations.quote: Us, his elders, one and all,
annotations.note: The meeting is σύγκλητον (l. 160, _synkleton_), 'specially convened', the Athenian term for an extraordinary session, and it is a λέσχην (l. 161, 'council') of γερόντων, old men. They have been called κοινῷ κηρύγματι (l. 161b), 'by a common proclamation'. Both words are from the prologue: _kerygma_ was Antigone's word for the edict (l. 8) and _koinon_ the first word she spoke. So the play sets two summonses side by side. Antigone called one sister outside the gates to hear in private; Creon calls the elders by herald to hear in public. Neither of them is asking for advice.

links.why: The second hymn to Bacchus, sung in hope just before the catastrophe, answers this one sung in relief just before the trouble starts.
The same Polyneices the elders picture as an eagle is the corpse Creon now legislates about.

s3.essay:
Creon's first speech is good, and it should be allowed to be good. He does not come on as a tyrant. He comes on as a man who has inherited a city one day after it nearly burned, and who says, sensibly, that nobody knows what a ruler is made of 'till he be proved by exercise of power.' His principle is that the city is the ship everyone sails in, and that a man who puts a friend before it is contemptible. A century later Demosthenes quoted these lines to an Athenian jury as a model of what a statesman ought to think. Polyneices led a foreign army against his own walls. Refusing him honours is not madness.

But listen to how the elders receive it. 'Thy word is law; thou canst dispose of us.' That is assent without agreement. They say he has the power, and they do not say he is right, and when he asks them to help enforce the order they suggest he find younger men. The speech about the ship of state has landed on people who are already keeping their heads down.

Then the Guard arrives, and the play turns briefly into comedy. He has argued with himself the whole way, he wants it on record that he neither did it nor saw it done, and he has to be told to shoot his bolt and go. I like him a great deal. He is what people are actually like under a threat, and he is there so that we can measure Antigone against the usual thing.

His news is strange. The body is covered with dust, there are no tracks, and no animal has touched it. The elders wonder aloud whether a god did this, and Creon explodes. That explosion is the first crack. He knows, he says, that the gods could have no thought for this dead man, and since it cannot be the gods it must be money: malcontents have bribed the guards. He has no evidence. He reaches for bribery again when the prophet comes in [[s11]]. A man who can explain every opposition as corruption never has to ask whether the opposition has a point.

annotations.quote: Elders, the gods have righted one again
annotations.note: Creon's first word is plain ἄνδρες (_andres_, 'men', l. 162), and his first subject is θεοὶ (_theoi_, 'the gods'), placed at the end of the line for weight. He opens by crediting heaven with the victory. Hold on to that, because this scene ends with him telling the same old men that it is 'intolerable' to suggest the gods had anything to do with the burial. He is pious as long as the gods agree with the government.

annotations.quote: Our storm-tossed ship of state, now safe in port.
annotations.note: Storr has built the ship and the harbour himself. The Greek (l. 163) says only that the gods, having shaken the city's affairs πολλῷ σάλῳ (_pollōi salōi_, 'in a great sea-swell'), ὤρθωσαν (_ōrthōsan_, 'set them upright') again. The same gods do the shaking and the righting. The word to track is the 'upright' one: Oedipus 'kept the city upright' at l. 167, the city sails 'upright' at l. 190, and in [[s11]] Teiresias will remind Creon that he once steered this city straight, just before telling him he has run it aground.

annotations.quote: But you by special summons I convened
annotations.note: The Greek is ἐκ πάντων δίχα (_ek pantōn dicha_, 'apart from everyone', l. 164). This is a hand-picked audience, old men chosen for a record of obedience, and the people are not asked. Haemon will tell his father in [[s7]] what the unpicked city is saying. Ask who is on stage: a king one day in office, fifteen elders, attendants, and nobody who can say no.

annotations.quote: I knew you loyal to Laius of old;
annotations.note: Loyal is too mild. He says they were σέβοντας (_sebontas_, 'revering', l. 166) the power of Laius' throne, and _sebein_ is the verb of religious awe. From his second sentence Creon uses the vocabulary of worship for obedience to rulers. The play's quarrel over _eusebeia_, what reverence is and to whom it is owed, begins here, before Antigone has been mentioned.

annotations.quote: Brother by brother murderously slain,
annotations.note: Storr's 'murderously' covers a harder phrase: αὐτόχειρι σὺν μιάσματι (_autocheiri syn miasmati_, 'with the pollution of a kindred hand', l. 172). Creon knows what _miasma_ is and names it in his first minute. He will then manufacture a larger one by leaving a corpse above ground, and it is the pollution, carried by birds to the altars, that Teiresias reports in [[s11]]. Note also _autocheir_, 'own-handed': it comes back at l. 306 in a place Creon does not intend.

annotations.quote: By right of kinship to the Princes dead,
annotations.note: ἀγχιστεῖα (_anchisteia_, l. 174) is a legal word, 'nearness of kin', the title under which an Athenian inherited. The same nearness carried the duty to bury the dead man. Creon claims the throne by his kinship with the brothers and in the next breath forbids the chief office kinship imposes. Antigone never makes this point against him, but the audience had the law in their heads.

annotations.quote: I claim and hold the throne and sovereignty.
annotations.note: The line begins ἐγὼ (_egō_, l. 173) and has πάντα, 'all', in the middle: 'I hold all the powers and the throne.' Count the first-person pronouns in this speech; they come at ll. 164, 173, 178, 184, 191, and twice in the last four lines. A man who has just said power is the test of character has started the test.

annotations.quote: The temper of a man, his mind and will,
annotations.note: Three nouns: ψυχήν τε καὶ φρόνημα καὶ γνώμην (_psychēn te kai phronēma kai gnōmēn_, l. 176), soul, cast of mind, judgment. The middle one, _phronēma_, is Creon's word. He closes this speech with it at l. 207, and the Chorus hand it back in the ode at l. 354. It belongs to the family of _phronein_, 'to think soundly', which is the last thing the play says anyone learns.

annotations.quote: Till he be proved by exercise of power;
annotations.note: The Greek is physical: until a man is shown ἐντριβὴς (_entribēs_, 'rubbed, worn', l. 177) against ἀρχαῖς τε καὶ νόμοισιν, 'offices and laws'. Storr keeps the offices and drops the laws. The thought was proverbial, and Greeks credited one of the Seven Sages with the saying that rule shows the man. Creon sets the terms of his own examination, and the rest of the play is the test he asks for here, failed by his own standard.

annotations.quote: Swerve from the highest policy, tongue-tied
annotations.note: The bad ruler is one who keeps γλῶσσαν ἐγκλῄσας (_glōssan enklēisas_, 'his tongue locked up', l. 180) ἐκ φόβου, out of fear. That is a fair maxim for a king and an exact description of his subjects by the end of the day. Antigone tells him in [[s5]] that the elders would approve her if fear did not shut their mouths, and the guards in this very scene bow their heads φόβῳ (l. 270). He also praises 'the best counsels' here and will refuse every piece of counsel offered him until Teiresias has left.

annotations.quote: And I contemn the man who sets his friend
annotations.note: φίλον (_philon_, l. 183) is the word, and 'friend' is too thin for it. A _philos_ is first of all one's own: kin, household, those to whom one is bound before any choosing. Antigone used it of Polyneices in [[s1]]. Creon says that whoever counts a _philos_ above his fatherland he counts 'nowhere', οὐδαμοῦ λέγω. He is ranking family beneath the city in general terms, before he knows the offender will be his niece and his son's bride.

annotations.quote: To witness Zeus, whose eyes are everywhere,
annotations.note: ἴστω Ζεὺς (_istō Zeus_, 'let Zeus know it', l. 184): the first of two oaths by Zeus in this episode; the second is at l. 304. A Zeus who sees everything always also sees the body on the plain. In [[s5]] Antigone's opening move is that it was not Zeus who made this proclamation. Both of them call the same witness.

annotations.quote: If I perceive some mischievous design
annotations.note: Storr turns a great word into a conspiracy. Creon says he would not be silent on seeing τὴν ἄτην (_tēn atēn_, 'ruin, the blindness that leads to ruin', l. 185) 'walking toward the citizens in place of safety'. _Atē_ is the subject of [[s6|the second stasimon]], where it is the thing that walks through a house generation after generation. Here it is on its way to the townsmen and the man watching for it is the one bringing it. The pairing of _atē_ with safety returns in the last line of his next speech (l. 314).

annotations.quote: Nor would I reckon as my private friend
annotations.note: 'Private' and 'public' are Storr's antithesis. The Greek is blunter: 'I would never make a man hostile to the land a _philos_ for myself' (ll. 187–188), with δυσμενῆ, 'ill-minded', standing against φίλον. The verb is the telling part. For Creon a _philos_ is something you appoint. Polyneices is his sister's son and was his _philos_ before either of them could choose.

annotations.quote: Is the good ship that holds our fortunes all:
annotations.note: ἡ σῴζουσα (_hē sōizousa_, 'she who keeps us safe', l. 189): the city is the saviour, and the ship appears only in the next word, πλέοντες, 'sailing'. This is where the image Storr planted in the first line actually stands in the Greek. It is an old and honourable figure, and Creon is not wrong that everyone drowns when the ship goes down. What he leaves out is that the helmsman can sink her. In [[s13]] he calls what he has reached a harbour of Hades.

annotations.quote: Farewell to friendship, if she suffers wreck.
annotations.note: Storr gives a sigh where the Greek gives a doctrine. Literally: 'only while we sail on her upright do we make our friends', τοὺς φίλους ποιούμεθα (_tous philous poioumetha_, l. 190). Friends are made, on the deck of the city, and by implication unmade there. This is _philos_ redefined by the polis: for Antigone you are born with your _philoi_ and cannot resign from them. The whole collision of [[s5]] is contained in that one verb.

annotations.quote: Such is the policy by which I seek
annotations.note: 'Policy' is νόμοισι (_nomoisi_, 'laws, principles', l. 191): 'by such _nomoi_ I make this city great.' It is Creon's first use of _nomos_ for his own maxims. The Chorus will say at l. 213 that he may use any _nomos_ he pleases, and Antigone will answer in [[s5]] with laws nobody enacted. Watch how easily a ruler's rules of thumb become 'the laws' when he is the one speaking.

annotations.quote: I have proclaimed an edict as concerns
annotations.note: Storr's 'conformably' in the line above stands for ἀδελφὰ τῶνδε (_adelpha tōnde_, 'brother to these', l. 192): the decree is 'brother' to his principles. The metaphor is ordinary Greek for 'akin', but it is a strange word to reach for when introducing an order about two brothers. The verb is κηρύξας, 'having had it heralded'. Antigone will insist on that word: a herald's proclamation, a _kērygma_, which she will not allow to be a law.

annotations.quote: That are the guerdon of the heroic dead.
annotations.note: The Greek says the rites 'go down to the best of the dead below', τοῖς ἀρίστοις ... κάτω νεκροῖς (l. 197). Creon believes that what is done at a grave reaches someone underneath. He is no rationalist about burial; he knows what the offerings are for and is deliberately withholding them. That makes the next clause an act against the dead man and the powers below, and it is how Teiresias will describe it.

annotations.quote: But for the miscreant exile who returned
annotations.note: 'Miscreant' is Storr's word. What Creon says first is τὸν δʼ αὖ ξύναιμον τοῦδε, 'but his brother of the same blood', and ξύναιμον (_xynaimon_, l. 198) is one of the play's kinship words. He states the tie in his own decree and then legislates as if it were not there. φυγὰς (l. 200), 'an exile', is the only hint of Polyneices' side of the story, and nobody on stage takes it up.

annotations.quote: His father’s city and his father’s gods,
annotations.note: θεοὺς τοὺς ἐγγενεῖς (_theous tous engeneis_, 'the gods of his race', l. 199). The charge is sacrilege as well as treason, and Creon repeats it with more heat at ll. 285–287. It matters to his reasoning: he infers that the gods must hate the man who came to burn their temples. That is an inference about the gods' feelings, and at no point does he ask a god or a prophet.

annotations.quote: And glut his vengeance with his kinsmen’s blood,
annotations.note: αἵματος κοινοῦ πάσασθαι (_haimatos koinou pasasthai_, 'to taste of shared blood', ll. 201–202): Creon makes him a cannibal. The adjective κοινοῦ, 'common, shared', is the one Antigone opens the play with, in her first line, addressed to her sister's head. For her the shared blood is the bond that obliges; for Creon it is the aggravation of the crime. They use the same word and mean opposite things by it.

annotations.quote: For Polyneices ’tis ordained that none
annotations.note: After a speech full of 'I', the decree itself comes in the impersonal perfect passive: ἐκκεκήρυκται (_ekkekēryktai_, 'it stands proclaimed', l. 203), 'to this city'. The author disappears at the moment of the order and the polis is put in his place. When Haemon asks in [[s7]] whether the city belongs to one man, this grammatical sleight is what he is exposing.

annotations.quote: Shall give him burial or make mourn for him,
annotations.note: Two prohibitions, μήτε κτερίζειν μήτε κωκῦσαί (l. 204): no funeral gifts and no keening. _Kōkyein_ is the shrill wail of women at a death, and the Guard will use a compound of it when he describes Antigone over the body in [[s5]]. Laying out and lamenting were women's work in a Greek household, so the edict, though addressed to 'anyone', falls on the two surviving women of the family. For the Athenian audience: a traitor could be refused burial in Attic soil, but his kin might bury him across the border. Creon forbids burial anywhere and posts a watch.

annotations.quote: For dogs and carrion crows, a ghastly sight.
annotations.note: The last word in the Greek is ἰδεῖν (_idein_, 'to look upon', l. 206): the body is to be eaten and αἰκισθέν, 'disfigured', for people to see. He is making an exhibit as well as withholding honour. The birds are οἰωνῶν (_oiōnōn_, l. 205), the word for birds of omen too, and it is exactly these birds, gorged on this flesh, whose cries Teiresias can no longer read in [[s11]]. The audience would also hear the opening of the _Iliad_, where dogs and birds get the bodies of heroes.

annotations.quote: So am I purposed; never by my will
annotations.note: τοιόνδʼ ἐμὸν φρόνημα, 'such is my _phronēma_' (l. 207), the word from l. 176. He said a man's _phronēma_ cannot be known until he rules, and thirty lines later he displays his, complete. The speech that began with the gods righting the city ends twice with 'from me': ἔκ γʼ ἐμοῦ here and ἐξ ἐμοῦ at l. 210. Honour in Thebes now has a single source.

annotations.quote: But all good patriots, alive or dead,
annotations.note: θανὼν καὶ ζῶν ὁμοίως (_thanōn kai zōn homoiōs_, 'dead and living alike', ll. 209–210). Here is the overreach, stated as a boast: his jurisdiction covers the dead on the same terms as the living. The one test is being εὔνους, 'well-minded', toward the city. The Chorus pick the phrase up at l. 214 and hand it back to him with the order reversed.

annotations.quote: Son of Menoeceus, thus thou will’st to deal
annotations.note: ἀρέσκει (_areskei_, 'it pleases', l. 211): 'this is your pleasure, Creon'. The elders report his wish and add no word of their own. Compare what a compliant chorus could have said: wisely spoken, justly decreed. They address him by his father's name rather than as king, which may be courtesy and may be a reminder that he is new.

annotations.quote: Thy word is law; thou canst dispose of us
annotations.note: Read this coldly. νόμῳ δὲ χρῆσθαι παντί (_nomōi de chrēsthai panti_, l. 213): 'you have the power, I suppose, to use any law at all, about the dead and about us who live.' The little particle που, 'I suppose', is in the Greek and not in Storr. They describe his power and decline to praise his judgment. When Antigone claims in [[s5]] that the city agrees with her and is afraid to say so, this line is her evidence.

annotations.quote: See then ye execute what I ordain.
annotations.note: He asks them to be σκοποὶ (_skopoi_, 'watchers', l. 215) of his orders. They take it, or choose to take it, as a request to guard the corpse, and plead their age. He means something else: watch the city for me. Two lines later he has ἐπίσκοποι, 'overseers', on the body already. A regime one day old has sentries on a dead man and wants informers among the elders.

annotations.quote: On younger shoulders lay this grievous charge.
annotations.note: This is the first refusal in the play after Ismene's, and it is made by old men with perfect manners. They do not say the task is wrong. They say it is heavy and they are old. It is the Chorus's method throughout: never oppose, never quite endorse, until Teiresias gives them cover in [[s11]].

annotations.quote: Not to connive at disobedience.
annotations.note: τοῖς ἀπιστοῦσιν (_tois apistousin_, 'those who disobey', l. 219): he already assumes there will be some. The verb also means 'to disbelieve, to withhold trust', which suits a ruler who equates the two. The Chorus use the same participle of Antigone when she is led in at l. 381, so his category is ready for her before she fills it.

annotations.quote: No man is mad enough to court his death.
annotations.note: μῶρος (_mōros_, 'fool', l. 220), and the verb is ἐρᾷ (_erai_, 'is in love with'): no one is such a fool as to be in love with dying. We have just watched a scene in which someone was. In [[s1]] Antigone said it would be fine to die doing this, and Ismene told her she was in love with the impossible, using the same verb. The elders state as a law of human nature the exact thing the audience knows to be false. Antigone will throw 'fool' back at Creon in [[s5]].

annotations.quote: The penalty _is_ death: yet hope of gain
annotations.note: The first appearance of τὸ κέρδος (_to kerdos_, 'gain, profit', l. 222), and note where it comes: before any crime has been reported. Creon has the motive ready in advance. Death he calls ὁ μισθός, 'the wage', so even the penalty is put in terms of pay. From here to the end of the scene he explains everything by money, and in [[s11]] he will say the same of Teiresias. Antigone will use _kerdos_ once, in [[s5]], for dying before her time, which is the one gain he has not budgeted for.

annotations.quote: My lord, I will not make pretense to pant
annotations.note: Messengers in tragedy arrive at a run with their news already in their mouths. This one opens by announcing that he has not hurried, a joke at the convention's expense. He is nameless, a common soldier, and the only comic figure in the play. He speaks the same iambic trimeter as the king, but the syntax is that of talk: restarts, proverbs, reported arguments with himself. Sophocles lowers the register exactly when the plot's first shock is due.

annotations.quote: In sooth my soul beneath its pack of thought
annotations.note: The pack, and conscience with her spur and curb two lines on, are Storr's. The Greek has φροντίδων ἐπιστάσεις (_phrontidōn epistaseis_, 'haltings of thought', l. 225) and then ψυχὴ γὰρ ηὔδα, 'for my soul kept saying to me' (l. 227). There is no conscience in it; the argument is about which course will hurt less. It is a small parody of tragic deliberation, and worth noticing that he is the only character who weighs both sides aloud before acting. The heroes of this play do not deliberate.

annotations.quote: Thus leisurely I hastened on my road;
annotations.note: A lovely contradiction in Storr, and a textual question underneath it. This Greek text reads ἤνυτον σχολῇ βραδύς (_ēnyton scholēi bradys_, l. 231), 'I got it done, at leisure, slowly'. Storr's paradox translates a variant, _tachys_, 'quick', which many editors have preferred because it is funnier. Either way the dithering is the play's picture of ordinary fear under this king, and it is the natural product of the speech we have just heard.

annotations.quote: Much thought extends a furlong to a league.
annotations.note: The Greek is a flat proverb, ὁδὸς βραχεῖα γίγνεται μακρά (_hodos bracheia gignetai makra_, l. 232): 'a short road becomes long'. The Guard thinks in ready-made sayings, and there is another at l. 277. Storr's furlong and league dress him up. The line also tells us, in passing, that the corpse lies a short way from the palace.

annotations.quote: To face thee. I will speak though I say nothing.
annotations.note: τὸ μηδὲν (_to mēden_, 'the nothing', l. 234): his report has a hole where the culprit should be. He has an event and no agent, which is the worst thing to bring to a ruler who needs someone to blame. The phrase comes back at the end of the play, when Creon calls himself a man who is no more than nothing.

annotations.quote: For plucking courage from despair methought,
annotations.note: Storr reverses the Greek, which says he comes δεδραγμένος (_dedragmenos_, 'clutching tight', l. 235) to hope, τῆς ἐλπίδος: the hope that nothing can happen to him except τὸ μόρσιμον, what is fated. Fatalism is his comfort. Hope runs through these two sections: it destroys men in Creon's mouth at l. 221, the Guard clings to it here and is saved 'beyond hope' at l. 330, and the ode gives man skill 'beyond hope' at l. 365.

annotations.quote: I neither did the deed nor saw it done,
annotations.note: He asks to state τἀμαυτοῦ, 'my own position', first, and does so before any news. After forty lines of Creon on putting the city before oneself, the first citizen we meet puts himself before everything and says so. His phrase for the culprit is ὁ δρῶν (_ho drōn_, 'the doer', l. 239), a masculine participle. Everyone in this scene assumes a man.

annotations.quote: The bearer of dread tidings needs must quake.
annotations.note: Here is the word of the coming ode, ninety lines early: τὰ δεινὰ (_ta deina_, 'terrible things', l. 243) 'lay on a man much hesitation'. The Guard means frightening news. When the Chorus open [[s4]] with πολλὰ τὰ δεινά they repeat his phrase, and he will plant the adjective once more at l. 323a. The audience hear 'wondrous' in the ode with 'dreadful' already in their ears.

annotations.quote: Well, it must out; the corpse is buried; someone
annotations.note: After twenty-odd lines of preface the news takes three. The Greek order is the corpse, then τις, 'someone', then the participle θάψας, 'having buried', and at once βέβηκε, 'is gone' (ll. 245–246). 'Buried' is the Guard's own word for a sprinkling of dust. Ritually he is right: the handful of earth and the due rites make a burial, whatever the depth.

annotations.quote: E’en now besprinkled it with thirsty dust,
annotations.note: διψίαν κόνιν (_dipsian konin_, ll. 246–247), 'thirsty dust', and Storr is exact. Dry dust on a dry plain at the end of the summer's fighting, and thirsty also for the libations Antigone brings in [[s5]]. This is the image the episode is named for: a king has spoken for fifty lines, and the answer is a handful of dust.

annotations.quote: Performed the proper ritual—and was gone.
annotations.note: κἀφαγιστεύσας ἃ χρή (_kaphagisteusas ha chrē_, 'and having performed the rites that are due', l. 247). The soldier reporting a capital crime describes it as doing what one ought, χρή, without noticing. Creon used a cousin of the verb, ἀφαγνίσαι, at l. 196 for the rites Eteocles is to receive. So the offence is that Polyneices has been given what Creon himself calls the proper thing.

annotations.quote: What say’st thou? Who hath dared to do this thing?
annotations.note: Storr's 'who' drops a word: τίς ἀνδρῶν (_tis andrōn_, 'what man', l. 248). Creon asks which of the men did it, and the possibility of a woman does not occur to him here or anywhere before she is brought in. His word for the act is ὁ τολμήσας, 'the one who dared', and _tolma_, daring, is what the ode condemns in its last stanza. Half of his fury in [[s5]] comes from having asked this question in this form.

annotations.quote: Of pick or mattock—hard unbroken ground,
annotations.note: The Guard proves the burial by listing what was absent: no pick, no mattock, no wheel-rut, the ground στύφλος, hard, and unbroken. Put this beside the first stanza of [[s4]], where man's mark on the earth is the plough that wears her down year after year. Whoever buried Polyneices left the earth as it was. The act that defies the city is, by the ode's own measure, the least violent thing a human does in the play.

annotations.quote: No sign that human hands had been at work.
annotations.note: Storr goes a step past the Greek, which says the doer was ἄσημος (_asēmos_, 'one who left no mark', l. 252). That is the first of the play's cruxes. Why are there two burials, this one and the one Antigone is caught at in [[s5]]? Some readers have held that the gods performed the first, and the Chorus say so at once. Others say that Antigone did both and came back because the guards swept the body bare. I think Sophocles wants both thoughts available: she did it, and it looked like something a god might do.

annotations.quote: When the first sentry of the morning watch
annotations.note: ἡμεροσκόπος (_hēmeroskopos_, 'day-watcher', l. 253) fixes the time. The prologue was played before dawn and Antigone left it at l. 99, so she did this in the dark while the Chorus were singing in the sunrise. Storr's 'terror-stricken' in the next line translates θαῦμα δυσχερὲς (_thauma duscheres_, l. 254), 'an uncomfortable wonder'. The guards' first reaction is astonishment, which is the right preparation for an ode about wonders.

annotations.quote: The corpse had vanished, not interred in earth,
annotations.note: ἠφάνιστο (_ēphanisto_, 'had been made unseen', l. 255). Set that against the end of the edict, where the body was to be left for people 'to look upon'. Creon wanted a sight and the dust removes exactly that. The burial is ritually slight and answers precisely the purpose of the order.

annotations.quote: To avert the curse that haunts the unburied dead:
annotations.note: ἄγος (_agos_, 'pollution, guilt before the gods', l. 256): the dust lay 'as of one avoiding _agos_'. The Guard takes it for the minimum any passer-by owes a corpse so as not to be tainted by having left it. So even the soldiers read the act as a religious one, and their reading condemns the order they are enforcing. Creon knows the idea: in [[s7]] he leaves Antigone a little food in her tomb to keep _agos_ off the city, using this word.

annotations.quote: Of hound or ravening jackal, not a sign.
annotations.note: The jackal is Storr's; the Greek says 'beast or dog'. This is the detail that makes it uncanny, since a film of dust would keep no dog away from a body left out all night. It is what prompts the Chorus's suggestion at l. 278. Notice that Sophocles gives the evidence for the miracle to the least imaginative witness available.

annotations.quote: Guard railed at guard and blows were like to end it,
annotations.note: φύλαξ ἐλέγχων φύλακα (_phylax elenchōn phylaka_, 'guard accusing guard', l. 260): a small civil war among comrades, the morning after two brothers killed each other. The verb for their noise, ἐρρόθουν (_errothoun_, l. 259), 'they surged, muttered', returns in Creon's mouth at l. 290 for citizens he says are murmuring against him. Suspicion of everyone by everyone is what his Thebes sounds like at every level.

annotations.quote: The ordeal, or to handle red-hot iron,
annotations.note: Lumps of hot metal, walking through fire, and θεοὺς ὁρκωμοτεῖν, 'to swear by the gods' (l. 265). With no evidence available the soldiers turn at once to the gods as judges, and it does not occur to them that the gods might be parties. Creon will swear by Zeus on the other side of the same question forty lines later.

annotations.quote: And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds,
annotations.note: The reeds are Storr's. The Greek has one man speak and all the rest bend their heads to the ground φόβῳ (_phobōi_, 'in fear', l. 270). Go back to l. 180, where Creon despised the man who locks his tongue 'from fear'. Here are his subjects an hour into his reign, afraid to tell him a fact. At l. 291 he complains that citizens shake their heads in secret, which is the same gesture seen from the throne.

annotations.quote: And I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize.
annotations.note: πάλος (_palos_, 'the lot', l. 275) condemns him 'to win this good thing', τοῦτο τἀγαθὸν, with a soldier's sarcasm. The scapegoat is Storr's addition. The guards settle it by lot, the device Athens used to fill offices, and the lot produces a man who then argues with his king to his face. It is a small democratic procedure inside a play about one-man rule.

annotations.quote: Unwelcome; no man cares to hear ill news.
annotations.note: A jingle in the Greek, ἄκων οὐχ ἑκοῦσιν (_akōn ouch hekousin_, 'unwilling, to the unwilling', l. 276), and then another proverb. His verb is στέργει (_stergei_, 'loves', l. 277): nobody loves the bringer of bad words. Creon uses the same verb at l. 292 for what he wants from his subjects, necks under the yoke 'so as to love me'. The Guard knows he will not be loved; the king expects to be.

annotations.quote: Of something more than natural at work.
annotations.note: The word is θεήλατον (_theēlaton_, 'god-driven, sent by a god', l. 278), and Storr's phrase is too vague for it. The elders say this thought has been with them πάλαι, 'for some time', which means since the Guard began. It is their one unprompted religious instinct in the first half of the play and it is correct in spirit: the gods do turn out to want this burial. Creon silences it in a line, and it is Teiresias in [[s11]] who has to say it again before they will act on it.

annotations.quote: O cease, you vex me with your babblement;
annotations.note: Storr hides a tracked word. Creon says 'stop, before your talk fills me with ὀργῆς' (_orgēs_, 'anger', l. 280). _Orgē_ is temper, the passion that governs a man, and the ode will list ἀστυνόμους ὀργάς, 'the tempers that order cities', among human achievements (l. 356). Here is one such temper at work. He adds that they risk being found ἄνους τε καὶ γέρων, 'mindless as well as old'. Here the objection is age; with Haemon in [[s7]] it will be youth. No age turns out to be the right one for contradicting him.

annotations.quote: That gods would have a thought for this dead man?
annotations.note: πρόνοιαν (_pronoian_, 'forethought, care', l. 283). Here Creon stops speaking for the city and starts speaking for heaven. He calls the suggestion οὐκ ἀνεκτὰ, 'not to be borne', which is a statement about himself and not about the gods. He is sure he knows whom they despise. Teiresias exists in this play to tell him he does not.

annotations.quote: And as some benefactor bury him,
annotations.note: Follow the argument, because it is an argument: the gods honour benefactors, Polyneices came to burn their temples, therefore they cannot have honoured him. The hidden premise is that burial is a reward, to be earned by services like a civic crown. Antigone's reply in [[s5]] is that burial is owed to the dead as such, and that Hades does not sort them by their record. Creon models the gods on a city council and then finds that they vote as he does.

annotations.quote: And scout their ordinances? Or perchance
annotations.note: νόμους (_nomous_, l. 287): Polyneices came 'to scatter their land and laws'. Creon concedes in passing that the gods have _nomoi_ of their own. It is on precisely that ground that Antigone will stand, with laws unwritten and unfailing. He assumes the gods' laws and his own must coincide, and the ode's last stanza makes the same assumption at l. 367.

annotations.quote: Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke,
annotations.note: ὑπὸ ζυγῷ (_hypo zygōi_, 'under the yoke', l. 291) and λόφον (_lophon_, 'the neck', l. 292): his picture of a citizen is a draught animal that should keep its neck where it is put. The ode repeats both words at l. 351, where man's triumph is the yoke about the horse's neck. Either the Chorus are echoing their king or Sophocles is, and the echo makes the taming stanza sound like politics. Ask too how he can have 'long' noted this, πάλαι, on his first day. Perhaps he means the war, when he held command; perhaps suspicion supplies its own history.

annotations.quote: By bribes. Of evils current upon earth
annotations.note: Storr's 'current' is a hit. The Greek calls silver the worst _nomisma_ ever to grow among men (ll. 295–296), a word that means both 'coinage' and 'established custom' and shares its root with _nomos_. The noun for silver is ἄργυρος (_argyros_). The tirade that follows is stock moralising and good of its kind. Its fault is that it has no connection with the facts. Nobody has been paid, and he has a theory of the crime before he has a suspect.

annotations.quote: Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home;
annotations.note: Money πορθεῖ (_porthei_, 'sacks', l. 297) cities. An hour ago it was Polyneices who came to sack this one, for a throne. The enemy has changed from the invader to the coin without Creon remarking on it. For him every opponent turns out to be the same opponent, greed, and the list will grow to include his guards, his niece's accomplices, and a blind prophet.

annotations.quote: And breeds a habit of dishonesty.
annotations.note: Storr loses the religious word. Money teaches men to know δυσσέβειαν (_dyssebeian_, 'impiety', l. 301) in every act. Creon is the first to use it, and he uses it of men he imagines taking bribes to bury a corpse. Antigone speaks it last, on her way to the tomb in [[s9]]: by being pious she has earned the name of impiety. Between those two uses the play decides who was entitled to the word.

annotations.quote: Yea, as I still revere the dread of Zeus,
annotations.note: σέβας (_sebas_, 'reverence', l. 304), and he declares himself ὅρκιος, on oath. Literally: 'if Zeus still has reverence from me'. It is a strong form of oath, and the conditional is ugly in hindsight. He swears by Zeus to torture innocent men over a burial that Zeus's own laws, on Antigone's account, require.

annotations.quote: Who carried out this lawless burial,
annotations.note: 'Lawless' is Storr's; no such word is in the line. What is there is τὸν αὐτόχειρα τοῦδε τοῦ τάφου (_ton autocheira_, 'the one whose own hand did this burial', l. 306). _Autocheir_ is ordinarily the word for one who kills with his own hand, and Creon used it at l. 172 for the brothers' mutual slaughter. He reaches for the vocabulary of murder to describe covering a body. Antigone will accept the description; her whole claim is that her own hand did it.

annotations.quote: Death for your punishment shall not suffice.
annotations.note: 'Hades alone will not be enough for you' (l. 308). He treats Hades as an instrument within his gift, to be supplemented by torture when it is too mild. The ode answers within sixty lines: Hades is the single thing from which man contrives no escape (l. 360). He will use the same instrument on Antigone and find that it reaches his son and his wife.

annotations.quote: Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make
annotations.note: No cross in the Greek: ζῶντες κρεμαστοὶ (_zōntes kremastoi_, 'strung up alive', l. 309), until they reveal τήνδε ... ὕβριν (_hybrin_), 'this outrage'. It is the first _hybris_ in the play and it is Creon's name for a burial. He will use it twice of Antigone in [[s5]]. Mark what the test of l. 177 has produced within a hundred and fifty lines: a threat of torture against men he has no evidence against.

annotations.quote: There are some villainies that bring no gain.
annotations.note: τὸ κέρδος (l. 310) and τὸ κερδαίνειν (_to kerdainein_, 'profit-making', l. 312) inside three lines, with sarcasm: you will be tortured 'so that you may know where profit is to be got'. Add the hirelings and wages of ll. 294 and 302, the silver of l. 295 and l. 322, and κέρδη again at l. 326. That makes eight words for money in forty lines, about a deed done for nothing by someone who expects to die for it.

annotations.quote: The many come to ruin and disgrace.
annotations.note: ἀτωμένους (_atōmenous_, 'brought to ruin', l. 314) set against σεσωσμένους, 'saved': the same pair, _atē_ and safety, with which he defined his duty at ll. 185–186. He closes on a general maxim, as he usually does. It is true, and it is about him.

annotations.quote: Is it thy ears that suffer, or thy heart?
annotations.note: δάκνει (_daknei_, 'it bites', l. 317): 'in the ears, or in the soul, does it bite?' Something has changed in the Guard. Having heard an accusation he knows to be false, he is less afraid, and begins to examine the king like a doctor locating a pain. His answer two lines later is accurate and impertinent: the doer hurts your mind, I only hurt your ears. Creon's reply shows he cannot bear to be described.

annotations.quote: What an inveterate babbler! get thee gone!
annotations.note: λάλημα (_lalēma_, 'a piece of chatter', l. 320), a neuter noun, as if the man were a thing that makes noise. Watch Creon's habit: he does not answer what is said, he classifies the speaker. The elders are senile, the Guard is a chatterbox and a hireling, Ismene will be a viper, Haemon a woman's slave, Teiresias a profiteer. Each label saves him from weighing an argument.

annotations.quote: Twice guilty, having sold thy soul for gain.
annotations.note: τὴν ψυχὴν προδούς (_tēn psychēn prodous_, 'having betrayed your soul', l. 322), for silver. At l. 176 Creon said it is impossible to learn any man's ψυχήν, his soul, until he has been tested in office. He now reads a stranger's soul in four minutes and finds a bribe in it. The Guard's next line is the comment that this deserves.

annotations.quote: Alas! how sad when reasoners reason wrong.
annotations.note: ἦ δεινὸν (_ē deinon_, l. 323a): 'terrible indeed, when the one who judges judges falsely.' Storr's 'sad' is far too mild, and the word is the ode's word, spoken ten lines before the ode. The verb δοκεῖν (_dokein_) means to think or seem, and it is also the verb of resolutions, of what 'seems good' to a ruling body. So the line concerns a man whose opinions are decrees. The lowest person on stage tells the king the truth and the king hears only insolence. He is the first of several he outranks to do so.

annotations.quote: The wages of ill-gotten gains is death.
annotations.note: Storr has slipped St Paul into Sophocles. The Greek says only that τὰ δειλὰ κέρδη (_ta deila kerdē_, 'base gains', l. 326) 'produce pains', and death is not mentioned. It is a good example of how a 1912 verse translation gives a pagan king a Christian cadence. Creon leaves into the palace on this line, the fourth time in the scene he has ended a speech on profit.

annotations.quote: Shalt see me here returning; that is sure.
annotations.note: He is back within fifty lines, leading Antigone, and he opens [[s5]] by admitting that a man should swear to nothing. The joke has a point. In this play confident statements about the future are refuted quickly, the Guard's in fifty lines and Creon's by nightfall.

annotations.quote: And for my safety owe the gods much thanks.
annotations.note: σωθεὶς (_sōtheis_, 'saved', l. 331) and τοῖς θεοῖς: the scene began with the gods saving the city and ends with a soldier thanking them for saving his skin, ἐκτὸς ἐλπίδος, 'beyond hope'. His religion is simple and, as far as it goes, sound. Chance, he says at l. 328, will decide whether the man is caught: τύχη, where Creon sees a paid plot and the Chorus a god. With both actors gone the elders are alone, and what they have just heard, a deed with no visible doer, is what they sing about.

links.why: The Guard swears he will never come back and returns almost at once with the culprit.
Creon's reflex here, that opposition means bribery, is repeated word for word against the prophet.
The ship of state and the fear of disorder get their fullest and most damaging statement to Haemon.

s4.essay:
This is the most famous ode in Greek tragedy, and it is odd that it is here. The elders have just heard that someone has defied the king and left no trace, and what they sing is a hymn to human cleverness: man crosses the sea, wears down the earth with ploughs, snares birds, breaks horses, teaches himself speech and cities and shelter. Storr sets it in long rhymed lines that roll like a Victorian hymn, and it is easy to hear it as plain praise.

It is not plain praise. The Greek word behind 'wondrous' also means terrible, formidable, uncanny; the first line could as fairly run 'many things are fearsome, and nothing more fearsome than man.' Read it that way and the catalogue darkens. Everything in it is something being mastered, the eldest of the gods included. And the list ends on its one exception: 'for death he hath found no cure.' The play is about a corpse and is heading for a tomb, and the ode has just named the one power nobody on stage can legislate.

The last stanza turns to judgment. Cleverness goes either way; the man who keeps the laws stands high in his city, and the bold transgressor is 'cityless.' The elders mean whoever buried the body. I think the description fits Creon at least as well, and by [[s13]] he is the one with no city worth having. Then, as if to mock the song about man the tamer, the Guard walks in with a girl.

annotations.quote: Many wonders there be,
annotations.note: πολλὰ τὰ δεινὰ (_polla ta deina_, l. 333). _Deinos_ comes from the word for fear: terrible first, then awe-inspiring, then formidably clever, and never simply admirable. 'Wonders' keeps the sunny half. The Guard has used the word twice in the last hundred lines, both times for something frightening (ll. 243, 323a), so the audience hear the dark sense first. Aeschylus began an ode in the _Libation Bearers_ in almost the same way, about the many dread things earth breeds, and went on to human daring and passion as the worst of them. Sophocles' hearers knew that song.

annotations.quote: but naught more wondrous than man;
annotations.note: δεινότερον (_deinoteron_, l. 333) is a comparative: man does not stand outside the class of dreadful things, he tops it. The noun is ἀνθρώπου, the human being, not yet the male. Why do the elders sing this now? They have just heard of a deed done against a king's order by someone who left no trace. The ode is their response to that daring, which is the crux: is it a hymn to human progress, or a warning that the cleverest creature is the most dangerous? I think the first line already makes it the second, with the hymn carried inside it.

annotations.quote: Over the surging sea, with a whitening south wind wan,
annotations.note: The first art is seafaring, and it is reckless from the start: the sea is πολιοῦ (_poliou_, 'grey', l. 334) and the wind is χειμερίῳ νότῳ, the stormy south wind of winter, when sensible Greeks kept their ships ashore. Man is called τοῦτο, 'this thing', a neuter, as though the Chorus were pointing at a specimen. The ship comes first in the list, and we have just listened to a ruler who thinks of his city as one.

annotations.quote: Through the foam of the firth, man makes his perilous way;
annotations.note: περῶν (_perōn_, 'passing through', l. 336) picks up πέραν (_peran_, 'across', l. 334): man is the creature that crosses. Storr's 'perilous' is his own, though fair, since the swells are περιβρυχίοισιν, 'engulfing'. Keep the idea of passage in mind. The second strophe turns it into a single word, 'all-passing', and then names the one crossing from which nobody finds a way back.

annotations.quote: And the eldest of deities Earth that knows not toil nor decay
annotations.note: The Greek is θεῶν τε τὰν ὑπερτάταν, Γᾶν (l. 337), 'the highest of the gods, Earth', which is a claim of rank where Storr has one of age. She is ἄφθιτον, ἀκαμάταν, imperishable and unwearied. Even so she is man's object. And it is earth, a handful of it, that has just been scattered on Polyneices; the ode and the crime share a substance. One act does violence to her and the other gives the dead back to her.

annotations.quote: Ever he furrows and scores, as his team, year in year out,
annotations.note: ἀποτρύεται (_apotryetai_, 'he wears away', l. 338). The verb is harsh and it is set right against 'unwearied': he wears out the one who cannot be worn. A song of plain praise would not describe ploughing as attrition of the highest goddess. ἔτος εἰς ἔτος, 'year into year', makes it relentless.

annotations.quote: With breed of the yoked horse, the ploughshare turneth about.
annotations.note: ἱππείῳ γένει (_hippeiōi genei_, 'with the offspring of horses', l. 340) is usually taken to mean mules, the standard plough-animal, which are themselves a human contrivance. The yoke in Storr's line is imported from the next stanza, where it belongs. Note the pattern so far: sea and earth are both elements that are also gods, and both are treated as material.

annotations.quote: The light-witted birds of the air, the beasts of the weald and the wood
annotations.note: κουφονόων (_kouphonoōn_, 'light-minded', l. 343): the birds lose because they think lightly, and man wins by thought. The verb for what he does to them is ἄγει (_agei_, 'leads off', l. 343), the word for carrying away captives. When Antigone is brought in at the end of this section the guards ἄγουσι, 'are leading', her (l. 382), and in [[s5]] the Guard says they 'hunted' her and compares her cry to a bird's over an emptied nest. The elders sing of snaring creatures while the snare is closing on someone they know.

annotations.quote: He traps with his woven snare, and the brood of the briny flood.
annotations.note: σπείραισι δικτυοκλώστοις (_speiraisi diktyoklōstois_, 'coils of woven net', l. 346), a showpiece compound, the language itself knotted like the mesh. Air, land and sea each give up their creatures, so the conquest is total across the three realms. Hunting is the first human activity in the ode that is directed at other living things, and it is done by enclosure.

annotations.quote: Master of cunning he: the savage bull, and the hart
annotations.note: περιφραδὴς ἀνήρ (_periphradēs anēr_, 'man, thoughtful all round', l. 347). The noun has changed: the ode began with the human being and now says ἀνήρ, the male. The elders, like Creon, picture the burier as a man. Then κρατεῖ δὲ μηχαναῖς (_kratei de mēchanais_, l. 348), 'he masters by devices', and _kratos_ is the word Creon used twice for his own power at ll. 166 and 173. Storr's hart is not in the Greek, which has only 'the beast that roams the hills'.

annotations.quote: And the shaggy rough-maned steed is broken to bear the bit.
annotations.note: The Greek has no bit: the horse is tamed with ζυγῶν (_zygōn_, 'yoking') ἀμφὶ λόφον, 'about its neck' (l. 351), and the bull is ἀκμῆτα (_akmēta_, 'untired', l. 352), like the unwearied earth before it. Yoke and neck are the two words Creon used for his subjects at ll. 291–292. Storr's bit arrives all the same in [[s5]], where Creon says of Antigone that spirited horses are schooled with a small one. The stanza on taming animals is, word for word, the king's theory of government.

annotations.quote: Speech and the wind-swift speed of counsel
annotations.note: φθέγμα (_phthegma_, 'voice, speech', l. 354) and ἀνεμόεν φρόνημα (_anemoen phronēma_, 'thought like the wind'). There is _phronēma_ again, Creon's word for his own cast of mind at l. 207. Wind-swift is praise, but wind is also what changes direction and blows ships off course, and Creon's thinking in the last scene moved very fast indeed. Speech stands first among the inward arts, in a play where nearly every scene is a contest of speeches and no one is persuaded until too late.

annotations.quote: and civic wit,
annotations.note: Storr has tamed this. The Greek is ἀστυνόμους ὀργάς (_astynomous orgas_, ll. 354–356), 'the tempers that give law to towns'. _Orgē_ is disposition, passion, and commonly anger: it is the word Creon used at l. 280 when the Chorus's piety began to fill him with it. And _nomos_ sits inside the adjective. So the Chorus count among man's wonders the very thing we have just watched, a city-ruling temper, and the phrase can be heard with a shudder.

annotations.quote: He hath learnt for himself all these; and the arrowy rain to fly
annotations.note: ἐδιδάξατο (_edidaxato_, 'he taught himself', l. 356). No god gives any of this. In the _Prometheus Bound_ every art is the gift of Prometheus; here man is his own teacher, which is the account of progress associated with thinkers such as Protagoras. The absence of the gods as givers is the most striking thing about the list, and the last stanza supplies them only as a limit. The play's closing lines return to teaching: great blows teach good sense in old age.

annotations.quote: And the nipping airs that freeze, ’neath the open winter sky.
annotations.note: Housing, the last of the outward arts, is put negatively: he has learned φεύγειν (_pheugein_, 'to flee', l. 357) the shafts of frost and rain. It is the first of three words for flight within five lines, with φεῦξιν at l. 360 and φυγὰς at l. 361. Under the mastery, human skill turns out to be a set of escapes. The sentence is being built so that the one thing without an escape arrives with full weight.

annotations.quote: He hath provision for all:
