annotations.note: παντοπόρος· ἄπορος (_pantoporos; aporos_, l. 358): 'all-resourceful; resourceless', set side by side with only a pause between. The usual construal joins the second to what follows: 'without resource he meets nothing that is to come'. But the ear takes the two words together first, and the jolt is meant. The same device closes the ode with ὑψίπολις· ἄπολις. _Poros_ is a way through, so the crosser of seas from the first stanza has become the one who finds a passage everywhere.

annotations.quote: fell plague he hath learnt to endure;
annotations.note: Storr has reversed the order and weakened the verb. In the Greek death comes first and medicine after, as a concession: 'yet from baffling diseases he has contrived escapes', ξυμπέφρασται (l. 361). He does not endure them, he thinks his way out. The diseases are ἀμηχάνων (_amēchanōn_, 'without remedy'), the word Creon used at l. 175 for the impossibility of knowing a man's soul. Even what has no device, man has found a device for, with the one exception.

annotations.quote: yet for death he hath found no cure.
annotations.note: Ἅιδα μόνον φεῦξιν οὐκ ἐπάξεται (_Haida monon pheuxin ouk epaxetai_, l. 360): 'from Hades alone he will procure no escape.' This is the hinge of the ode, and the one thing man has not mastered is named as a god, Hades, where Storr has 'death'. The verb is future: he never will. Creon said at l. 308 that 'Hades alone' would not suffice as a punishment and is about to use death as an instrument of policy twice. He learns that it does not stay where it is put. The dead man lying on the plain belongs to the one power the arts cannot reach, and that is what the edict ignores.

annotations.quote: Passing the wildest flight thought are the cunning and skill,
annotations.note: Here is the summary of the list: σοφόν τι τὸ μηχανόεν τέχνας (_sophon ti to mēchanoen technas_, l. 365), 'a clever thing, the inventiveness of art', possessed _hyper elpida_, beyond expectation. Count the _technai_: sailing, ploughing, fowling, hunting, fishing, taming, speech, thought, civic order, building, medicine. Now ask what is missing. Reverence and justice are not among them. In the myth Plato gives Protagoras, those have to be sent separately by Zeus because the arts alone leave men destroying one another. The last stanza is about that gap.

annotations.quote: That guide man now to the light, but now to counsels of ill.
annotations.note: Storr puts the good first; the Greek puts the bad: τοτὲ μὲν κακόν, 'now to evil', then to good (l. 366). And the verb is ἕρπει (_herpei_, 'he creeps, he moves along'), a slow word after so much crossing and outrunning. Skill has no direction of its own. This sentence is the plainest evidence that the ode is not a hymn, since four stanzas of achievement end in a coin-toss.

annotations.quote: If he honors the laws of the land,
annotations.note: νόμους ... χθονὸς (_nomous chthonos_, l. 367). The participle in this text, γεραίρων (_gerairōn_, 'honouring'), is an editor's correction; the manuscripts have a word meaning 'weaving in', which some keep. χθονός is 'of the land', and that is what the elders mean: the law of Thebes, which today is Creon's edict. But _chthōn_ is also the earth and what lies beneath it, and the gods below are the chthonic ones. The phrase can mean the laws Antigone obeys, though the singers do not know it.

annotations.quote: and reveres the Gods of the State
annotations.note: A mistranslation that takes Creon's side. The Greek is θεῶν τʼ ἔνορκον δίκαν, 'and the justice of the gods, sworn by oath' (l. 367). The word is δίκαν (_dikan_, 'justice'), and there is no State in it. The Chorus name two things, the laws of the land and the gods' justice, and assume they are one, so that honouring both is a single act. The whole play happens in the space between them. In [[s5]] Antigone will appeal to the Justice who dwells with the gods below, against the law of the land.

annotations.quote: Proudly his city shall stand;
annotations.note: ὑψίπολις (_hypsipolis_, l. 370), one word, and ambiguous: 'high in his city' or 'having a high city'. Storr chooses the second. I prefer the first, because the next word is about a person. Creon believes this stanza describes him, since by his _nomoi_ he makes the city great (l. 191). The Chorus probably believe it too, at this point.

annotations.quote: but a cityless outcast I rate
annotations.note: ἄπολις (_apolis_, l. 370), set directly against ὑψίπολις with only a stop between, like 'all-resourceful; resourceless' above. Whom does it condemn? In the singers' minds, the unknown burier who defied the edict. In the event it fits two people. Antigone becomes literally cityless, at home among neither the living nor the dead, as she says in [[s9]]. Creon, who dishonoured the gods' justice while enforcing the law of the land, ends [[s13]] asking to be led away, a man who is nothing. The elders think they are describing a criminal and have described the alternatives open to their king.

annotations.quote: Whoso bold in his pride from the path of right doth depart;
annotations.note: Two phrases matter. τὸ μὴ καλὸν (_to mē kalon_, 'what is not fine', l. 370): in [[s1]] Antigone used exactly that adjective for dying in this act. And τόλμας χάριν (_tolmas charin_, 'for daring's sake', l. 371), which answers Creon's 'who dared?' at l. 248. So the vocabulary points at the burier. The question the play puts is which of the two, the girl with the dust or the king with the edict, was keeping company with what is not _kalon_.

annotations.quote: Ne’er may I sit by his side, or share the thoughts of his heart.
annotations.note: παρέστιος (_parestios_, 'at my hearth', l. 371) and ἴσον φρονῶν (_ison phronōn_, 'thinking the same', l. 375), with _phronein_ once more. This is a formula of excommunication: the offender is to be kept from the household fire as one keeps away a polluted man. The irony needs no forcing. These elders will share Creon's counsels for another seven hundred lines, and the pollution, when it comes, comes from his act.

annotations.quote: What strange vision meets my eyes,
annotations.note: The metre changes to marching anapaests as the Guard leads Antigone in. Their words are δαιμόνιον τέρας (_daimonion teras_, 'a portent from the gods', l. 376), and ἀμφινοῶ, 'I am of two minds'. A _teras_ is a prodigy, one more _deinon_, and they have no idea how apt the adjective is. The staging is the comment on the ode: four stanzas on what 'man' dares, and the answer that walks in is a girl.

annotations.quote: Hapless child of hapless sire,
annotations.note: δυστήνου πατρὸς Οἰδιπόδα (l. 380): they identify her through her father before she has said a word in their presence, as they will again at l. 471 once she has spoken, and as [[s6|the next ode]] will at length. For the elders the explanation of Antigone is heredity. It is kinder than Creon's explanation, money, and it is equally a way of not listening to what she is about to say.

annotations.quote: Madly brave the King’s decree?
annotations.note: Three words in the Greek settle the Chorus's position for now. She is ἀπιστοῦσαν (_apistousan_, 'disobeying', l. 381), Creon's participle from l. 219. What she disobeys is τοῖς βασιλείοισιν ... νόμοις (l. 382), 'the royal laws', so the proclamation has become _nomoi_, fifteen lines after 'the laws of the land'. And she was taken ἐν ἀφροσύνῃ (_en aphrosynēi_, 'in folly', l. 383), the absence of _phronein_. They have judged before the hearing. Yet they call her 'child' twice and sound appalled, and that divided response is the one they keep until the end.

links.why: The man who ends 'a cipher, less than nothing' is the cityless figure this ode imagines, and it is not the one the elders meant.
The next ode drops this confidence in human skill entirely and sings of a family that nothing can save.

s5.essay:
The Guard is back, 'forsworn' and cheerful, and before the great argument begins he gives the best piece of description in the play. They brushed the dust off the body and sat upwind of the smell. At noon a whirlwind blotted out the sky, and when it cleared the girl was standing there, crying 'as when the mother bird beholds her nest / Robbed of its nestlings.' She then poured the offering three times and did not run. The Guard is 'glad—and grieved,' and concludes that a man's first duty is to himself. It is exactly the principle Antigone lacks, stated by a decent man with no shame about it.

Then Creon asks whether she knew the law, and she says 'I knew, all knew,' and makes the speech the play is remembered for. Look closely at what it claims. She does not say that conscience outranks the State, or that she may break any law she dislikes. She says something narrower: that the care of the dead belongs to the gods below, that their rules 'were not born today nor yesterday,' and that a mortal cannot 'by a breath annul' them. It is a claim about jurisdiction. Creon governs the living city. The corpse has passed out of it.

Creon's side deserves a fair hearing, and the stichomythia, the rapid line-for-line exchange, gives it one. Eteocles died defending the walls his brother came to burn. 'Why cast a slur on one by honoring one?' is a real question. If the defender and the attacker receive the same rites, what has the city said about the difference between them? Athens itself refused traitors burial in home soil. And Creon is doing the thing we normally ask of a magistrate: he will not make an exception because the offender is his sister's child. On the day after a civil war, a ruler who let his own household flout the first order of his reign would be inviting the next war.

The usual grand reading, Hegel's, is that this is right against right, family against State, each justified and each one-sided. I think that is half true, and I do not land in the middle. Both are defending something real. But Antigone answers his best question with a line he cannot touch: 'Who knows if this world’s crimes are virtues there?' She is saying that the city's categories of patriot and outlaw may not apply where her brother now is, and that Creon is legislating in a country he has never seen. And listen to what happens to his reasons as he loses. He begins with the law and ends with 'I am woman, she the man' and 'No woman shall be the master while I live.' What started as the city's safety has become his own standing. The gods of this play side with her before it is over. So do I, on the deed. Refusing a traitor a hero's funeral was within a ruler's gift. Keeping the body above ground as a spectacle, and killing whoever covers it, reaches past the city into ground no king holds. And an order that the lawgiver's own niece, son and prophet must each in turn break or protest is, at the least, a badly made law.

On the person I am less sure, and the Ismene scene is why. Ismene comes out and lies to share her sister's death: 'I did the deed, if she will have it so.' It is the bravest thing she does, and Antigone refuses it flat. 'A friend in word is never friend of mine.' The woman who has just said her nature is for love and not hate cannot find any for the sister standing in front of her. Some of it may be rescue; 'save thyself; I grudge not thy escape' can be heard as protection. Some of it is plain pride of ownership in the deed. 'Thou livest, I died long ago' is the coldest line in the scene, and it is true.

One more thing surfaces only now, and from Ismene: Antigone is engaged to Creon's son. She has not thought it worth mentioning.

annotations.quote: Here is the culprit taken in the act
annotations.note: Before this line the Chorus have chanted eight lines of marching anapaests as she is led in (ll. 376–383, printed at the end of [[s4]]). They call the sight a δαιμόνιον τέρας (_daimonion teras_, "a portent sent by a god", l. 376), which is how the ode on man looks when its abstract law-breaker turns out to be a girl they know. Their first guess at a motive is ἀφροσύνῃ (_aphrosynei_, "want of sense", l. 383), and they speak of the king's νόμοις (_nomois_, "laws", l. 382): two words she is about to take away from them. Storr's "culprit" is his own; the Guard says only "this is she, the one who did the deed" (l. 384).

annotations.quote: Of giving burial. But where’s the King?
annotations.note: The Greek is _tende heilomen thaptousan_ ("we caught her burying", l. 385). The verb is plain "burying", with no "attempting" about it, and the Guard repeats it at ll. 402 and 404. Creon's men never doubt that a handful of dust counts as burial. That matters for everything Creon says later about the body being unburied.

annotations.quote: There from the palace he returns in time.
annotations.note: The Greek is _eis deon_ ("just when needed", l. 386). Creon enters on cue here and answers with the word for coincidence, _tychei_ (l. 387). Keep the punctual entrance in mind: in the last third of the play his whole catastrophe is a matter of arriving minutes late.

annotations.quote: No man, my lord, should make a vow, for if
annotations.note: Like his first entrance in [[s3]], the Guard starts with a proverb before he gets to the news. Here it is that mortals should call nothing _apomoton_ ("sworn off, out of the question", l. 388). It is comic, but it is also the play's subject seen from below: here is a man for whom nothing is fixed, a few lines before a woman for whom one thing is.

annotations.quote: His afterthoughts belie his first resolve.
annotations.note: Literally "second thought makes a liar of judgement", with _gnomen_ (l. 389) for the judgement. The Guard means his own oath never to come back. But this is a fair summary of what happens to Creon, whose second thought arrives after Tiresias has left and is correct and useless.

annotations.quote: When from the hail-storm of thy threats I fled
annotations.note: The Greek is _echeimasthen_ ("I was storm-tossed", l. 391). In his first speech Creon was the helmsman keeping the ship of state upright. To the man actually on deck he is the weather. The storm word also prepares the real storm in the Guard's narrative.

annotations.quote: But the wild rapture of a glad surprise
annotations.note: The Greek is cooler than Storr: joy that comes _par' elpidas_ ("beyond one's hopes", l. 392) is bigger than any other pleasure. Nobody is "intoxicated". Note what the joy is about: another person's capture. The Guard is likeable and I think Sophocles means him to be, and this is still what he is pleased by.

annotations.quote: Decking the grave. No lottery this time;
annotations.note: The participle _kosmousa_ ("putting in order, adorning", l. 396) is the proper word for dressing the dead, and the Guard gives it to her without irony, along with the word "grave" for what is a body under dust. The lottery is the one in [[s3]], where the watch drew lots for who should carry bad news. This time he volunteered.

annotations.quote: This prize is mine by right of treasure-trove.
annotations.note: θοὔρμαιον (_to hermaion_, l. 397) is a windfall, a lucky find, the sort of thing Hermes drops in your path. Creon accused this man of working for pay. Here is the only profit he makes in the play, and it is her.

annotations.quote: So take her, judge her, rack her, if thou wilt.
annotations.note: Storr's "rack" brings in the torture chamber. The Greek pair is forensic: _krine_ ("judge", l. 399) and a verb meaning to question and refute. The Guard expects a hearing. He is right that there will be one and wrong about who will be examined in it.

annotations.quote: Hence to depart well quit of all these ills.
annotations.note: The word Storr spreads into "well quit" is _eleutheros_ ("free", l. 399), and Creon grants it in the same word at l. 445. Watch the free/slave vocabulary from here: Creon calls Antigone a slave at l. 479 and she answers with the same word at l. 517. The only person who leaves this scene free is the one who looked after himself.

annotations.quote: Burying the man. There’s nothing more to tell.
annotations.note: αὕτη τὸν ἄνδρʼ ἔθαπτε (_haute ton andr' ethapte_, l. 402): "this woman was burying the man". Four words, a feminine pronoun at one end and the male noun in the middle. In [[s3]] Creon asked "what man dared this?" and built a theory of bribed male conspirators. The grammar corrects him before anyone argues with him.

annotations.quote: Hast thou thy wits? Or know’st thou what thou say’st?
annotations.note: Creon cannot take it in, and the question shows why his earlier certainty was worthless. He had a complete account of the crime, with motive and paymasters, and none of it was true. He will do the same with Ismene in a hundred lines.

annotations.quote: Driven from thy presence by those awful threats,
annotations.note: τὰ δείνʼ ἐκεῖνʼ (_ta dein' ekein'_, "those terrible things", l. 408). This is the adjective of the ode just sung, where many things are _deina_ and nothing more so than man. The Guard uses it of Creon's threats without a thought. The word has gone from the cosmic to the petty in thirty lines.

annotations.quote: Than straight we swept away all trace of dust,
annotations.note: Here is the crux of the two burials. The first dusting was complete enough to alarm Creon, so why does she return? Some have argued the first was not hers at all (the Chorus in [[s3]] wondered about the gods; a few critics have proposed Ismene). I take the plain reading. She could not have known the guards would undo it, she comes back with a jug for the libations the first report never mentioned, and she finds the body stripped. Sophocles also simply needs her caught, and caught in the act.

annotations.quote: And bared the clammy body. Then we sat
annotations.note: "Clammy" is polite. _mydon_ (l. 410) means oozing, wet with decay, and the next line has the men sitting where the _osmen_ ("smell", l. 412) cannot reach them. The Guard is the one character who has stood near what Creon's decree actually is. When Tiresias later describes altars fouled with carrion, this is the body he means.

annotations.quote: So all night long we watched, until the sun
annotations.note: There is no night in the Greek, only "this went on until the sun's bright disc stood in mid-sky" (ll. 415–416). The prologue was before dawn, the first burial was found by the first day-watch, and it is now noon of the same day. Storr's extra night hides how fast the play moves: edict, crime, arrest and sentence inside a morning. Midday is also the hour at which, in Greek stories, gods tend to show themselves.

annotations.quote: Smote us. A sudden whirlwind then upraised
annotations.note: A _typhos_, a whirlwind (l. 418), lifts from the ground a column of dust that the Guard calls "a trouble in the sky". It fills the plain and tears the leaves from the trees. A dust-storm, in a play where dust on a corpse is the whole issue, is either weather or help. Sophocles gives no ruling.

annotations.quote: And waited till the heaven-sent plague should pass.
annotations.note: The Greek is _theian noson_ ("a divine sickness", l. 421). The Guard is not a theologian and may just mean "terrible", but the word is there, and the Chorus's earlier suspicion that the gods had a hand in the first burial has never been answered. Notice also _mysantes_ ("with our eyes shut"). The watchmen are not watching at the one moment that matters, and when they open their eyes she is there.

annotations.quote: At last it ceased, and lo! there stood this maid.
annotations.note: The Greek is _he pais horatai_ ("the child is seen", l. 423), a present passive, as if she had been produced by the storm. _Pais_ is "child" or "girl". The Chorus used it at l. 378, the Guard uses it here, and Creon will use it too. The men of the play keep her small in their nouns while she is doing the largest thing in it.

annotations.quote: A piercing cry she uttered, sad and shrill,
annotations.note: The verb is the one for the women's funeral shriek, and the sound is that of a _pikras ornithos_ ("a bitter bird", l. 423–424). Birds have been against Polynices so far. He came on Thebes as a screaming eagle in the entry song, and the edict leaves him for birds to eat. Now a bird is mourning him.

annotations.quote: As when the mother bird beholds her nest
annotations.note: The only tender image anyone gives her, and it comes from the man arresting her. It makes her a mother at the moment she gives up any chance of being one. The Greek presses this harder than Storr: the nest is called both εὐνῆς (_eunes_) and λέχος (_lechos_, l. 425), and both are ordinary words for the marriage bed, the second returning at l. 573 for her own marriage. Behind it is the Odyssey, where Odysseus and Telemachus weep more shrilly than birds whose young have been taken.

annotations.quote: Robbed of its nestlings; even so the maid
annotations.note: Storr's "robbed" stands for ὀρφανὸν (_orphanon_, "orphaned", l. 425). The simile says the bed is orphaned of its young, a strange use that lets the word for the bereaved child fall on a bereaved parent. Antigone is the orphan here. The image has her as mother, child and bride in two lines, which is the confusion of roles she inherits from her family.

annotations.quote: And cursed the ruffians who had done this deed.
annotations.note: The Greek phrase for the ruffians is "those who had done the deed" (l. 428), and it is word for word what the Guard called her at l. 384. Burial and unburial are the same "deed" in his mouth. And she curses, as her father did. The curse is aimed at the guards and lands on the man who gave the order.

annotations.quote: Anon she gathered handfuls of dry dust,
annotations.note: She gathers _dipsian konin_ ("thirsty dust", l. 429), carried in her bare hands. In the prologue she spoke of heaping up a tomb. What one person can do is this. It is enough ritually, and the smallness of the act against the size of the penalty is something the play wants you to feel.

annotations.quote: Thrice on the dead she poured a lustral stream.
annotations.note: Not lustral water. χοαῖσι τρισπόνδοισι (_choaisi trispondoisi_, l. 431) are the three drink-offerings poured to the dead, and the verb is στέφει (_stephei_, "she crowns"). She brought a bronze jug with her, so this visit was planned. Storr's "lustral" makes it a cleansing. The Greek makes it a gift, and a coronation of a body the city has declared rubbish.

annotations.quote: Our quarry. Undismayed she stood, and when
annotations.note: The Greek is _therometh'_ ("we hunted her down", l. 433). The ode on man praised him for netting the light-minded birds, and she has just been a bird. The praise of human skill and the arrest of Antigone use the same picture. She is "not at all frightened", which is the first thing we learn of her manner since the prologue.

annotations.quote: And yet to bring disaster to a friend
annotations.note: The Greek is _tous philous_ (l. 438). The Guard, a servant of the house, counts the princess among his _philoi_, his own people. So the great word of the scene is first used here, casually, by someone who then weighs it against his skin and finds it lighter. He feels both pleasure and pain and says so. Antigone does the same sum of pains at ll. 465–468 and gets the opposite answer.

annotations.quote: A man’s first duty is to serve himself.
annotations.note: Storr makes a maxim of it. The Guard is more personal: all this πέφυκε (_pephyke_, "is by nature", l. 440) less to me than my own σωτηρίας, safety. Hold on to the verb. At l. 523 Antigone uses the same one of herself: my nature is to join in love. Set the two natures side by side and the distance between an ordinary decent person and her is measured exactly.

annotations.quote: Speak, girl, with head bent low and downcast eyes,
annotations.note: This is a description in the Greek, and Storr has turned it into an order: "You there, you with your head bowed to the ground" (l. 441). She has stood silent and looking down through forty lines of the Guard's story. In a masked theatre posture is the face. I do not read it as shame, since nothing she goes on to say is ashamed. She is looking at the earth, where her business is.

annotations.quote: Guilty. I did it, I deny it not.
annotations.note: There is no "Guilty" in the Greek. She says "I say I did it and I do not deny it" (l. 443), affirming the act in Creon's own two verbs and pleading nothing. With that she takes the question of fact off the table. Only the question of right is left, and that is the ground she wants.

annotations.quote: Now answer this plain question, yes or no,
annotations.note: "Not at length, but briefly" (l. 446). She gives him one word, _eide_ ("I knew"), and then, when he asks the next question, twenty-one lines. Creon calls his edict here "what was proclaimed" (l. 447). It is still a proclamation. Watch what he calls it two lines later.

annotations.quote: I knew, all knew; how should I fail to know?
annotations.note: It was _emphane_ ("public, out in the open", l. 448). Is Creon offering his niece a way out through ignorance? I think he may be. If so she shuts it at once, as she told Ismene in [[s1]] she would: she wanted the deed proclaimed.

annotations.quote: And yet wert bold enough to break the law?
annotations.note: τούσδʼ ὑπερβαίνειν νόμους (_tousd' hyperbainein nomous_, "to overstep these laws", l. 449). The proclamation of two lines ago has become _nomoi_. And ἐτόλμας, "you dared", is the last ode's word for the daring that makes a man cityless. Creon thinks he is quoting the Chorus's verdict. Her whole reply is an attack on that one noun.

annotations.quote: Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus,
annotations.note: Storr gives away what she refuses to concede. She does not say "laws". She says: it was not Zeus who was ὁ κηρύξας (_ho keryxas_, "the one who proclaimed", l. 450) these things to me. She keeps Creon's edict in the herald's vocabulary where it started. A proclamation needs a proclaimer with standing, and the first thing she asks is who issued this one.

annotations.quote: And she who sits enthroned with gods below,
annotations.note: Δίκη (_Dike_, Justice) is ξύνοικος (_xynoikos_, "sharing a house", l. 451) with the gods below. That is unusual. In Hesiod, and elsewhere in Sophocles, Justice sits beside Zeus. Antigone names Zeus for the upper world and then moves Justice downstairs to live with the dead. Her justice is the claim the dead have on the living, and she is not offering a general theory of right.

annotations.quote: Justice, enacted not these human laws.
annotations.note: The verb ὥρισεν (_horisen_, l. 452) is from the word for a boundary stone: Justice "marked out" no such laws among men. This is the one place she lets _nomoi_ near Creon's edict, and it is inside a negation. The manuscripts read the line differently, making it the gods who did mark out "these laws", meaning burial. On either text the point holds: the boundary was set by someone else, before Creon.

annotations.quote: Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man,
annotations.note: τὰ σὰ κηρύγμαθʼ (_ta sa kerygmath'_, "your proclamations", l. 453–454), set against the _nomima_ of the gods in the next line. That contrast of nouns is the argument. θνητὸν ὄνθʼ (_thneton onth'_, "being mortal", l. 455) is left loose in the Greek and can mean "you, a mortal" or "anyone who is mortal". Storr chooses the insult. The looser sense is better: no mortal can do this, herself included.

annotations.quote: Could’st by a breath annul and override
annotations.note: "By a breath" is Storr's ornament. The verb is ὑπερδραμεῖν (_hyperdramein_, "to outrun", l. 455), and it answers Creon's ὑπερβαίνειν at l. 449. You say I stepped over your laws. You tried to run past the gods'. She returns his charge of transgression to him in a stronger form of his own verb.

annotations.quote: The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.
annotations.note: ἄγραπτα κἀσφαλῆ θεῶν νόμιμα (_agrapta kasphale theon nomima_, l. 454–455). Not _nomoi_ but νόμιμα, "usages, things held lawful", the word for observances. And _asphale_ is "unfailing, not to be tripped up", which is firmer and more physical than "immutable". This phrase made the play a founding text for every later argument about higher law, so notice how specific she is: these are the rites owed to the dead. She claims no general licence for conscience. An Athenian audience was proud of written law, and Pericles in Thucydides also speaks of unwritten laws whose breach brings agreed disgrace.

annotations.quote: They were not born today nor yesterday;
annotations.note: The edict is a few hours old. She heard of it before dawn in the prologue as something just announced. Against that she sets _aei pote_ ("always, at all times", l. 456). The contrast is of age, and in Greek thinking about custom age is authority.

annotations.quote: They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang.
annotations.note: The Greek is positive: ζῇ ταῦτα (_zei tauta_, "these things live", l. 457). And κοὐδεὶς οἶδεν, "no one knows", from when they appeared. She claims no revelation and names no lawgiver. That is a strength, since she cannot be asked for her source, and a limit, since she cannot produce one. The same "who knows?" comes back at l. 521 as her last argument.

annotations.quote: I was not like, who feared no mortal’s frown,
annotations.note: ἀνδρὸς οὐδενὸς φρόνημα δείσασʼ (_andros oudenos phronema deisas'_, "fearing no man's will", l. 458–459). The word is ἀνδρὸς, a male's, so gender enters the scene from her side first. And φρόνημα is the ode's word for the wind-swift thought man taught himself, here meaning mere temper. Creon picks the word up at l. 473 and throws it back.

annotations.quote: The wrath of Heaven. I knew that I must die,
annotations.note: What she says is "to pay the penalty among the gods" (ll. 459–460). So her first stated motive is not love. It is fear of a higher court, and she has compared two penalties and chosen the lighter. A tutor would ask whether that makes her prudent rather than heroic. I think it shows she reasons more coldly than her admirers allow.

annotations.quote: Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain.
annotations.note: The Greek is _kerdos_ ("profit", l. 462). In [[s3]] this was Creon's word for what corrupts men: money, bribes, the hope of gain that has destroyed many. He assumes everyone has a price. She now names hers, and it is an early death. The word does not fit his meaning any more.

annotations.quote: For death is gain to him whose life, like mine,
annotations.note: _Kerdos_ again (l. 464), now as a general rule for anyone who lives among many evils. This is the voice of the play's first lines, where she counted over the family's sufferings. It weakens her case a little: if death is a profit, what is she giving up? She answers that herself in the Kommos ([[s9]]), where the losses are finally counted and this armour comes off.

annotations.quote: To leave my mother’s son unburied there,
annotations.note: τὸν ἐξ ἐμῆς μητρὸς (_ton ex emes metros_, "the one from my own mother", l. 466–467). Kinship for her is measured through the womb, as it will be again at l. 511. With it comes ἄθαπτον (_athapton_, "unburied"), the condition the whole play is about. She does not say "a human being" or "a Theban". Remember this when the speech is read as a charter of universal rights.

annotations.quote: Methinks the judge of folly’s not acquit.
annotations.note: The word "fool" comes three times in two lines: μῶρα, μώρῳ, μωρίαν (ll. 469–470), ending on ὀφλισκάνω (_ophliskano_), a law-court verb for losing a suit. "I am convicted of folly in a fool's court." After twenty lines on Zeus and Justice she closes with an insult. It is magnificent and it is also the moment she makes it impossible for Creon to give way without being seen to lose.

annotations.quote: A stubborn daughter of a stubborn sire,
annotations.note: Storr's "stubborn" tames ὠμὸν ἐξ ὠμοῦ πατρὸς (_omon ex omou patros_, l. 471). _Omos_ is "raw", the word for uncooked meat and for savagery. The elders hear the unwritten laws and their comment is on her breeding, her γέννημʼ (_gennema_). Filing her under Oedipus spares them an opinion on her argument.

annotations.quote: This ill-starred maiden kicks against the pricks.
annotations.note: Storr borrows from the King James Bible, where an ox kicks the goad and hurts only itself. The Greek has no ox: "she does not know how to εἴκειν (_eikein_, "yield") to troubles" (l. 472). That verb belongs to the whole play. Haemon in [[s7]] tells his father about trees that bend in the flood and live, and in the end it is Creon who has to yield. Here the Chorus fasten on her the fault that will turn out to be his.

annotations.quote: Well, let her know the stubbornest of wills
annotations.note: He says _skler' agan phronemata_ ("over-hard spirits", l. 473), taking her word from l. 459, and he says it to the Chorus. He will not address her directly for another twenty lines. The iron that shatters and the horse broken with a small bit are both from the ode's list of human mastery. Every image fits Creon better than her, and his son will tell him so with trees and ships.

annotations.quote: Who in subjection lives must needs be meek.
annotations.note: "In subjection" softens δοῦλός (_doulos_, "slave", l. 479): there is no room to think big for one who is the slave of those around him. He is speaking of his sister's daughter, a king's child. This is how Creon sees rule: one master and a household of slaves. She gives him the word back at l. 517.

annotations.quote: First overstepped the established law, and then—
annotations.note: νόμους ὑπερβαίνουσα τοὺς προκειμένους (_nomous hyperbainousa tous prokeimenous_, "overstepping the laws laid down", l. 481). He repeats his own phrase from l. 449 as if she had not spoken. This is the thing to notice about the central scene: Creon never answers her on Zeus or Justice, here or later. He charges her with ὕβρις (_hybris_, l. 482) twice over, which in Athenian usage is outrage that shames its victim. He is the one who feels shamed.

annotations.quote: She boasts and glories in her wickedness.
annotations.note: The second outrage is γελᾶν (_gelan_, "to laugh", l. 483). Being laughed at is what a Sophoclean hero cannot stand. It drives Ajax to kill himself. Antigone has not laughed. Creon hears laughter because he is afraid of it, and at l. 551 she will use the verb herself, of Ismene, with pain.

annotations.quote: Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
annotations.note: There is no "woman" in the line. He says ἐγὼ μὲν οὐκ ἀνήρ, αὕτη δʼ ἀνήρ (_ego men ouk aner, haute d' aner_, l. 484): then I am no man, and she is the man, if this κράτη (_krate_, "mastery", l. 485) rests with her unpunished. This is the first time Creon says what is at stake for him. It was not in his opening speech about the ship of state. From here he says it in nearly every scene.

annotations.quote: But though she be my sister’s child or nearer
annotations.note: ὁμαιμονεστέρα (_homaimonestera_, "closer in blood", l. 486) than all of Ζηνὸς ἑρκείου, Zeus of the Courtyard, the god at the household altar who stands for the family itself. Storr's "all who worship at my hearth" loses the god. Creon names the divine guardian of kinship in order to say that kinship will count for nothing. And he condemns Ismene in the same breath on no evidence at all.

annotations.quote: Within the palace, frenzied and distraught.
annotations.note: He calls her _lyssosan_ ("raving", l. 492), and not in possession of her wits. He saw a girl beside herself and concluded guilt. It is his habit: bribery behind the first burial, conspiracy behind this one. Ismene was distraught because she knew what her sister had gone to do.

annotations.quote: When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.
annotations.note: καλλύνειν (_kallynein_, "to make beautiful", l. 496). Creon cannot know it, but he has hit her exact word. In [[s1]] she told Ismene it would be _kalon_, beautiful, to die doing this. He begins the sentence with μισῶ (_miso_, "I hate", l. 495). Count the verbs of hating in his part of this scene and then read l. 523 again.

annotations.quote: Would’st thou do more than slay thy prisoner?
annotations.note: Her first words since the insult, and they ask for the sentence. _helon_ ("having caught", l. 497) keeps the Guard's hunting language. The dry answer to her question is yes. He will think of something beyond killing her, a walled cave with a ration of food. And he has already done more than kill her brother.

annotations.quote: Not I, thy life is mine, and that’s enough.
annotations.note: The Greek is _tout' echon hapant' echo_ ("having this I have everything", l. 498). Storr gives the sense but not the boast. It is the sentence of a man who thinks killing her settles things. By the end of the day he has that and nothing else.

annotations.quote: A name so glorious as by burying
annotations.note: The Greek is _kleos eukleesteron_ (l. 502), literally "a more glorious glory". _Kleos_ is what Homeric warriors die for. So there is a third motive beside fear of the gods and love of kin: she wants fame, and says so. I do not think that discredits her. It does mean the Hegelian picture of her as pure family piety leaves out how much of the male heroic code she has taken over.

annotations.quote: A brother? so my townsmen all would say,
annotations.note: The brother is τὸν αὐτάδελφον (_ton autadelphon_, "my very own brother", l. 503), the word of the play's first line, where it was Ismene. And "townsmen" is too wide. She says τούτοις πᾶσιν (_toutois pasin_, "all these men here", l. 504) and means the fifteen elders standing in the orchestra. She appeals to them directly, to their faces. They do not answer.

annotations.quote: A king’s prerogatives, and not the least
annotations.note: Storr's "king" is _he tyrannis_ (l. 506). The word can be neutral in tragedy, but she defines it as the power to do and say what it likes, which is the Athenian democrat's definition of tyranny: rule that answers to no one. And she says it "is blessed", in a word the next ode opens with in earnest (l. 583).

annotations.quote: These think as I, but bate their breath to thee.
annotations.note: ὑπίλλουσιν στόμα (_hypillousin stoma_, l. 509): they curl their mouths under, as a dog tucks its tail. Creon has just said she alone of the Thebans sees it this way. Who is right about the city? Haemon will report in [[s7]] that the town mourns her in whispers. The proof on stage now is the Chorus's silence under a direct appeal.

annotations.quote: To reverence kith and kin can bring no shame.
annotations.note: "Kith and kin" is far too mild for τοὺς ὁμοσπλάγχνους (_tous homosplanchnous_, l. 511): those of the same _splanchna_, the same womb, the same inward parts. The verb is σέβειν (_sebein_, "to revere"), the root of the play's word for piety. She puts religious reverence and bodily kinship in one phrase. For her they are one thing.

annotations.quote: One mother bare them and the self-same sire.
annotations.note: Creon has made his best point: Eteocles was _homaimos_ ("of the same blood", l. 512) too. She grants it in full and adds "from one mother and the same father" (l. 513). In this family the phrase is loaded, since the same father is also their mother's son. She does not flinch from it. Sameness of blood is her whole argument.

annotations.quote: Why cast a slur on one by honoring one?
annotations.note: Creon now takes the piety words for his side. Her favour to Polynices is _dyssebe_ ("impious", l. 514) in Eteocles' eyes, and at l. 516 Polynices is simply "the impious one". So both of them claim _eusebeia_, and the play will not say who holds it until Tiresias does. Creon's premise is that honour is a fixed sum, so that giving some to one brother takes it from the other. She replies that the dead man will not testify to that, which she cannot know.

annotations.quote: The slain man was no villain but a brother.
annotations.note: οὐ γάρ τι δοῦλος, ἀλλʼ ἀδελφὸς ὤλετο (_ou gar ti doulos, all' adelphos oleto_, l. 517): it was no slave who died, but a brother. I suspect Storr's "villain" keeps its old sense of serf, but a modern reader hears "wicked man" and loses the point. She is answering Creon's "slave" of l. 479. And she shows the edge of her principle: it is for a brother. She does not say what a slave's body would be owed.

annotations.quote: The patriot perished by the outlaw’s brand.
annotations.note: The Greek puts each brother in half a line: one _porthon de tende gen_ ("ravaging this land", l. 518), the other standing up for it. This is Creon's real case and she never denies the fact. Athenians would have felt its force, since their own practice refused a traitor burial in Attic soil. Creon goes further than that practice did: he forbids burial anywhere and leaves the body exposed.

annotations.quote: Nathless the realms below these rites require.
annotations.note: Here she does say "laws": ὅ γʼ Ἅιδης τοὺς νόμους τούτους ποθεῖ (_ho g' Haides tous nomous toutous pothei_, l. 519). The noun she kept from Creon's edict she gives to burial, and makes Hades the party interested. The verb ποθεῖ is "longs for", a word for missing someone absent. Storr's "require" is too official. Her god of the dead wants these rites the way the bereaved want the dead.

annotations.quote: Who knows if this world’s crimes are virtues there?
annotations.note: Storr inflates it. She says τίς οἶδεν (_tis oiden_, "who knows", l. 521) whether these things are εὐαγῆ (_euage_, "free of pollution, holy") below. "These things" may be her act, or it may be Creon's distinction between the good brother and the bad. It is her best argument and her most modest. She does not claim to know the mind of the dead. She says he does not either, and that he is punishing on the assumption that he does.

annotations.quote: Not even death can make a foe a friend.
annotations.note: οὑχθρός and φίλος (_ho echthros_, _philos_, l. 522): the two poles of the play in one line. For Creon these are positions a man earns. In his first speech in [[s3]] he said he would never count an enemy of the city as a _philos_. For Antigone _philos_ is a fact of birth that conduct cannot cancel. They are using one word for two different things, and neither notices.

annotations.quote: My nature is for mutual love, not hate.
annotations.note: οὔτοι συνέχθειν, ἀλλὰ συμφιλεῖν ἔφυν (_outoi synechthein, alla symphilein ephyn_, l. 523). Both verbs appear to be coined for this line: I was born to join in loving, not to join in hating. The prefix matters. She is refusing to take a side in her brothers' enmity and choosing to share in the _philia_ she owes both. And ἔφυν, "I was born", makes it a matter of birth and so of family. It is the line everyone remembers, but she is not announcing love for mankind. She has shown Creon none, and within a minute she is refusing her sister.

annotations.quote: No woman shall be the master while I live.
annotations.note: He hears her verb and sneers with it three times: go below and φίλει, love them, if love you must (l. 524). Then he says ἐμοῦ δὲ ζῶντος οὐκ ἄρξει γυνή (_emou de zontos ouk arxei gyne_, l. 525), with γυνή, "woman", as the last word of the exchange. He has lost the stichomythia on every point of kinship and piety. He ends it on force and sex, with no civic argument left.

annotations.quote: Weeping o’er her sister’s fate,
annotations.note: Anapaests again, as for Antigone's entrance, though Storr turns them into a rhymed jingle. Ismene's tears are _philadelpha_ ("sister-loving", l. 527), a _phil_- word given to her three lines after Antigone's great one. Her face is _haimatoen_ ("blood-red", l. 528) with weeping. Storr's "angry" is his invention. The Chorus describe a face because the mask cannot show one.

annotations.quote: Two plagues I nurtured blindly, so it proved,
annotations.note: δύʼ ἄτα (_dy' ata_, l. 533), a dual: "a pair of ruins", with "uprisings against my throne" added. _Ate_ is the ruin the gods send through a man's own blinded judgement, and the ode that follows this scene ([[s6]]) is about nothing else. Creon uses it as abuse for two girls. He says οὐδʼ ἐμάνθανον, "I did not notice", and his failure to learn in time is the plot. Two unarmed nieces have become a coup, and one of them a viper.

annotations.quote: I did the deed, if she will have it so,
annotations.note: She says _dedraka tourgon_ ("I did the deed", l. 536), on the condition that her sister _homorrothei_, "rows in time with me". It is a lie, a loving one, and it comes with a glance sideways for permission. Is this the timid Ismene of the prologue? She told Antigone then that she could not act against the city. She can, it turns out, die for her sister. Those are different things, and Sophocles gives her full credit for the second.

annotations.quote: That were unjust. Thou would’st not act with me
annotations.note: Justice, _he dike_ (l. 538), will not allow it. This is the Justice of l. 451, now turned on Ismene. Antigone is exact about the record: you were not willing, and I did not make you a partner. Both halves are true to [[s1]], where she said she would not accept the help even if it were offered later. She forgets nothing.

annotations.quote: But now thy bark is stranded, I am bold
annotations.note: She calls herself _xymploun_ ("fellow-voyager", l. 541) in suffering, after the rowing verb of l. 536. Ismene thinks in ships. Creon's ship in [[s3]] was the city, on which alone one can make friends. Hers has two people in it. Storr's "stranded" is his addition, and "I am bold" underplays the Greek, "I am not ashamed".

annotations.quote: A friend in word is never friend of mine.
annotations.note: λόγοις δʼ ἐγὼ φιλοῦσαν οὐ στέργω φίλην (_logois d' ego philousan ou stergo philen_, l. 543). Three words of loving in one line, used to refuse love, twenty lines after "my nature is to join in love". The test is deed against word, τοὔργον against λόγοις. Is she being cruel, or keeping Ismene out of the grave? I think both. She needs the deed to be hers alone, and refusing Ismene also saves Ismene's life.

annotations.quote: One death sufficeth. Wherefore should’st thou die?
annotations.note: The question is Storr's. She says _arkeso thneskous' ego_ ("my dying will be enough", l. 547). Before it comes a prohibition: do not make your own what you never touched. Burial is done with the hands, and Ismene's were not there. In the same line she says "do not die with me", using _koina_ ("in common"), the word with which she first greeted Ismene.

annotations.quote: What would life profit me bereft of thee?
annotations.note: No "profit" here. Storr has borrowed the scene's other key word by mistake. Ismene asks what _bios_ ("life") is _philos_ ("dear") to her without her sister (l. 548). She is speaking Antigone's language of _philia_ back to her, and it is refused.

annotations.quote: Ask Creon, he’s thy kinsman and best friend.
annotations.note: One word does the work of Storr's two: κηδεμών (_kedemon_, l. 549), the one who has you in his care, a guardian. Its root covers family care, connexion by marriage and the tending of the dead, which is everything Antigone thinks Creon has betrayed. It is the cruellest line she speaks, and it throws the prologue back at a sister who has come to die with her.

annotations.quote: ’Tis a sad mockery, if indeed I mock.
annotations.note: The participle _algousa_ ("in pain", l. 551) is the first word: it is in pain that I laugh at you, if I do laugh. This is the one crack in her manner in the whole scene. Creon accused her of laughing over her deed (l. 483). She admits to this laughter, and to what it costs her.

annotations.quote: No, save thyself; I grudge not thy escape.
annotations.note: The Greek is _soson seauten_ (l. 553). It is the Guard's creed, safety first, recommended to Ismene. Does she mean it kindly? This is the strongest line for the protective reading, and I think the tone has changed since l. 549. She will not share the deed, but she does want her sister alive.

annotations.quote: Well, some approved thy wisdom, others mine.
annotations.note: Storr loses who the "some" and "others" are. The verb is _phronein_ ("to think rightly", l. 557). The usual reading, which I accept, is that Ismene seemed wise to those up here and Antigone to those below. Good sense has two juries in this play, the living and the dead. The Chorus's last lines award the prize for it, too late.

annotations.quote: Fear not; thou livest, I died long ago
annotations.note: The Greek is _he d' eme psyche palai tethneken_ (l. 559–560): my soul has long been dead. Since when? Since the decision before the play began, or since the family's ruin that she counted over in its first lines. The end of the sentence is "so as to help the dead", which Storr turns into a heroic "gave my life". She speaks as someone already below. Creon's sentence, a living woman shut in a tomb, will make her claim literal.

annotations.quote: Both maids, methinks, are crazed. One suddenly
annotations.note: Creon has stood silent for twenty-five lines while the sisters talk past him. His word is _anoun_ ("mindless", l. 562), and it is the word Ismene used of Antigone at the end of [[s1]]. One of them, he says, has been so from birth. He has heard the scene's two great speeches and put both down to a defect of mind.

annotations.quote: thy sister’s dead.
annotations.note: Ismene has said "without her", using the pronoun for someone present, ἥδε (_hede_, "this woman here"). Creon forbids it: do not say ἥδε, for she no longer exists (l. 567). She is standing a few feet away. Antigone said the same of herself a moment ago, so on this one point they agree.

annotations.quote: What, wilt thou slay thy own son’s plighted bride?
annotations.note: Line 568, nearly halfway through the play, and this is the first we hear that Antigone is betrothed to Creon's son. Ismene says it. Antigone did not mention him in the prologue or in her defence, and Creon has not thought of him. Sophocles held the fact back so that it falls here, after the sentence. We now know the edict will reach into Creon's own house.

annotations.quote: Aye, let him raise him seed from other fields.
annotations.note: Storr's biblical "raise seed" dignifies a barnyard line: ἀρώσιμοι γὰρ χἀτέρων εἰσὶν γύαι (_arosimoi gar chateron eisin gyai_, "others have furrows that can be ploughed", l. 569). The Athenian betrothal formula gave a daughter "for the ploughing of legitimate children", so the metaphor is conventional and he makes it brutal. The ode praised man for wearing down the Earth with the plough. For Creon a wife is a field, and one field is as good as another.

annotations.quote: No new espousal can be like the old.
annotations.note: The Greek is _hermosmena_ ("fitted together", l. 570): not as things were fitted between him and her. This is all the testimony the play gives that the match was more than an arrangement, and it comes from Ismene. Antigone says nothing. Haemon, when he comes, will argue politics and never plead love.

annotations.quote: A plague on trulls who court and woo our sons.
annotations.note: Storr's "trulls who court and woo" is his own invention. The line is κακὰς ἐγὼ γυναῖκας υἱέσι στυγῶ (_kakas ego gynaikas hyiesi stygo_, "I hate bad wives for my sons", l. 571). The verb is one of loathing, the second such verb Creon has used since l. 495. Against her "I was born to join in love" he has now said "I hate" twice in so many words.

annotations.quote: O Haemon, how thy sire dishonors thee!
annotations.note: Storr drops the most important word: ὦ φίλταθʼ Αἷμον (_o philtath' Haimon_, "dearest Haemon", l. 572), the superlative of _philos_. The manuscripts give the line to Ismene. A Renaissance edition moved it to Antigone, and Jebb and Storr follow, because it seems too warm to leave her silent. I can believe it either way but I lean to Ismene: the exchange around it is hers and Creon's line for line, and Antigone's silence about Haemon then runs unbroken to her death. If the line is hers, it is the only time she names him.

annotations.quote: A plague on thee and thy accursed bride!
annotations.note: No curse in the Greek: "you vex me too much, you and _to son lechos_", l. 573. The phrase means "your marriage-bed" if Antigone has just spoken, or "this marriage you keep on about" if Ismene has, so it settles nothing about the speaker. _Lechos_ is the word the Guard used for the bird's emptied nest at l. 425.

annotations.quote: ’Tis death that bars this marriage, not his sire.
annotations.note: Ἅιδης ὁ παύσων τούσδε τοὺς γάμους ἔφυ (_Haides ho pauson tousde tous gamous ephy_, l. 575): Hades is the one who will stop this marriage. "Not his sire" is Storr's addition, though it is the evasion Creon intends. Read the line again after the Messenger's speech, where Haemon lies with his arms round her in the tomb and gets his wedding in the house of Hades. Hades does not stop the marriage. He hosts it.

annotations.quote: By you, as first by me; off with them, guards,
annotations.note: The Chorus have said _dedogmen'_ ("it is resolved", l. 576), the verb of formal decrees. Creon's reply is "yes, by you and by me" (l. 577). He writes the elders into the sentence and they let him. Their one protest in the scene was about the son's marriage, not the niece's life or the corpse. Antigone said fear had locked their tongues. This is what that looks like.

annotations.quote: To live as women use, not roam at large.
annotations.note: The Greek is _gynaikas einai tasde med' aneimenas_ (l. 579): these must be women, and not let loose. The participle is used of animals turned out to range. The play began with two sisters outside the house gates before dawn, where they should not have been. Creon's last order is to put them back indoors. Ismene goes in condemned too, and is not spared until l. 771.

annotations.quote: When they perceive death pressing on life’s heels.
annotations.note: Even the _thraseis_ ("the bold", l. 580) run when they see Hades close. He has misjudged her to the last. She does not run. The one who gives way when death comes near his house is Creon. The Chorus begin the next ode on the word _eudaimones_ ("blessed", l. 583), which no one on stage now is.

links.why: Ismene's refusal before dawn is the thing Antigone will not let her take back here.
Haemon confirms what Antigone asserts in this scene, that the city thinks as she does and holds its breath.
The certainty of the unwritten-laws speech gives way to doubt and to a far stranger argument.
Teiresias settles the question of jurisdiction she raises: the dead and the gods below are not Creon's to command.

s6.essay:
The confidence of the last ode is gone. There the elders sang of what man can do; here they sing of a family for whom doing makes no difference. Once heaven's curse touches a house, trouble passes from generation to generation like a sea driven by the north wind, 'billow on billow.' It is the best image in the ode, and its cold, heavy rhythm survives even Storr's rhyming quatrains.

I read this as the elders finding a way not to judge. They have just watched their king condemn two girls, and what they offer is an explanation by inheritance: she is a daughter of Labdacus's line, the last shoot of a doomed tree, so of course this is happening. The Greek speaks of light spreading over the last root of the house, meaning the sisters; Storr's 'last born son' blurs that. Either way, nobody is responsible. Fate did it.

Then the ode lifts to Zeus, whom neither sleep nor time can touch, and comes down on a proverb about hope and delusion: when evil starts to look good to a man, ruin is close. They are thinking of Antigone, who called her death a gain. But who in this play mistakes a harm for a good and cannot be told otherwise? This is the pattern I find in every ode: aimed at her, it lands on Creon. He is about to prove it at length with his son.

annotations.quote: Thrice blest are they who never tasted pain!
annotations.note: The sisters have just been led indoors under sentence, and Creon probably stays on stage through the song. The Greek is quieter than Storr: εὐδαίμονες (_eudaimones_, 'fortunate, with a good daimon') are those whose life is κακῶν ἄγευστος (_kakon ageustos_, 'without a taste of evils', l. 583). 'Thrice' is Storr's. The ode on man in [[s4]] sang of what man can do; this one, its dark twin, sings of what is done to him.

annotations.quote: If once the curse of Heaven attaint a race,
annotations.note: Storr's legal 'attaint' hides an earthquake. The Greek says 'those whose house is shaken from the gods', σεισθῇ θεόθεν δόμος (l. 584), and the thing that then never fails them is ἄτας (_atas_, from _ate_: ruin, and the delusion that brings it). That word comes four times in this ode (ll. 584, 614, 623, 625) and is the song's real subject. Note that it is a house, _domos_, that is shaken: the unit of suffering here is the family, never the individual.

annotations.quote: The infection lingers on and speeds apace,
annotations.note: The Greek has no infection; _ate_ is ἕρπον (_herpon_, 'creeping', l. 585) over the whole length of the family. The verb comes back twice (ll. 613, 617), so that ruin, the law of Zeus and the unwary man's foot all move at the same crawl. It is the idea Antigone opened the play with, the evils that come from Oedipus, but from her it was a grievance and from the elders it is an excuse: if the house is cursed, nobody in the room has to be blamed.

annotations.quote: Sweep o’er the blackening main and whirl to land
annotations.note: The simile is a Thracian north wind driving a swell across ἔρεβος ὕφαλον (_erebos hyphalon_, 'the darkness under the sea', l. 587). Set it beside the ode on man in [[s4]], where man crosses the grey sea in a winter gale and comes through. Here the same sea is seen from the shore, and nobody is steering anything. I take the pairing as deliberate: Sophocles lets the Chorus unsay its own optimism.

annotations.quote: From Ocean’s cavernous depths his ooze and sand,
annotations.note: The storm rolls up κελαινὰν θῖνα (_kelainan thina_, 'black sand') from the bottom, βυσσόθεν (_byssothen_, 'from the depths', l. 590). That is the point of the comparison, and Storr keeps it well. What a family curse does is bring up old sediment: things done generations ago, long settled, are churned to the surface and thrown on the present.

annotations.quote: Billow on billow thunders on the shore.
annotations.note: Storr's 'billow on billow' anticipates the 'woe upon woe' of the next stanza and is not in the Greek. What the Greek has is sound: the headlands, beaten head-on, στόνῳ βρέμουσι (_stonoi bremousi_, 'roar with a groan', l. 591). _Stonos_ is a human noise, the groan of mourning, so the landscape is already lamenting before the Chorus names the family.

annotations.quote: On the Labdacidae I see descending
annotations.note: Labdacus was the grandfather of Oedipus. The troubles are ἀρχαῖα (_archaia_, 'ancient', l. 593), and they fall 'on the troubles of the dead', πήματα φθιτῶν ἐπὶ πήμασι (l. 595). The elders say 'I see', and what they see is a pattern. Ask what the pattern leaves out: Creon's edict, issued this morning, appears nowhere in their account of why this girl is to die.

annotations.quote: Laid on the race a malison, and his rod
annotations.note: 'Malison' is the opposite of benison: a curse. The Greek is vaguer and bleaker. 'Generation does not release generation, but some one of the gods strikes them down', θεῶν τις (_theon tis_, l. 597), 'and there is no deliverance', οὐδʼ ἔχει λύσιν. No god is named and no offence is given. The vagueness is the point; a curse with no author needs no remedy and permits no protest.

annotations.quote: The light that dawned upon its last born son
annotations.note: A mistranslation that matters. The Greek speaks of a light spread over 'the last root' in the house of Oedipus, ἐσχάτας and ῥίζας (ll. 597 and 600), and the last root is Antigone, with Ismene; there is no son. The elders are saying that the family's one remaining hope of continuing was this girl and her marriage. Storr's 'son' sends the reader looking for Polynices or Eteocles and loses the fact that the ode is about the person who has just left the stage.

annotations.quote: Is vanished, and the bloody axe of Fate
annotations.note: A famous crux. The manuscripts, and the Greek text shown here, read κόνις (_konis_, 'dust', l. 602): 'the bloody dust of the gods below mows it down'. Many editors, Jebb among them, print the conjecture _kopis_, 'chopper', and Storr's 'axe' follows them, since dust is an odd thing to reap with. I would keep the dust. It is the handful Antigone scattered on her brother in [[s3]], the thinnest substance in the play, and the elders are saying that it has cut down a royal house.

annotations.quote: Has felled the goodly tree that blossomed late.
annotations.note: The tree is half Storr's; the Greek has only the root and the verb ἀμᾷ (_amai_, 'mows, reaps', l. 602). But the instinct is good, because vegetable images are about to matter. In [[s7]] Haemon will show his father trees on a riverbank that survive by bending and others that go under 'root and branch'. The house of Oedipus is already cut to the root; Creon's is still standing and can still choose.

annotations.quote: O Oedipus, by reckless pride undone!
annotations.note: There is no address to Oedipus in the Greek. The line names the two things that, with the dust, cut the root down: λόγου τʼ ἄνοια (_logou anoia_, 'folly of speech') and φρενῶν ἐρινύς (_phrenon erinys_, 'a Fury of the mind', l. 602). This is the elders' judgment on Antigone: her defiant speech to Creon in [[s5]] was mindlessness, and the avenging spirit of the family now lives inside her head. It is the first of this stretch's many verdicts on who has _phrenes_, good sense, and who has lost them.

annotations.quote: Thy might, O Zeus, what mortal power can quell?
annotations.note: Storr's 'mortal power' translates ὑπερβασία (_hyperbasia_, 'overstepping, transgression', l. 605): what human trespass could hold down the power of Zeus? The word is loaded. Creon asked Antigone in [[s5]] whether she had dared to overstep his laws, and in [[s7]] he will damn anyone who 'oversteps' and forces the law (l. 663). The Chorus means Antigone. A listener who remembers her speech about the laws of Zeus may wonder which of the two has stepped over a line that belongs to him.

annotations.quote: Not sleep that lays all else beneath its spell,
annotations.note: Sleep is ὁ πάντʼ ἀγρεύων (_ho pant' agreuon_, 'the one who hunts down everything', l. 606), and even he cannot take Zeus. The ode on man ([[s4]]) made man the great hunter, netting birds, beasts and fish. Here the hunting is done to mortals, and the only being beyond the net is a god.

annotations.quote: Thou reignest King, omnipotent, sublime.
annotations.note: Three English adjectives for one Greek noun, δυνάστας (_dynastas_, 'ruler, potentate', l. 610), who is 'unaged by time' and holds the μαρμαρόεσσαν αἴγλαν (_marmaroessan aiglan_, 'the flashing radiance') of Olympus. The picture is of rule that does not get old. It is sung in front of a king who took power yesterday and whose first decree has already produced a death sentence in his own family.

annotations.quote: All bow to thy decree,
annotations.note: The Greek word is νόμος (_nomos_, 'law', l. 613): 'for the future and the past this law will hold'. So the play now has three things called law. Creon's proclamation is a _nomos_; Antigone appealed past it to the unwritten _nomima_ of the gods in [[s5]]; and the elders now announce Zeus's law, which is neither a command nor a custom but a regularity, like gravity. It tells you what will happen to the great and nothing about what you ought to do.

annotations.quote: All that exceeds the mean by Fate
annotations.note: The Greek here (ll. 613-614) is corrupt and much emended, but its drift is: nothing vast, πάμπολύ (_pampoly_), creeps into mortal life ἐκτὸς ἄτας (_ektos atas_, 'outside ruin'). Storr's 'the mean' brings in a doctrine of moderation that the text only implies, and 'Love or Hate' is filler for the rhyme. Still, he catches the elders' philosophy: do not be big. It suits old men who have survived several kings, and it has nothing to say when the moderate course is to leave a brother to the dogs.

annotations.quote: Hope flits about never-wearying wings;
annotations.note: ἐλπὶς (_elpis_) in Greek is expectation as much as hope, and it is not a comfort. Here it is πολύπλαγκτος (_polyplanktos_, 'far-wandering', l. 615), which Storr turns into a bird. The elders are explaining how ruin gets in: through what people expect to gain. That was Creon's theory of everyone else in [[s3]], where every opponent was after _kerdos_, profit; it will turn out to describe him.

annotations.quote: Profit to some, to some light loves she brings,
annotations.note: Storr drops the key noun. Hope is a benefit, ὄνασις, to many, but to many it is ἀπάτα κουφονόων ἐρώτων (_apata kouphonoon eroton_, 'the deception of light-minded desires', l. 616). _Apata_ will be heard again within a dozen lines, when Haemon is said to come 'cheated' of his marriage. And 'light-minded' was the ode on man's word for the birds that clever man traps: the trapper is now the bird. With _eroton_ the ode also slips in the subject of the next one ([[s8]]).

annotations.quote: Till ’neath his feet the treacherous ashes burn.
annotations.note: A man walking over ground he thinks is cold; the Greek says the thing creeps on him 'knowing nothing', εἰδότι δʼ οὐδὲν (l. 617), until he scorches his foot in hot fire. The elders mean it for Antigone, but she knew exactly what she was walking on and said so. The one on stage who does not yet feel the heat is Creon.

annotations.quote: Sure ’twas a sage inspired that spake this word;
annotations.note: The Chorus now quotes a proverb and says so: a κλεινὸν ἔπος (_kleinon epos_, 'famous saying', l. 620), revealed 'by someone's wisdom'. They do not know whose. This is how the elders think throughout the play: when events become frightening they reach for something everybody already says.

annotations.quote: If evil good appear
annotations.note: The centre of the ode, and Storr's couplet removes the god from it. The Greek runs: evil seems good to the man whose wits a god is leading towards ruin, φρένας θεὸς ἄγει πρὸς ἄταν (ll. 622-623). The later Latin tag about the gods first maddening those they mean to destroy descends from this thought. The frightening part is that the victim's judgment is the instrument: he does not choose evil knowing it, he sees it as ἐσθλὸν (_esthlon_, 'good, noble'). The elders mean the girl who called a crime holy. Within a hundred lines we will watch a man defend obedience to unjust orders as the highest civic good.

annotations.quote: And brief the respite from her flaming sword.
annotations.note: The flaming sword comes from Genesis, not Thebes. The Greek is flat and exact: such a man fares 'the briefest time outside ruin', ὀλίγιστον χρόνον ἐκτὸς ἄτας (l. 625). The phrase _ektos atas_ closed the previous stanza too (l. 614), so both halves of the song end on the same two words. Taken as a prediction about Creon it is accurate to the hour: his respite lasts until Tiresias leaves the stage in [[s11]].

annotations.quote: Hither comes in angry mood
annotations.note: Storr prejudges the entrance. The Greek asks whether Haemon comes ἀχνύμενος (_achnymenos_, 'grieving', l. 627) for Antigone's fate, and the next scene depends on the fact that he arrives perfectly controlled. The metre shifts here from song to marching anapaests, the usual way of announcing a new arrival. The Chorus speaks to Creon, so 'thy brood' is his.

annotations.quote: Haemon, latest of thy brood;
annotations.note: νέατον γέννημʼ (_neaton gennema_, 'last-born offspring', l. 627). The elders have just sung of the 'last root' of Oedipus's house, and without drawing breath they introduce the last child of Creon's. We learn only at the end ([[s13]]) that another son is already dead. The curse the Chorus thinks it is watching in one family is about to be manufactured, from nothing, in the other.

annotations.quote: Or her marriage-bed deceived,
annotations.note: ἀπάτης λεχέων (_apates lecheon_, 'the cheating of his marriage-bed', l. 630): the word used a moment ago for the deception worked by light-minded desire (l. 616). The elders have already decided what Haemon's business is. He is a young man in love, deceived of his bride, and whatever he says will be heard as that. Creon makes the same assumption, and Haemon will spend the whole scene refusing to speak in those terms.

links.why: Set this beside the ode to human ingenuity sung one scene earlier; the elders' mood has turned completely.
Antigone takes up the family curse herself on the way to the tomb, and it is her 'most poignant pain,' not a theory.

s7.essay:
Haemon begins with a submission so complete, 'O father, I am thine,' that I cannot tell whether it is sincere or tactical, and I suspect he could not either. Creon takes it at face value and delivers his fullest statement of what he believes. Much of it is still reasonable. A man who cannot govern his household will not govern a city; an army holds only while discipline holds; these people were under siege two days ago. Then he says the thing that loses the argument: whoever the State appoints must be obeyed in everything, 'just and unjust alike.' He has stopped claiming the edict is right. He is claiming that it need not be.

Haemon's reply is a model of how to tell a powerful man he is wrong. He does not plead for his bride. He never once says he loves her. He reports, as a loyal son who hears what a king cannot, that the city is mourning the girl and thinks her name should be 'writ in gold.' So Antigone was right in [[s5]] about those bated breaths. Then come two pictures of bending: trees that give way to a flood and keep their twigs, a sailor who will not slacken the sheet and goes over.

None of it gets through, because Creon can only hear a boy besotted with a woman. The quick exchange that follows is the political heart of the play. 'A State for one man is no State at all.' 'The State is his who rules it.' That second line is where the ship of state from [[s3]] ends up. Then Haemon says one will die with her, meaning himself, and his father hears a threat on his own life.

Two small decisions close the scene, and both tell on Creon. Asked whether he really means to kill both sisters, he says 'I stand corrected' and spares Ismene in half a line; he can change his mind when nothing rides on it. And the stoning announced in [[s1]] becomes a cave with a little food, so that technically no one has killed her. It is a lawyer's device for avoiding pollution, and Teiresias will see straight through it.

annotations.quote: Soon shall we know, better than seer can tell.
annotations.note: μάντεων ὑπέρτερον (_manteon hyperteron_, 'better than seers', l. 631) is a throwaway idiom, and one of the cruellest ironies in the play. A real seer is coming in [[s11]], and what Creon learns from him he learns one hour too late. For the moment he thinks knowledge is something a king gets by asking a direct question.

annotations.quote: Learning may fixed decree anent thy bride,
annotations.note: The line is garbled in this printing; read 'my fixed decree'. The Greek is τελείαν ψῆφον (_teleian psephon_, 'the final vote', l. 632). A _psephos_ is the pebble an Athenian dropped in the urn in court or assembly, so Creon dignifies one man's decision with the word for a collective verdict. Haemon will take him at his word and report how the city would actually vote.

annotations.quote: Thou mean’st not, son, to rave against thy sire?
annotations.note: λυσσαίνων (_lyssainon_, 'raging', l. 633) comes from _lyssa_, the fury of a rabid dog. Creon's first thought about his son is that he may have gone mad. Keep the word in mind: the scene ends with the son telling the father that he is the one who raves (l. 765). The charge of madness travels the whole length of the episode and changes hands.

annotations.quote: Know’st not whate’er we do is done in love?
annotations.note: Storr softens this. The Greek asks: 'or are we φίλοι (_philoi_, 'dear, your own') to you whatever we do?' (l. 634). It is a demand for unconditional loyalty, made in advance of knowing what has been done. This is Creon's notion of _philia_ throughout: in [[s3]] he chose his friends by their service to the city, and from his son he expects kinship to work as a blank cheque. He means it; he does love his son. The line is unbearable on a second reading.

annotations.quote: O father, I am thine, and I will take
annotations.note: σός εἰμι (_sos eimi_, 'I am yours', l. 635). Haemon opens with exactly what was asked for, in the fewest possible words. Is it sincere? I think so, and I think it is also strategy: he knows his father, and knows that anything said before these words would not be heard. Nothing in the scene suggests he came intending to quarrel.

annotations.quote: Thy wisdom as the helm to steer withal.
annotations.note: The Greek is more careful than the English. 'You, having good judgments, set me straight, and those I will follow': γνώμας and χρηστὰς (ll. 635-636). The participle 'having' can mean 'since you have' or 'if you have', and the relative clause promises obedience only to the good ones. Creon hears the first sense. The verb ἀπορθοῖς (_aporthois_, 'you keep straight') belongs to the vocabulary of the upright ship of state from his opening speech in [[s3]], which is why Storr's helm, though his own, is apt.

annotations.quote: More precious than thy loving goverance.
annotations.note: 'Goverance' is a slip for 'governance', and 'loving' is not in the Greek, which says σοῦ καλῶς ἡγουμένου (_sou kalos hegoumenou_, l. 638): 'you leading well'. Again the grammar leaves a door open: 'since you lead well' or 'so long as you lead well'. Haemon has made two statements of submission and put a condition inside each. The rest of the scene is the condition being called in.

annotations.quote: In all deferring to a father’s will.
annotations.note: 'To stand behind a father's judgment in everything', ὄπισθεν ἑστάναι (_opisthen hestanai_, l. 640). It is a drill-ground image: the son is posted in the rank behind. Creon cannot describe a family except as a formation, and by the end of this speech the household, the city and the phalanx will have become one thing with one rule.

annotations.quote: A brood of sons submissive, keen to avenge
annotations.note: Sons are prayed for so that they will be κατηκόους (_katekoous_, 'obedient', literally 'listeners', l. 642), repay the father's ἐχθρὸν (_echthron_, 'enemy') with harm and honour his φίλον (_philon_, 'friend') as he does (ll. 643-644). This is the ordinary Greek ethic of helping friends and harming enemies, but note who decides which is which. A son inherits his father's list. Antigone's list in [[s5]] was fixed by birth; Creon's is fixed by Creon.

annotations.quote: But who begets unprofitable sons,
annotations.note: ἀνωφέλητα (_anopheleta_, 'useless, bringing no benefit', l. 645). Children are assessed as assets, in the same accounting Creon applies to everyone. The worst consequence he can imagine is γέλων (_gelon_, 'laughter', l. 647) from his enemies, the dread of being mocked that drives Sophoclean heroes. He shares that fear with the girl he has condemned, and neither would thank you for saying so.

annotations.quote: And let no woman fool away thy wits.
annotations.note: 'Do not throw out your φρένας (_phrenas_, 'wits, good sense') under pleasure, ὑφʼ ἡδονῆς, for a woman's sake' (ll. 648-649). Creon assumes his son's only possible motive is sexual, as the Chorus did when it announced him. Haemon will not say one word about love in the entire scene. Who is thinking about pleasure here is a fair question.

annotations.quote: And her embraces very soon wax cold.
annotations.note: ψυχρὸν παραγκάλισμα (_psychron parankalisma_, 'a cold thing to hold in your arms', l. 650). Creon means a bad wife. The Messenger in [[s13]] describes Haemon dying with his arms round Antigone's body in the tomb, and the phrase comes true to the letter. Sophocles has given the father the image of his son's death and let him use it as a joke about shrews.

annotations.quote: As a false friend? So spue and cast her off,
annotations.note: φίλος κακός (_philos kakos_, 'a bad _philos_', l. 652): Antigone is family, Creon's niece and ward, and he has to concede the word even while disowning her. Then πτύσας (_ptysas_, 'spitting', l. 653): spit her out like an enemy. In the tomb, the Messenger reports, Haemon answers his father's pleading by spitting in his face. The gesture Creon prescribes here is the one he will receive.

annotations.quote: Bid her go find a husband with the dead.
annotations.note: 'Let the girl marry someone in Hades', ἐν Ἅιδου and νυμφεύειν (l. 654). This is where the bride-of-death motif enters the play, as a sneer. Antigone turns it into lament in [[s9]], calling the tomb her bridal chamber, and in [[s13]] it becomes simple fact, when Haemon is said to have got his marriage rites in the house of Hades. Creon never says anything in this scene that the plot does not hold him to.

annotations.quote: Of all my subjects the one malcontent,
annotations.note: 'Alone out of the whole city', πόλεως and ἐκ πάσης μόνην (l. 656). This is a factual claim, and it is the one Haemon will contradict, first tactfully (the city mourns her, l. 693) and then flatly (the whole people of Thebes denies it, l. 733). Watch the word 'alone', _monos_, through the scene. Creon pins it on Antigone here, and by line 739 it has been pinned on him.

annotations.quote: I will not prove a traitor to the State.
annotations.note: Storr overstates. The Greek is ψευδῆ (_pseude_, 'false, a liar', l. 657): I will not make myself a liar to the city. Having announced the penalty in public, he cannot now let it lapse, and that, not her guilt, is the reason he gives. It is an honest glimpse of the mechanism: what locks him in is his own proclamation and what it would look like to retreat from it.

annotations.quote: She surely dies. Go, let her, if she will,
annotations.note: The Greek is two words, ἀλλὰ κτενῶ (_alla kteno_, 'no, I will kill her', l. 658), in the first person. Storr's 'She surely dies' turns an act into an event. Creon himself will retreat to a formula very like Storr's at the end of the scene, when he devises a death in which nobody's hand does the killing.

annotations.quote: Appeal to Zeus the God of Kindred, for
annotations.note: Δία ξύναιμον (_Dia xynaimon_, 'Zeus of shared blood', ll. 658-659), and the verb is ἐφυμνείτω (_ephymneito_, 'let her chant her hymn to him'), which is contempt. This is the second time Creon has waved away Zeus in his family aspect; in [[s5]] it was Zeus of the household hearth. A man who invokes the gods for the city and mocks them for the family has divided what the Greeks did not divide. The Chorus will use the same adjective of his own quarrel with his son (l. 792).

annotations.quote: If thus I nurse rebellion in my house,
annotations.note: ἄκοσμα (_akosma_, 'disorderly', l. 660): if I rear my own kin to be without _kosmos_, order. The root returns at l. 677 and l. 730, and it is Creon's master value in this speech, as the city's safety was in [[s3]]. The argument is from the smaller to the larger: indulgence at home will be read as weakness abroad. As political psychology it is not stupid. It is the argument of every ruler who has punished a relative to prove a point.

annotations.quote: For whoso rules his household worthily,
