annotations.note: The man who is χρηστός (_chrestos_, 'sound, good') among his own will be found δίκαιος (_dikaios_, 'just') in the city (ll. 661-662). Set the maxim against the ending: Creon's management of his household costs him his son and his wife within the day. By his own test he stands condemned as a ruler. Some editors rearrange the lines that follow, because the 'such a one' praised at l. 668 fits the obedient man better than the transgressor; Storr translates the transmitted order and the join shows.

annotations.quote: But he who overbears the laws, or thinks
annotations.note: ὑπερβὰς (_hyperbas_, 'overstepping', l. 663) and νόμους βιάζεται ('does violence to the laws'). The Chorus has just sung that no human _hyperbasia_ can check the power of Zeus (l. 605), and Creon claims the word for offences against his own _nomoi_. The second offence he names is new and aimed at the son in front of him: thinking to give orders to those in power. He has scented advice coming.

annotations.quote: Appoints must be obeyed in everything,
annotations.note: 'Whomever the πόλις (_polis_) sets up, him one must hear', κλύειν (l. 666). Notice where Creon locates his authority at this stage: in the city's appointment. Seventy lines on he asks with scorn whether the city is to tell him what to order (l. 734). The speech and the stichomythia cannot both be true, and the scene is built to make him say both.

annotations.quote: But small and great, just and unjust alike.
annotations.note: 'But' looks like a slip in this printing for 'Both'. The Greek is 'in small things and just things and their opposites', καὶ δίκαια καὶ τἀναντία (l. 667); he cannot quite bring himself to say 'unjust' and uses a euphemism. This is the turning point of his case: obedience is owed even to wrong commands. Nothing in his opening speech required this, and nothing after it recovers. It is also the exact position Antigone refused in [[s5|the unwritten laws speech]].

annotations.quote: Would shine, as King or subject; such a man
annotations.note: καλῶς μὲν ἄρχειν, εὖ δʼ ἂν ἄρχεσθαι (l. 669): to rule well and to be willing to be ruled well. Ruling and being ruled in turn was the Athenian citizen's ideal, and the audience would have nodded. The question the play puts is whether Creon possesses the second half. In this scene he is offered advice by his son, his council and (by report) his people, and treats each offer as mutiny.

annotations.quote: A comrade leal and true; but Anarchy—
annotations.note: παραστάτην (_parastaten_, 'the man who stands beside you', l. 671) is the hoplite next in the line, whose shield covers your right side. Young Athenians swore in their oath of service not to desert that man. Creon is at his most persuasive here, and it would be a mistake to read the speech as a tyrant's rant. It is the creed of a citizen-soldier whose city was nearly sacked two nights ago.

annotations.quote: What evils are not wrought by Anarchy!
annotations.note: The Greek is a flat superlative: there is no greater evil than ἀναρχίας (_anarchias_, 'absence of rule', l. 672). Compare the superlatives elsewhere: for Haemon the highest of possessions is good sense (l. 684), and for the Messenger in [[s13]] the worst of evils is bad counsel. The play is partly an argument about what goes at the top of that list, and Creon's answer, disorder, is the only one that makes obedience the supreme virtue.

annotations.quote: She ruins States, and overthrows the home,
annotations.note: Anarchy makes houses ἀναστάτους (_anastatous_, 'laid waste, emptied', l. 673). Cities, homes, armies: the three institutions fall in one sentence, each introduced by a pointing 'she'. Which house in Thebes is laid waste by nightfall? Creon's, and what empties it is the insistence on rule, not any failure of it.

annotations.quote: While discipline preserves the ordered ranks.
annotations.note: πειθαρχία (_peitharchia_, 'obedience to command', l. 676) is the opposite pole to _anarchia_, and what it saves is τὰ πολλὰ σώμαθʼ, 'most of the bodies', men's lives. It is a soldier's truth. It is also an awkward noun to hear from a man in a play about a body, whose refusal to release one corpse is about to cost three more.

annotations.quote: And yield to title to a woman’s will.
annotations.note: Read 'no title'. After forty lines on fathers, cities and armies the speech lands here: γυναικὸς οὐδαμῶς ἡσσητέα (_gynaikos oudamos hessetea_, 'we must on no account be worsted by a woman', l. 678). I think this is the real conclusion and the rest is its justification. In [[s5]] he said no woman would rule while he lived; a principle that needs repeating this often is covering a fear.

annotations.quote: Than hear it said, a woman proved his match.
annotations.note: Better to fall πρὸς ἀνδρὸς (_pros andros_, 'at a man's hands', l. 679) than be called γυναικῶν ἥσσονες (_gynaikon hessones_, 'weaker than women', l. 680). 'Be called': it is reputation again. He gets the alternative he asks for. He is brought down by men, a son and a blind prophet, and it makes no difference to how far he falls. Haemon will throw the word 'weaker' back at him at l. 747.

annotations.quote: To me, unless old age have dulled wits,
annotations.note: 'Unless we have been robbed by time', τῷ χρόνῳ κεκλέμμεθα (l. 681), 'you seem to speak sensibly', φρονούντως (_phronountos_, l. 682). The elders endorse Creon with an escape clause already attached. In forty lines they will endorse Haemon as well. Their value as a moral guide in this scene is nil, and their value as a picture of how a council behaves under a strong ruler is considerable.

annotations.quote: Reason, the choicest gift bestowed by heaven.
annotations.note: Haemon's first word after 'Father' is θεοὶ, 'the gods', and what they plant in men is φρένας (_phrenas_, 'wits, good sense', l. 683), the faculty Creon warned him not to throw away at l. 648. He accepts his father's term and changes its owner: sense is the gods' gift to human beings generally, so no one man holds all of it. He calls it the highest of κτημάτων (_ktematon_, 'possessions', l. 684), meeting Creon's talk of profitable sons in its own currency.

annotations.quote: ’Tis not for me to say thou errest, nor
annotations.note: This is the tact the scene is famous for. 'That you do not speak ὀρθῶς (_orthos_, 'rightly, straight') I could not say, and may I never know how to' (ll. 685-686). He disclaims both the ability and the wish to criticise, and then criticises for forty lines by reporting what others say. It is how one speaks to a man whose 'eye is terrible': the truth has to arrive as hearsay.

annotations.quote: And yet wise thoughts may come to other men
annotations.note: γένοιτο μέντἂν χἀτέρῳ καλῶς ἔχον (l. 687): 'yet something good might come to another man too'. The whole speech is in this modest potential clause. Haemon never argues that the burial was right. He argues that a second opinion can exist, and Creon will be unable to grant even that.

annotations.quote: And, as thy son, it falls to me to mark
annotations.note: προσκοπεῖν (_proskopein_, 'to look out ahead', l. 688) is scouting, and he says he was born to do it for his father. It turns Creon's military idea of the son to a better use than standing in the rear rank. A son who watches on his father's behalf will sometimes see what the father does not want seen. Creon asked for a subordinate who hates his enemies; he is offered an intelligence service.

annotations.quote: The commons stand in terror of thy frown,
annotations.note: τὸ γὰρ σὸν ὄμμα δεινὸν (_to son omma deinon_, 'your eye is terrible', l. 690) to the ἀνδρὶ δημότῃ, the ordinary man of the people. _Deinos_ is the ode on man's great word, 'formidable, wonderful, dreadful', and here it has only its ugly sense. Antigone told Creon in [[s5]] that the elders would agree with her if fear did not lock their tongues, and he ignored it from her. The defect of one-man rule shown here is practical before it is moral: the ruler stops receiving information.

annotations.quote: But I can overhear their muttered plaints,
annotations.note: He hears it ὑπὸ σκότου (_hypo skotou_, 'under cover of darkness', l. 692). There is no assembly in this Thebes and nobody speaks in the open; opinion exists only as something overheard. An Athenian audience, used to settling public questions by open debate, is being shown a city that has to whisper.

annotations.quote: Know how the people mourn this maiden doomed
annotations.note: ὀδύρεται πόλις (_odyretai polis_, 'the city laments', l. 693). Up to now the _polis_ has been Creon's word, the thing he defends against her. Haemon makes it the subject of a verb of mourning for Antigone, in direct reply to 'alone out of the whole city' at l. 656. From this line on the scene's question is who gets to say 'the city'.

annotations.quote: For noblest deeds to die the worst of deaths.
annotations.note: Three superlatives in two Greek lines: of all women the least deserving, ἀναξιωτάτη, dying most foully, κάκιστʼ, for deeds most glorious, εὐκλεεστάτων (ll. 694-695). The last is from _eukleia_, 'good fame', and it is what Antigone told Creon in [[s5]] she had won by burying her brother. She claimed it defiantly and with no sign that anyone agreed. She never learns that the city gave it to her.

annotations.quote: When her own brother slain in battle lay
annotations.note: αὐτάδελφον (_autadelphon_, 'her very own brother', l. 696) is the word of the play's first line, where Antigone used it of Ismene. The citizens, as Haemon reports them, describe the deed in her vocabulary and not in Creon's: Polynices is a brother fallen in the slaughter and unburied, with no mention of treason. Dogs that eat flesh raw, ὠμηστῶν κυνῶν (l. 697), keep the physical horror in view, which Creon's abstractions never do.

annotations.quote: Should not her name (they cry) be writ in gold?
annotations.note: Storr invents the inscription. The Greek asks whether she does not deserve χρυσῆς (_chryses_, 'golden') honour, _time_ (l. 699). This is our only report of what ordinary Thebans think, and it reaches us third-hand through a son with a motive. I believe it anyway, because the elders' chilly 'Thy word is law' in [[s3]] pointed the same way, and because Tiresias in [[s11]] confirms that the city is suffering.

annotations.quote: Such the low murmurings that reach my ear.
annotations.note: ἐρεμνὴ σῖγʼ ἐπέρχεται φάτις (_eremne sig' eperchetai phatis_, 'a dark rumour comes on in silence', l. 700). Rumour here moves the way ruin moved in the ode just sung, quietly and under cover. Haemon closes the report and turns at once to affection. He knows that this was the dangerous part.

annotations.quote: Than thy well-being, for what higher good
annotations.note: 'No κτῆμα (_ktema_, 'possession') is more precious to me than your prospering' (ll. 701-702), picking up the 'possessions' of l. 684. A father's good name is his children's ἄγαλμα (_agalma_, 'ornament, glory', l. 704), and theirs is his. It answers Creon's doctrine that sons exist to serve the father's interests by agreeing with it and drawing the right conclusion: your interest is your reputation, and your reputation is going bad in the dark.

annotations.quote: Therefore, my father, cling not to one mood,
annotations.note: 'Do not wear one single ἦθος (_ethos_, 'cast of mind, character') in yourself', with φόρει (_phorei_, 'carry, wear', l. 705), as one wears a garment. The diagnosis is exact: Creon has one way of being right and puts it on every morning. With μοῦνον, 'one only', the word 'alone' starts to migrate towards him.

annotations.quote: That he alone can speak or think aright,
annotations.note: φρονεῖν μόνος δοκεῖ (_phronein monos dokei_, 'thinks that he alone has sense', l. 707), or a tongue or a ψυχὴν, a soul, that no one else has. Tongue, soul and thinking: in [[s3]] Creon said you cannot know a man's soul, thought and judgment until he has been tested in office. His son is handing him back his own test.

annotations.quote: Such oracles are empty breath when tried.
annotations.note: There are no oracles in the Greek. Such men, διαπτυχθέντες (_diaptychthentes_, 'opened up, unfolded', l. 709), like a folded writing-tablet or a box, are seen to be κενοί (_kenoi_, 'empty'). Storr loses the picture of the man as a container with nothing in it. 'Empty' will be traded as an insult later in the scene (ll. 753, 754), and Creon in [[s13]] will call himself a man who no longer exists, no more than nothing.

annotations.quote: By others’ wisdom and relax in time.
annotations.note: Two infinitives carry the advice: τὸ μανθάνειν (_to manthanein_, 'to learn') and τὸ μὴ τείνειν ἄγαν (_to me teinein agan_, 'not to strain too tight', ll. 710-711). 'Learn' is the play's last idea; its closing lines say that the proud are taught good sense in old age, by blows. 'Strain' sets up the two images that follow, since the tree that 'strains against' the current and the sailor who 'strains' his sheet use the same verb.

annotations.quote: See how the trees beside a stream in flood
annotations.note: The trees that ὑπείκει (_hypeikei_, 'give way', l. 713) beside the winter torrent save their twigs. A few minutes ago the elders sang of a sea-storm no one could resist and a family cut down to the root; Haemon offers flood and tree again, but as a situation in which there is still a choice. The image should sound familiar to Creon. In [[s5]] he told Antigone that the stiffest wills fall hardest and the hardest iron snaps, and he does not recognise his own argument when it comes back.

annotations.quote: But by resisting perish root and branch.
annotations.note: ἀντιτείνοντʼ (_antiteinont'_, 'straining against') and αὐτόπρεμνʼ (_autopremn'_, 'trunk and all', l. 714). The ode spoke of the 'last root' of Oedipus's house (l. 600); now the phrase is held out to Creon as a warning about his own. It is prophecy in a strict sense. He loses the whole tree, son and wife and the son before, and survives as the stump.

annotations.quote: The mariner who keeps his mainsheet taut,
annotations.note: πόδα (_poda_, literally 'foot', l. 715) is the sheet, the rope at the sail's lower corner, kept ἐγκρατῆ, 'under tight control'. The choice of a ship is pointed. Creon introduced himself in [[s3]] as the helmsman of the city, the vessel that keeps everyone safe if it sails upright. His son accepts the metaphor and tells him he does not know how to sail.

annotations.quote: To sail with thwarts reversed, keel uppermost.
annotations.note: The Greek has a grim joke that Storr keeps: he capsizes and 'voyages for the rest of the trip', τὸ λοιπὸν and ναυτίλλεται, with his rowing-benches upside down, ὑπτίοις and σέλμασιν (ll. 716-717). The tree was about the ruler; the ship has a crew. If the man at the sheet will not ease it, everyone aboard goes into the water with him.

annotations.quote: Relent then and repent thee of thy wrath;
annotations.note: εἶκε (_eike_, 'yield', l. 718) is the third appearance of the verb in six lines, and the first direct imperative Haemon has allowed himself. He asks for a μετάστασιν (_metastasin_, 'change, shift') in his father's θυμῷ (_thymoi_, 'temper'). Creon does yield, in [[s11]], to the Chorus, in almost these terms. Why can he do for the elders, an hour later, what he cannot do for his son now? Partly fear of Tiresias, and partly, I think, that the elders are old.

annotations.quote: With absolute wisdom; but, if that’s denied,
annotations.note: The close paraphrases Hesiod, who in the _Works and Days_ ranks the man who thinks everything out for himself first and the man who listens to good advice second, with the man who does neither called useless. Haemon discreetly leaves out the third. He ends on μανθάνειν (_manthanein_, 'to learn', l. 723) again, and prefaces it with an apology for being young (l. 719), having guessed which objection is coming.

annotations.quote: Heed thou thy sire too; both have spoken well.
annotations.note: εὖ γὰρ εἴρηται διπλῇ (_eu gar eiretai diplei_, 'it has been well said on both sides', l. 725). The two speeches are not compatible: one says obey in everything, the other says the order is wrong and the city knows it. The elders' evenhandedness is a refusal to judge, and it removes the one restraint that might have worked on Creon, a clear word from his council.

annotations.quote: Lessoned in prudence by a beardless boy?
annotations.note: διδαξόμεσθα and φρονεῖν (_didaxomestha_, _phronein_, 'shall we be taught to have sense', ll. 726-727) by a man of his age? Creon answers none of the arguments. He answers the speaker's birth certificate. The last lines of the play will say that good sense is taught in old age by great blows, so the question he asks in scorn gets a literal yes.

annotations.quote: Weigh me upon my merit, not my years.
annotations.note: Look at τἄργα (_targa_, 'the deeds, the facts', l. 729), not at my age. From here the scene is in stichomythia, one line each for thirty lines, which in Greek tragedy is the form for a quarrel that has stopped being a discussion. Each speaker takes a word from the other's line and turns it, and you can follow the whole exchange by the stolen words.

annotations.quote: Strange merit this to sanction lawlessness!
annotations.note: Creon takes 'deed' and twists it: is it a deed to σέβειν (_sebein_, 'revere') those who are disorderly, τοὺς ἀκοσμοῦντας (l. 730)? _Sebein_ is religious vocabulary, the word for what one owes the gods, and it now enters the quarrel and will not leave: ll. 731, 744, 745, 777, 780. The question of the play, what deserves reverence, is being fought out in a single verb.

annotations.quote: For evil-doers I would urge no plea.
annotations.note: 'I would not ask you to show piety towards the wicked', εὐσεβεῖν and κακούς (l. 731). Haemon gives up nothing here. He grants the principle and denies that it applies to her. He is still arguing; the anger has not started.

annotations.quote: Is not this maid an arrant law-breaker?
annotations.note: Storr drops the metaphor. Creon asks whether she has not been seized by such a νόσῳ (_nosoi_, 'disease', l. 732). Wrongdoing as sickness is his habit of speech, and it rebounds: Tiresias will tell him in [[s11]] that the city is sick and that the source is his own mind.

annotations.quote: The Theban commons with one voice say, No.
annotations.note: ὁμόπτολις λεώς (_homoptolis leos_, 'the people who share this city', l. 733). _Homoptolis_ is a rare word, 'of the same polis', and it is chosen to make the point that the city is a thing held in common. Haemon has dropped the hearsay and the tact. This is a flat statement of fact against his father's flat statement at l. 656.

annotations.quote: What, shall the mob dictate my policy?
annotations.note: The Greek word is πόλις (_polis_, l. 734), and Storr's 'mob' badly obscures what happens. Creon does not sneer at a rabble. He asks whether the city is to tell him what orders to give. The man whose whole case was the city's safety and the city's appointment (l. 666) now sets himself against the city by name. This is the line where the polis and the one man come apart, and he is the one who separates them.

annotations.quote: ’Tis thou, methinks, who speakest like a boy.
annotations.note: ἄγαν νέος (_agan neos_, 'altogether too young', l. 735). Haemon returns the taunt of l. 727. It is fair: the idea that the ruler owes no account to anyone is an adolescent's idea of power, and Creon is new to the job. It is also the moment the son stops managing his father and starts scoring off him.

annotations.quote: Am I to rule for others, or myself?
annotations.note: The Greek dative is ambiguous between 'by another's judgment' and 'for another's benefit' (l. 736), and Creon means both: this land is to be ruled, ἄρχειν χθονός, by him and for him. Notice that 'city' has become 'land'. He is talking about territory he holds.

annotations.quote: A State for one man is no State at all.
annotations.note: 'That is no πόλις (_polis_) which belongs to one man', ἀνδρός and ἑνός (l. 737). An Athenian audience, proud of governing itself, would have gone with this line at once. Haemon has shifted the ground from what his father may forbid to whose city it is. It is a definition, and by it Creon's Thebes has ceased to be a city while he was speaking.

annotations.quote: The State is his who rules it, so ’tis held.
annotations.note: 'Is the city not considered to belong to the one in power?', τοῦ κρατοῦντος and νομίζεται (l. 738). The verb is from _nomos_: it is 'customarily held'. So here, at the bottom of the argument, is Creon's _nomos_: the city is property. In [[s3]] it was a ship carrying everyone, and its safety was the measure of a man. The audience has watched a decent political creed turn into ownership in the course of one day.

annotations.quote: As monarch of a desert thou wouldst shine.
annotations.note: 'You would rule well, alone, over an empty land', ἐρήμης and μόνος (l. 739). The deferential son is gone and this is sarcasm. _Monos_, 'alone', which Creon fixed on Antigone at l. 656, has come home to him. It is also prophecy: by the end he rules a palace with nobody left in it, and within forty lines he will send Antigone to a place he calls by the same word, 'desolate' (l. 773).

annotations.quote: This boy, methinks, maintains the woman’s cause.
annotations.note: Beaten on the city, Creon changes ground to gender, and changes addressee: 'this fellow' is said to the Chorus, over his son's head. συμμαχεῖ (_symmachei_, 'fights as ally of', l. 740) is military. At l. 674 anarchy was what broke the allied spear, and Creon now files his son under the enemy's alliance.

annotations.quote: If thou be’st woman, yes. My thought’s for thee.
annotations.note: εἴπερ γυνὴ σύ (_eiper gyne sy_, 'if you are a woman', l. 741). A hit at the sorest point, since being bested by a woman is the thing Creon cannot bear, and then at once the truth of the scene: σοῦ and προκήδομαι, 'it is you I am anxious for'. I believe him. The speech was not a lover's plea in disguise, and reading it that way is Creon's mistake and the Chorus's.

annotations.quote: O reprobate, would’st wrangle with thy sire?
annotations.note: διὰ δίκης ἰὼν (_dia dikes ion_, 'going to law with', l. 742) your father. Creon takes disagreement for litigation, a son suing his parent, which in Greek eyes is monstrous. The word _dike_, justice, has entered, and Haemon uses it against him in the next line.

annotations.quote: Because I see thee wrongfully perverse.
annotations.note: οὐ γὰρ δίκαιά (_ou gar dikaia_, 'not just', l. 743): I see you going wrong against justice. For the first time Haemon says in his own voice what he began by saying he could never say (l. 685). The verb for erring, here and in Creon's reply, gives the noun Creon will use of his own mistakes in his lament in [[s13]].

annotations.quote: And am I wrong, if I maintain my rights?
annotations.note: τὰς ἐμὰς ἀρχὰς σέβων (_tas emas archas sebon_, 'revering my own office', l. 744). The reverence verb again, with Creon's own authority as its object. Storr's 'rights' is too modern and too mild. Creon is describing a piety, and the god it is paid to is his position.

annotations.quote: Talk not of rights; thou spurn’st the due of Heaven
annotations.note: 'You do not revere, οὐ γὰρ σέβεις, when you trample the honours of the gods', τιμάς and πατῶν (l. 745). This is the first time Haemon makes the religious charge, forty lines after a speech that kept the gods out of it except as givers of sense. He has reached Antigone's position by a different road. The verb 'trample' is physical and is meant to be.

annotations.quote: O heart corrupt, a woman’s minion thou!
annotations.note: μιαρὸν ἦθος (_miaron ethos_, 'polluted character', l. 746). _Miaros_ belongs with _miasma_, religious defilement, and Creon throws it at his son as abuse. Thirty lines later he is taking careful steps to keep _miasma_ off the city (l. 776). The actual pollution, as Tiresias will report, comes from the corpse he left out, and it is on every altar in Thebes.

annotations.quote: Slave to dishonor thou wilt never find me.
annotations.note: ἥσσω (_hesso_, 'weaker than, beaten by', l. 747): you will not catch me giving in to what is shameful, τῶν αἰσχρῶν. He picks up his father's word from l. 680, 'weaker than women', and corrects its object. Being beaten by a woman is not a disgrace; giving in to a base act is.

annotations.quote: And thee and me, and for the gods below.
annotations.note: Creon says the whole speech was for her; Haemon adds three more clients, 'you, and me, and the gods below', θεῶν τῶν νερτέρων (l. 749). The phrase is the Chorus's from the ode (l. 601), where the nether gods' dust cut down the last root. It is an exact list of who is injured by what Creon is doing, in the order in which he will find it out last.

annotations.quote: Living the maid shall never be thy bride.
annotations.note: 'You shall never marry her while she still lives', ἔτι ζῶσαν (l. 750). Creon means it as a simple veto and builds the loophole himself. Haemon marries her dead: the Messenger in [[s13]] says he lies corpse embracing corpse, having won his marriage rites in Hades' house.

annotations.quote: So she shall die, but one will die with her.
annotations.note: The Greek is more open than Storr: θανοῦσʼ ὀλεῖ τινα (_thanous' olei tina_, 'in dying she will destroy someone', l. 751). Haemon means himself. Creon assumes he is being threatened, since by now he hears every sentence as an attack on his authority. He is not wholly wrong: in the tomb Haemon draws his sword on his father first, misses, and only then turns it on himself. The indefinite 'someone' covers both, and Sophocles surely chose it for that.

annotations.quote: What threat is this, vain counsels to reprove?
annotations.note: κενὰς γνώμας (_kenas gnomas_, 'empty judgments', l. 753). 'Empty' is Haemon's word from l. 709 for the man who thinks he alone has sense, now applied without disguise. At l. 635 he promised to follow his father's judgments, _gnomas_, provided they were good. This is the proviso being exercised.

annotations.quote: Vain fool to instruct thy betters; thou shall rue it.
annotations.note: Creon catches both words and throws them back: 'you will teach sense in tears, being yourself empty of sense', φρενώσεις and κενός (l. 754). The quarrel has shrunk to two men each telling the other he has no _phrenes_. The ode's proverb was that a god leads the wits of the doomed man towards ruin, and the audience is being invited to decide whose wits those are.

annotations.quote: Wert not my father, I had said thou err’st.
annotations.note: 'I would have said you are not in your right mind', οὐκ εὖ φρονεῖν (_ouk eu phronein_, l. 755). He says it by saying he will not. Set this beside l. 685, where he prayed never to know how to say such a thing, and you have the measure of how far the scene has travelled in seventy lines.

annotations.quote: Play not the spaniel, thou a woman’s slave.
annotations.note: δούλευμα (_douleuma_, 'slave-thing', l. 756) is a neuter abstract, a chattel and not a person, and κώτιλλέ (_kotille_) means to wheedle or chatter. Creon has now called his son an ally of a woman, lower than a woman, and a woman's property. Three times is a pattern: gender is where he goes whenever an argument has cornered him.

annotations.quote: When thou dost speak, must no man make reply?
annotations.note: 'Do you want to speak and, having spoken, hear nothing?', λέγειν and κλύειν (l. 757). It is the best short description of Creon in the play. 'Hearing' was what he required of the citizen (l. 666) and of sons, who should be 'listeners' (l. 642). Haemon's point is that the verb ought to work in both directions.

annotations.quote: Off with the hateful thing that she may die
annotations.note: Creon swears by Olympus (l. 758), the seat of the Zeus the Chorus has just hymned, and calls for Antigone as τὸ μῖσος (_to misos_, 'the hatred, the hateful thing', l. 760), another neuter. The order is given to attendants and is not carried out before Haemon leaves. Up to this line the scene has been an argument; this is a decision to hurt.

annotations.quote: At once, beside her bridegroom, in his sight.
annotations.note: κατʼ ὄμματʼ (_kat' ommat'_, 'before his eyes') and νυμφίῳ (_nymphioi_, 'bridegroom', ll. 760-761), the word spat out. The father proposes to kill the bride in front of the groom as a punishment for arguing. What happens is the mirror of it: the bridegroom dies beside the bride, before the father's eyes. Every cruelty Creon devises in this scene is returned to him with the roles changed.

annotations.quote: Or by my side; never shalt thou again
annotations.note: 'You will never look on my face with your eyes', προσόψει (l. 764). It sounds like a vow of exile or of suicide, and Haemon may not know which. It is also untrue, and the play needs it to be: Creon sees him once more, alive, in the tomb, where the son looks at him 'with wild eyes' and says nothing. These are the last words we hear Haemon speak.

annotations.quote: With friends who like a madman for their mate.
annotations.note: μαίνῃ (_mainei_, 'you rave, you are mad', l. 765): rave on, among such of your φίλων (_philon_) as can bear it. The scene opened with the father asking whether the son came raging (l. 633) and whether the two were still _philoi_ (l. 634). It closes with the son answering both. Haemon goes out by the side passage towards the country, not into the palace; the audience is given no idea where, and neither is Creon.

annotations.quote: Fell is the wrath of youth beneath a smart.
annotations.note: He has gone ἐξ ὀργῆς ταχύς (_ex orges tachys_, 'swift from anger', l. 766), and a mind so young, when hurt, is βαρύς (_barys_, 'heavy, dangerous', l. 767). _Orge_, temper, is the ode on man's word for the civic disposition and Creon's ruling fault. The elders see the danger clearly and say it. They said nothing useful while he was on stage, and the same pattern returns in [[s13]] with Eurydice, whose silent exit they also remark on too late.

annotations.quote: Let him go vent his fury like a fiend:
annotations.note: No fiend in the Greek: 'let him do it, let him go and think thoughts greater than befit a man', φρονείτω μεῖζον ἢ κατʼ ἄνδρʼ (l. 768). Thinking beyond mortal measure is the standard Greek description of the offence the gods punish. Creon diagnoses it in a son who asked him to listen to other people, and he is, at this moment, the play's chief case of it.

annotations.quote: These sisters twain he shall not save from death.
annotations.note: The Greek uses the dual number, τὼ and κόρα (_to kora_, 'the two girls', l. 769). Ismene, who did nothing, is still under sentence from [[s5]]. Creon has not thought about her since; she is simply included, as part of a pair.

annotations.quote: I stand corrected; only her who touched
annotations.note: One mild question from the Chorus and Ismene is reprieved: 'not the one who did not touch it', θιγοῦσαν, 'you are right', εὖ γὰρ οὖν λέγεις (l. 771). Two things follow. Her sentence was temper and nothing else. And Creon can be turned by a single line when it comes from old men and costs him nothing, which makes his deafness to Haemon a matter of who was speaking. It is the elders' one successful intervention before [[s11]], and they do not try a second.

annotations.quote: She shall be taken to some desert place
annotations.note: ἔρημος (_eremos_, 'deserted', l. 773), Haemon's word from l. 739 for the land Creon is fit to rule. The edict announced death by public stoning ([[s1]]). Why the change? Stoning needs the hands of the citizens, and Creon has just been told that the citizens are on her side. I think the new sentence is a silent admission that Haemon's report was true.

annotations.quote: By man untrod, and in a rock-hewn cave,
annotations.note: κρύψω and ζῶσαν (_krypso_, _zosan_, 'I will hide her, living', l. 774). The verb is the ordinary one for covering the dead with earth. So the decree that kept a dead man above ground ends by putting a living woman below it. Tiresias states the inversion to Creon's face in [[s11]], as the offence against both sets of gods.

annotations.quote: With food no more than to avoid the taint
annotations.note: The ration is a legal fiction: if she starves with food beside her, the city has not shed kindred blood. The Greek has two technical terms, ἄγος (_agos_, here 'what discharges the guilt', l. 775) and μίασμα (_miasma_, 'pollution', l. 776), which the whole city is to escape. Creon, who scoffed at the gods' interest in a corpse, turns out to be scrupulous about ritual when it protects him. The care is real and wholly misdirected: the pollution is already in the city, spreading from the unburied body.

annotations.quote: The King of Death, the one god she reveres,
annotations.note: 'Hades, whom alone of gods she reveres', μόνον σέβει θεῶν (l. 777). A taunt, and a false one: she appealed to Zeus and to Justice in [[s5]]. But it fixes how Creon sees the conflict, as his gods of the city against her god of the dead. The play will say that this division of the gods into parties is the mistake.

annotations.quote: ’Tis labor lost, to reverence the dead.
annotations.note: πόνος περισσός (_ponos perissos_, 'wasted, excessive labour', l. 780). _Perissos_ was Ismene's word in [[s1]] for the senselessness of doing too much. The scene's last word in Greek is σέβειν (_sebein_, 'to revere'), the verb the two men have fought over since l. 730. Creon expects Antigone to learn this lesson in the cave. He learns its opposite at the cave mouth.

links.why: The messenger's account of the cave is the last meeting of this father and son, and it answers every line of this quarrel.
The elders at once explain the scene as the work of Love, which is to hear it exactly as Creon did.
The ship of state that sounded statesmanlike there becomes 'the State is his who rules it' here.

s8.essay:
The shortest ode in the play, and the elders' quickest verdict. They have just listened to a young man argue, carefully and politically, that a ruler should heed his people, and what they conclude is that Love did it. Love is unbeatable, Love sends the wisest mad, Love 'didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin.' That is Creon's own reading of his son, a boy turned by a woman, set to music.

I think they are wrong about Haemon, who talked about justice and the city and never about desire. But the ode is truer than they intend. Something like love is behind every act in this story: Antigone's for a brother, which she called her nature; Haemon's, which he will prove in the only way left to him; even Creon's for the son he is about to lose. The elders name a god to dismiss a quarrel and name the engine of the play instead.

Then Antigone is brought out under guard and the song breaks off. 'Lo I myself am borne aside' is as close as these cautious men come to confessing that the sight of her undoes their loyalty to the edict. Storr has them swept 'from Justice'; the Greek is nearer to being carried outside the ordinances, past what they are allowed to feel. They weep. They still do nothing. And 'Death’s bower,' a bridal chamber, sets the figure for the scene that follows.

annotations.quote: Love resistless in fight,
annotations.note: Ἔρως ἀνίκατε μάχαν (_Eros anikate machan_, 'Eros, unconquered in battle', l. 781). The scene just ended was about winning: Creon would not be 'worsted' by a woman, and no one has given way. The Chorus now names the one combatant nobody beats. Ask what they are doing by singing this now. A girl has just been sentenced to be walled up alive, a son has left in despair, and the elders sing a hymn to desire. It lets them explain the quarrel without judging it.

annotations.quote: all yield at a glance of thine eye,
annotations.note: Storr's own line. The Greek says something odder: Eros 'who falls upon possessions', ἐν κτήμασι πίπτεις (l. 781), like a raider. _Ktemata_ was Haemon's word twice in [[s7]], for good sense as the best of possessions and for his father's welfare as his own. I hear the Chorus picking it up: love descends on what men own and value, and makes havoc of it.

annotations.quote: Love who pillowed all night on a maiden’s cheek dost lie,
annotations.note: The one soft picture in a hard ode: Eros who ἐννυχεύεις (_ennycheueis_, 'keep the night watch', l. 782) on the μαλακαῖς παρειαῖς (_malakais pareiais_, 'soft cheeks') of a girl. Even here the verb is a sentry's. The Greek names Eros, and later Aphrodite; Storr makes both 'Love'. The girl we are about to see has no such nights ahead of her.

annotations.quote: Over the upland holds. Shall mortals not yield to thee?
annotations.note: Storr drops half the range. Eros roams ὑπερπόντιος (_hyperpontios_, 'over the sea', l. 785) and among the dwellings of the wild country, and no immortal can escape him, nor any of mankind, the creatures of a day. Sea and wilderness are exactly the realms man was praised for mastering in the ode on man ([[s4]]). This song is its correction: there is a power abroad in both that has not been tamed, and the gods are subject to it as well.

annotations.quote: Mad are thy subjects all, and even the wisest heart
annotations.note: ὁ δʼ ἔχων μέμηνεν (_ho d' echon memenen_, 'he who has you is mad', l. 790). Haemon's parting word to his father was 'rave' (l. 765); the elders quietly hand the madness back to Haemon. And 'wisest' is wrong: the Greek says Eros wrenches aside the minds of the δικαίων (_dikaion_, 'the just') and makes them ἀδίκους (_adikous_, 'unjust', l. 791). That is a verdict. In their view a good son has been made to do wrong.

annotations.quote: Straight to folly will fall, at a touch of thy poisoned dart.
annotations.note: The dart belongs to a later Cupid. The Greek says the just are dragged aside ἐπὶ λώβᾳ (_epi lobai_, 'to their ruin, to their disgrace', l. 791), and the verb παρασπᾷς (_paraspais_) is to jerk a horse off its line. Here I part company with the Chorus. Haemon made a political argument and never mentioned love, and the city, by his account, agrees with him. Calling it Eros turns a case that needed answering into a fever that only needs explaining.

annotations.quote: Thou didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin,
annotations.note: νεῖκος ἀνδρῶν ξύναιμον (_neikos andron xynaimon_, 'this quarrel of men of one blood', l. 792). _Xynaimon_ is the epithet Creon sneered at when he told Antigone to go and chant to Zeus of kindred blood (ll. 658-659). And _neikos_, 'strife', is the word inside the name Polynices, a pun the entry song made in [[s2]]. The war of brothers is over and the same strife has moved one generation and one household along. The elders' diagnosis lets them avoid asking which of the two was right, a question they dodged a moment ago by saying both had spoken well.

annotations.quote: By the eyes of a winsome wife,
annotations.note: 'Victory goes to the desire that shines plain from the eyes of the bride', νικᾷ and ἵμερος (_nikai_, _himeros_, l. 795). 'Wins' answers 'unconquered' in the first line. The bride is νύμφας (_nymphas_, l. 796), and she is εὐλέκτρου (_eulektrou_), 'of the happy marriage-bed'. Nothing in the play has shown us Antigone as an object of desire, and she has not spoken Haemon's name. The elders supply a love story from the outside, and then she walks in.

annotations.quote: For as her consort still, enthroned with Justice above,
annotations.note: A notorious crux; the text is doubted. As it stands, desire sits πάρεδρος (_paredros_, 'seated beside', as an assessor sits beside a magistrate) in rule with the great θεσμῶν (_thesmon_, 'ordinances', ll. 796-800). Storr's 'Justice' stands for those ordinances. If the reading is right it is an astonishing claim: desire holds office alongside the fundamental laws. The play has had Creon's _nomos_ and Antigone's unwritten _nomima_, and the Chorus now seats a third power on the same bench.

annotations.quote: Thou bendest man to thy will, O all invincible Love.
annotations.note: The Greek names her: ἄμαχος γὰρ ἐμπαίζει θεὸς Ἀφροδίτα (_amachos gar empaizei theos Aphrodita_, 'for the goddess Aphrodite, not to be fought, has her sport', l. 800). Storr loses the name and, worse, the verb. _Empaizei_ is to play, to mock. The ode ends by saying that the catastrophe gathering over two houses is, from where the goddess sits, a game.

annotations.quote: Lo I myself am borne aside,
annotations.note: The metre changes to anapaests as Antigone is brought out under guard. The elders have sung that Eros drags the just off their course, and now 'I myself am carried outside the ordinances', θεσμῶν and ἔξω φέρομαι (ll. 801-802), by pity. Which ordinances? I take them to be the loyalty they owe the king. It is their most honest line so far, and it changes nothing they do.

annotations.quote: (O sight an eye in tears to drown)
annotations.note: They can no longer hold back the πηγὰς (_pegas_, 'springs', l. 803) of their tears. Mark who is weeping: the men who told Creon his speech was sensible and who have just set the girl's rescue down to a young man's lust. The tears are real. They are also the cheapest thing the elders have to give, and they give nothing else until Tiresias has frightened them.

annotations.quote: Death’s bower with the dead to share.
annotations.note: τὸν παγκοίτην and θάλαμον (_ton pankoiten thalamon_, 'the chamber where all are laid to sleep', l. 804). A _thalamos_ is a bedroom, above all the bridal chamber, and Storr's 'bower' keeps that. So the hymn to Eros ends by handing its bride to death, and the image Creon coined as a sneer ('let her marry someone in Hades') is now the Chorus's pity. Antigone takes it over herself in [[s9]], where her whole lament is the lament of a bride.

links.why: This ode is the elders' reading of the quarrel just ended, and it is worth checking against what Haemon actually said.
The bridal chamber of Death, named in the ode's last line, becomes Antigone's own refrain.

s9.essay:
The woman who told Creon that death was gain now turns for 'one last fond, lingering, longing look' at the sun. I do not think this is inconsistency, and it is not Sophocles weakening her. It is the difference between defying a death sentence and walking to the place. For the first time she is not arguing with anyone, and what comes out is grief for an ordinary life: no wedding song, no flowers on the bed, no children. She never names Haemon, here or anywhere. What she mourns is marriage itself, the thing every girl in her city was raised to expect, and she sings of it in the lyric metres of a lament. She is conducting her own funeral because nobody else will.

The elders are worse than useless. They tell her she goes 'great and glorious,' that no disease has wasted her, that she alone descends alive. The Greek behind 'freely' is the word that gives us autonomous: she goes by her own law. It is meant as a tribute and she hears it as a taunt. 'Ye mock me.' When she reaches for Niobe, the grieving queen turned to weeping stone, they correct her: Niobe was a goddess and you are not. Then they return to her father, and to their real position: piety is all very well, but power is power, and she was 'a self-willed rebel.' These are the citizens Haemon said were on her side. They are, and this is what their sympathy is worth.

Creon comes in to hurry things, and his speech is a small masterpiece of hand-washing. She is to be left 'at liberty to die, / Or, if she choose, to live in solitude.' 'We in either case / Are guiltless.' He has persuaded himself that walling a girl in a cave is not killing her. Set this beside her 'Guilty. I did it, I deny it not' in [[s5]]. She owned her act in a single line before the whole city. He, with all the power, arranges his so that it will have no author. Of the two, she is the one behaving like a ruler.

Then comes her last speech, and the passage that has embarrassed admirers for two centuries. She says she would not have done this for a husband or a child. A husband can be replaced, another child can be born, but with both parents dead 'no second brother can be born for me.' Goethe wished some scholar would prove the lines spurious. They echo a story in Herodotus about a Persian woman allowed to save one relative. But Aristotle quotes them, so they were in the play he knew, and I have come round to keeping them.

My reason is this. The argument is bad; it is a sum, and it shrinks the 'unwritten laws of Heaven' to a rule about one kind of kinship. But look at where she is. Everyone has left her, the elders have just called her a rebel, and no god has given any sign. She reaches for a reason that might convince the people in front of her and comes up with a borrowed, clumsy one. People do this. And clumsy as it is, it tells the truth she told in the first scene, before the fine language: 'What right has he to keep me from my own?' It was always this brother. Storr softens it by calling her rule 'the law of conscience'; as far as I can tell the Greek says only 'such a law,' and conscience is his century's word, not hers.

What I find hardest is what follows. 'What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed?' She does not know. If the gods approve of this, she says, she will learn her sin by suffering; if the sin is Creon's, let him suffer no more than she has. She goes into the rock without her answer. It arrives in [[s11]], spoken to someone else, after she is past hearing it. That is why I call her brave and not merely certain.

annotations.quote: Friends, countrymen, my last farewell I make;
annotations.note: This is a kommos, a lament sung between an actor and the Chorus, and it is the first time Antigone sings. Storr's 'Friends, countrymen' is warmer than the Greek, where she calls them πολῖται (_politai_, "citizens", l. 806) of her father's land and her first word is _horate_, "look at me". The woman who has spoken all play of family and the dead now addresses the city and asks it to watch. Her last words in the scene will be the same demand: λεύσσετε (_leussete_, "look", l. 940).

annotations.quote: One last fond, lingering, longing look I take
annotations.note: Storr piles three adjectives where the Greek is spare: νεάταν ὁδὸν (_neatan hodon_, "the last road", l. 806) and then νέατον (_neaton_, "last") again for the sunlight, the same word twice. For once the Victorian excess seems right to me in spirit. This is the woman who told Ismene in [[s1]] that death would be a fine thing and told Creon in [[s5]] that it would be a gain, and she cannot take her eyes off the day. I do not think that is inconsistency. The courage was real, and so is the cost, which she is counting only now that nobody can call it a retreat.

annotations.quote: For Death who puts to sleep both young and old
annotations.note: The Greek has one compound, παγκοίτας (_pankoitas_, "who lays all to bed", l. 810), an epithet of Hades. The Chorus has just used it of her destination at the close of [[s8]], calling it the bridal chamber "where all are laid to rest", so she is picking up their word. Storr's 'puts to sleep' keeps the gentleness but loses the bed, and the bed matters: the whole scene turns on the confusion of marriage bed and grave.

annotations.quote: And beckons me to Acheron’s dark fold,
annotations.note: 'Beckons' is far too mild. The Greek is ζῶσαν ἄγει (_zosan agei_, "leads me, living", l. 810): Hades is taking her alive, and _agein_ is the ordinary verb for a bridegroom leading his bride home. Watch that verb through the scene. Hades leads her here, Creon is its subject at l. 916, and her last cry at l. 939 is ἄγομαι (_agomai_, "I am being led"). By then the bridegroom and the king have become one figure.

annotations.quote: No youths have sung the marriage song for me,
annotations.note: An Athenian wedding and an Athenian funeral looked alike: a procession by torchlight, a song, a washed and adorned body, a journey to a new house. A girl who died unmarried was said to have married Hades, as Persephone did. Antigone works through the list of what she has been denied (the hymn at the door, the hymn at the bed) and finds that the other ceremony supplies every item. Remember that she has a bridegroom, and that Haemon will be found with his arms round her in that chamber in [[s13]].

annotations.quote: ’Tis Death I wed.
annotations.note: The Greek is blunter and stranger: Ἀχέροντι νυμφεύσω (_Acheronti nympheuso_, "I shall be bride to Acheron", l. 815). Her husband is a river in the underworld. Storr's 'Death' turns it into an abstraction, and the earlier 'unwed wife' is his own paradox, not hers. Notice that Haemon's name does not occur anywhere in this scene. Whatever the Chorus sang about Eros in [[s8]], she laments marriage and children as a state she has lost, never a particular man.

annotations.quote: Great and glorious, to the dead.
annotations.note: κλεινὴ (_kleine_, "famous", l. 817) and ἔπαινον (_epainon_, "praise") are the elders' answer to her grief. It is the consolation one offers a warrior, and they have nothing else to offer. Is it kind? I think it is meant kindly and is tone-deaf. She asked to be looked at and pitied, and they tell her she will be well spoken of. It is also the first time these men have conceded in public that what she did is praiseworthy, which bears out Haemon's report in [[s7]] of what the city says under its breath.

annotations.quote: Thou the sword’s edge hast not tasted,
annotations.note: The elders reckon the ways people usually die, wasting sickness and what they grimly call the wages of swords, and observe that she has avoided both. It is the reasoning of old men who have seen many deaths. To a young woman about to be walled up it can only sound like being told she is lucky.

annotations.quote: Freely thou alone shalt go
annotations.note: Storr's 'freely' stands for the most discussed word in the scene: αὐτόνομος (_autonomos_, "living by one's own law", l. 821). It is a political term, used of cities that keep their own laws, and so far as I know this is its earliest surviving application to a person. A _nomos_ of her own is exactly what Creon accused her of setting against the city's. Do the elders intend praise or blame? I think the word is honestly double: of her own free choice and a law unto herself. Our 'autonomy' descends from it, and has lost the warning.

annotations.quote: Living to the dead below.
annotations.note: The Greek stresses that she is unique: μόνη (_mone_, "alone", l. 821) of mortals she will go down to Hades alive. The elders offer this as her distinction. It is in fact the horror of the sentence, since she will be neither buried nor alive. Creon has left one corpse above ground and is sending one living body under it, and that inversion is precisely the charge Teiresias will bring against him in [[s11]].

annotations.quote: Nay, but the piteous tale I’ve heard men tell
annotations.note: She does not answer the consolation at all. Offered glory, she reaches for a precedent of her own choosing, and it is the saddest one she knows: the superlative _lygrotatan_, "most wretched", is the first thing she says about it. A tutor's question: why does she want a mythical parallel at this moment? I think because nobody on stage will mourn her, and a myth is company.

annotations.quote: Of Tantalus’ doomed child,
annotations.note: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, boasted that her children outnumbered Leto's, lost them all to Apollo and Artemis, and turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, still weeping. Antigone calls her τὰν Φρυγίαν ξέναν (_tan Phrygian xenan_, "the Phrygian stranger", l. 823), which Storr drops. Niobe came to Thebes as a foreign bride, the wife of Amphion, so the comparison is local and it introduces the idea of the outsider that Antigone will shortly turn on herself. It is an odd choice all the same: the woman who will have no children picks the great bereaved mother, and a woman punished for a boast.

annotations.quote: That clung like ivy wild,
annotations.note: Storr has the simile backwards. In the Greek the stone is the ivy: κισσὸς (_kissos_, "ivy", l. 825) is what the growth of rock is compared to, and the verb is δάμασεν (_damasen_, "subdued", l. 826). The rock crept over Niobe and overpowered her as ivy overpowers a wall. _Damazein_ is also used for breaking in an animal and for taking a wife, so the stone is one more bridegroom.

annotations.quote: While on her frozen breast the tears aye flow—
annotations.note: The participle for Niobe is τακομέναν (_takomenan_, "melting, wasting away", l. 826): rain and snow never leave her and she dissolves in tears while remaining stone. Keep the verb in mind. It returns for the husband who might have "wasted" in death at l. 906 and for the blinded sons in the next ode. What Antigone envies in Niobe, I think, is that her grief is permanent and visible, a monument that weeps. Her own tomb will be sealed and seen by no one.

annotations.quote: Her fate is mine.
annotations.note: The Greek is more exact: a δαίμων (_daimon_, "divine power", l. 831) is putting her to bed, κατευνάζει (_kateunazei_), "most like" Niobe. The bed again. And she says a god is doing it. She does not say Creon, and this is the first moment in the play where she attributes her end to something larger than one man's decree.

annotations.quote: She was sprung of gods, divine,
annotations.note: The rebuke. θεός (_theos_, "a god", l. 834) and θεογεννής (_theogennes_, "god-born") are set against βροτοὶ (_brotoi_, "mortals", l. 835) and _thnetogeneis_, "mortal-born". Strictly Niobe was no goddess, only a granddaughter of Zeus, so the elders overstate their case to make it. It is a pedant's correction delivered to a girl on the way to her death. But see what they hear in her comparison: a claim to rank with the divine. Niobe was destroyed for exactly that, so the correction carries a warning too.

annotations.quote: Like renown with gods to gain
annotations.note: Having corrected her, they try to give the comparison back as a compliment. It is a great thing, they say, for one who has perished even to be said to share the lot of the ἰσοθέοις (_isotheois_, "the godlike", l. 837). σύγκληρα (_synklera_, "sharing an allotment") answers the word she used when she said she had no share in wedding songs. Their only currency is still reputation. Storr's 'recompenses all thy pain' promises more than the Greek, which says only that it is no small thing to hear.

annotations.quote: Hers in life and death thy doom.
annotations.note: So does the Chorus console or mock? I take them to be sincere and inept. They are old men who admire fame, fear power and believe in limits, and every consolation they offer is true by their lights. What they will not do is the one thing she came out for, which is to weep for her and say she was wronged. They did weep, at the end of [[s8]], before she spoke. Once she claims a likeness to Niobe they begin to judge, and judgment is all she gets from them until she is gone.

annotations.quote: Alack, alack! Ye mock me. Is it meet
annotations.note: 'Meet' means fitting. Her word is γελῶμαι (_gelomai_, "I am laughed at", l. 839), the thing a Sophoclean hero can least endure, and she follows it with ὑβρίζεις (_hybrizeis_, "you outrage me", l. 840). Both words have been used before, against her: in [[s5]] Creon said her _hybris_ was doubled because she laughed over what she had done. She now turns his two charges on the elders. And she adds ἐπίφαντον (_epiphanton_, "still in plain view"): could you not have waited until I was gone?

annotations.quote: Ye lordly rulers of a lordly race.
annotations.note: The Greek is ὦ πόλις (_o polis_, "O city", l. 841) and then πολυκτήμονες ἄνδρες (_polyktemones andres_, "men of many possessions"). Storr's 'lordly' hides the edge. She is addressing the propertied men of Thebes, the people with something to lose, and that is a diagnosis of why they have not spoken up. Note _andres_ too: in this play the word 'men' is seldom neutral.

annotations.quote: O fount of Dirce, wood-embowered plain
annotations.note: Since the citizens will not be her witnesses she appoints the landscape: she takes the springs of Dirce and the grove of Thebes as ξυμμάρτυρας (_xymmartyras_, "fellow witnesses", l. 845). These are the places the Chorus sang of in the victory ode of [[s2]], Dirce's streams and Thebes of the many chariots. She is claiming the city of that song, the physical and ancestral Thebes, over the heads of the men who now speak for it.

annotations.quote: the cruel laws that now have wrought my bane,
annotations.note: 'Cruel' is Storr's. The Greek is the exclamation οἵοις νόμοις (_hoiois nomois_, "by what sort of laws", l. 846), and the contempt is in the pronoun. This is the play's contest over _nomos_ in two words. In [[s5]] she set the gods' unwritten _nomima_ above a mortal's proclamation, and she has not moved: Creon's decree is called a law only with a sneer. She also calls the tomb a grave of a new and unheard-of kind, which is fair, since Creon invented the punishment in [[s7]].

annotations.quote: The friends who show no pity in my need!
annotations.note: φίλων ἄκλαυτος (_philon aklautos_, "unwept by friends", l. 846). _Philoi_ are one's own people, kin first, and the word has carried her whole case since [[s1]]. Is the complaint true? Ismene offered to die with her and was refused, and Haemon has just broken with his father for her sake. She seems not to know about Haemon, and she has cut Ismene out of the family. Her isolation is real, but she built some of it herself.

annotations.quote: And alien midst the living and the dead.
annotations.note: The word is μέτοικος (_metoikos_, l. 851), the Athenian term for a resident foreigner, someone who lives in a city without belonging to it. She will be a metic everywhere, housed with neither the living nor the dead. Every Athenian in the theatre knew exactly what status that was. She uses it again at l. 867, and Creon picks it up coldly at l. 890. It also answers her own 'Phrygian stranger': Niobe was a foreigner in Thebes, and Antigone will be one in both worlds.

annotations.quote: In thy boldness over-rash
annotations.note: From here the Chorus sings in lyric with her and its tone hardens from consolation to verdict. You went, they say, to the furthest edge of θράσους (_thrasous_, "daring, rashness", l. 853). _Thrasos_ is courage seen from the disapproving side. They still call her τέκνον (_teknon_, "child", l. 855), which Storr omits, and the tenderness of that word laid over the severity of the judgment is the Chorus's whole position.

annotations.quote: ’Gainst high Justice’ altar stair.
annotations.note: Δίκας βάθρον (_Dikas bathron_, "the pedestal of Justice", l. 854), with the verb προσέπεσες (_prosepeses_, l. 855). The verb can mean you fell against it, like someone stumbling, or you fell before it, like a suppliant, and some readers have wanted the second so as to make the elders kinder. I think collision is meant. But ask which Justice. In [[s5]] Antigone claimed the _Dike_ who lives with the gods below as her authority, and the elders now tell her she has run into the very power she invoked.

annotations.quote: Thou a father’s guild dost bear.
annotations.note: 'Guild' is a misprint for 'guilt'. The Greek is vaguer than Storr: πατρῷον (_patroion_, "of your father, ancestral", l. 856) and ἆθλον (_athlon_, "ordeal, contest"), which she is paying out in full. This is the explanation the elders gave in [[s6]], the ruin that runs down the house of Labdacus, now said to her face. It lets them hold two views at once: she chose this, and it was laid on her. It also spares them from having to say anything about Creon.

annotations.quote: At this thou touchest my most poignant pain,
annotations.note: ἔψαυσας (_epsausas_, "you have touched", l. 858) the sorest of her μερίμνας (_merimnas_, "cares"). She does not dispute the diagnosis. The lament for her father she calls τριπόλιστον (_tripoliston_, l. 859), thrice-ploughed, turned over and over like a field. In a family whose disaster was a son sowing where he was sown, and after Creon's remark in [[s5]] that there are other fields for Haemon to plough, the farming metaphor is hard to hear as innocent.

annotations.quote: Woe worth the monstrous marriage-bed where lay
annotations.note: The first word of her cry over the marriage bed is ἆται (_atai_, "ruins, delusions", l. 865). _Ate_ was the refrain of [[s6]], the ruin a god sends on a house, and here she accepts the Chorus's own term for her family. The union she calls by a word built on _auto-_ (_autogenneta_, "self-engendered"): a mother lying with a son she bore herself. This play is full of _auto-_ compounds for the family folded in on itself, from the _autadelphos_ of the first line onward. Her lament for the marriage she will not have runs straight back to the marriage that produced her.

annotations.quote: To meet them as an alien there below;
annotations.note: μέτοικος (_metoikos_, l. 867) again, and this time it contradicts everything she has said. From [[s1]] on, the dead of her family were the people she belonged with, and she would lie beside them as a loved one. Now she expects to be a resident alien even there, ἀραῖος ἄγαμος (_araios agamos_, "accursed, unmarried"). I take this as the lowest point of her confidence. It should be weighed against the hope she voices at l. 897: she holds both.

annotations.quote: And thee, O brother, in marriage ill-bestead,
annotations.note: The brother is Polyneices and the marriage is his to Argeia, daughter of Adrastus of Argos, the alliance that gave him an army to bring against Thebes. So there are three ruinous marriages in this stanza: her parents', her brother's, and her own to Acheron. In this family marriage is how catastrophe travels.

annotations.quote: ’Twas thy dead hand that dealt me this death-blow.
annotations.note: The Greek sets the two participles against each other: dead, you killed me while I still lived, with the heavy epic verb κατήναρές (_katenares_, "you slew", l. 871), a word for killing in battle. She has not said anything like this before. In [[s5]] the burial was a glory and a duty, and here, for one line, it is something her brother did to her. It is not regret, since she never wishes it undone. It is the first admission that the dead take as well as receive, and the play ends with Creon as a living man destroyed by his dead.

annotations.quote: Religion has her chains, ’tis true,
annotations.note: σέβειν (_sebein_, "to show reverence", l. 872) is εὐσέβειά τις (_eusebeia tis_, "a kind of piety"). The little word _tis_ is grudging: reverence of your sort is piety of a sort. Still, this is the Chorus conceding in so many words that what she did was _eusebeia_, the virtue she will claim with her last breath. Storr's 'chains' is his own invention and makes the concession sound like a complaint against religion, which it is not.

annotations.quote: The powers who hold by might the sway.
annotations.note: κράτος (_kratos_, "power", l. 873) twice in a line: for the man whose business power is, power is παραβατὸν (_parabaton_, "to be transgressed", l. 874) in no way at all. Read it carefully. The elders do not say Creon is right. They say power does not tolerate being crossed, which is an observation about power, and for a moral judgment it is close to an evasion. One line for piety, two for power: that ratio is as exact a statement of the Chorus's position as the play gives.

annotations.quote: A self-willed rebel, thou must die.
annotations.note: The Greek has no 'rebel' and no 'must die'. It says your αὐτόγνωτος (_autognotos_, "self-determined", l. 875) ὀργά (_orga_, "temper") destroyed you. _Autognotos_ is the partner of _autonomos_ fifty lines earlier, a temper that takes counsel only of itself, and the ambiguity of that word is now settled on the side of blame. _Orge_ is no less Creon's passion: in [[s3]] he warns these same elders to stop before they fill him with it. And the tense is past. They speak of her as already destroyed.

annotations.quote: Unwept, unwed, unfriended, hence I go,
annotations.note: She answers nothing. Three privatives stand in a row: ἄκλαυτος, ἄφιλος, ἀνυμέναιος (_aklautos, aphilos, anymenaios_, "unwept, friendless, without wedding song", l. 876). Storr keeps the hammering and shuffles the order. Then ἄγομαι (_agomai_, "I am led"), the bride's verb in the passive. The dialogue with the Chorus is over, and I think she has stopped expecting anything from them.

annotations.quote: No longer may I see the day’s bright eye;
annotations.note: The sun is the ἱερὸν ὄμμα (_hieron omma_, "sacred eye", l. 878) of the torch of day, and the word Storr renders 'may' is θέμις (_themis_, "what is right, what is sanctioned", l. 880). It is no longer _themis_ for her to look at the light. That is a bitter use of a religious word by someone who holds that everything she did was sanctioned. The Chorus greeted this same sun in [[s2]] as the eye of golden day rising on a rescued Thebes.

annotations.quote: Not one friend left to share my bitter woe,
annotations.note: οὐδεὶς φίλων (_oudeis philon_, "none of my own", l. 882) groans for a fate that is ἀδάκρυτον (_adakryton_, "untearful", l. 881). This is exactly the state she refused to leave Polyneices in. In [[s1]] the edict's cruelty was that he should lie unwept and unburied, and by curing that she has taken it on herself. She gave her brother a mourner and has none.

annotations.quote: If wail and lamentation aught availed
annotations.note: Creon cuts in with spoken verse after seventy lines of song, and the drop in register is the point. Whether he has stood there throughout or comes back on now is disputed, and I prefer to imagine him present and silent, so that the elders' deference to power is performed under his eye. His opening is a sneer in the form of a proverb: nobody would ever stop his ἀοιδὰς καὶ γόους (_aoidas kai goous_, "songs and wailings", l. 883) before death if it were allowed. He treats mourning as a delaying tactic, as he has all along.

annotations.quote: Leave her alone at liberty to die,
annotations.note: The Greek is ἄφετε μόνην ἔρημον (_aphete monen eremon_, "leave her alone, deserted", l. 887), whether she wishes to die or to go on living entombed. Storr's 'at liberty' is his, but it catches the grotesque tone. Creon is arranging matters so that her death will look like her own choice. In the event she takes him at his word and hangs herself, and that act, which he thinks keeps his hands clean, is what kills his son.

annotations.quote: Are guiltless as concerns this maiden’s blood,
annotations.note: ἁγνοὶ (_hagnoi_, "pure", l. 889) is a ritual term: free of _miasma_, the pollution of bloodshed. This is why she is walled up with a little food and not stoned as the edict first threatened. Leave a kinswoman to starve and technically no one has killed her. It is a legalism addressed to the gods by a man who scoffed in [[s3]] at the idea that the gods could care for this corpse. Teiresias will tell him in [[s11]] that the city's altars are polluted because of him. And he calls her κόρην (_koren_, "girl"). He does not address her once in this scene.

annotations.quote: Only on earth no lodging shall she find.
annotations.note: He has been listening. She called herself a _metoikos_ twice, and he answers that she will be deprived of her μετοικίας (_metoikias_, "residence as an alien", l. 890) up here. He takes her bitterest word and makes it administrative: her permit to stay is withdrawn. It also concedes something he may not notice, that she was never more than a lodger in his Thebes.

annotations.quote: O grave, O bridal bower, O prison house
annotations.note: The speech opens with a triple address: τύμβος (_tymbos_, "tomb", l. 891), νυμφεῖον (_nympheion_, "bridal chamber"), and a dwelling that is κατασκαφὴς (_kataskaphes_, "dug deep") and ἀείφρουρος (_aeiphrouros_, "keeping watch for ever", l. 892). Tomb, bride's room and guardhouse are one place. She has stopped singing and now speaks in the iambics of argument. That change matters for what follows: this is a speech of reasons, addressed to the dead, not a continuation of the lament.

annotations.quote: Of kinsfolk, Persephassa’s guests long dead,
annotations.note: Persephassa is Persephone, the girl Hades carried off to be his bride, so the hostess of this house is the pattern for Antigone's own fate. She says she is going πρὸς τοὺς ἐμαυτῆς (_pros tous emautes_, "to my own", l. 893). And she calls herself λοισθία (_loisthia_, "the last", l. 895) of them, which leaves no room for Ismene.

annotations.quote: And yet good hope is mine that I shall find
annotations.note: Against the fear of being an alien among the dead she sets a hope, and the Greek says she nurses it: ἐλπίσιν (_elpisin_, "hopes", l. 897) with the verb for feeding. She will come φίλη (_phile_, "dear", l. 898) to her father, προσφιλὴς (_prosphiles_) to her mother, φίλη again to her brother. This returns to her promise in [[s1]] that she would lie with Polyneices, dear with one who is dear. The order is father, mother, brother, the family she was born into. No husband, and nothing about Thebes.

annotations.quote: From with these hands, I laved and decked your limbs
annotations.note: 'From' is a misprint for 'For'. The word is αὐτόχειρ (_autocheir_, "with my own hand", l. 900): she washed, dressed and poured χοὰς (_choas_, "libations", l. 902) for father, mother and brother. That brother, addressed as κασίγνητον κάρα (_kasigneton kara_, "brother's dear head", l. 899), must be Eteocles, since Polyneices is named next. It is the idiom of the play's first line, where Ismene was a dear sister's head. _Autocheir_ will come back in [[s13]] for people who die by their own hands.

annotations.quote: I paid due rites, and this my recompense!
annotations.note: The verb is ἄρνυμαι (_arnymai_, "I win, I earn", l. 903), the word for carrying off a prize or a wage. For tending your body, Polyneices, such are my winnings. The play's long argument about _kerdos_, gain, lies behind it: Creon thinks everyone acts for profit, and in [[s5]] she called an early death a gain. Here she audits the account and the tone is not triumphant.

annotations.quote: Yet am I justified in wisdom’s eyes.
annotations.note: Here begins the most disputed passage in Sophocles, ll. 904 to 920. The line says she honoured him rightly in the eyes of τοῖς φρονοῦσιν εὖ (_tois phronousin eu_, "those who think well", l. 904). _Phronein_ is the play's contested word: Creon, Haemon and Teiresias each claim good sense and the last lines of the play award it to nobody on stage. She appeals over the heads of the Chorus, who have just denied her that quality, to a jury of the right-minded who are not present. The cautious reading is that everything from here to 'a living grave' may be an actor's addition. I do not think it is.

annotations.quote: For even had it been some child of mine,
annotations.note: The case against. In [[s5]] she appealed to laws of the gods that bind everyone and say the dead must be buried. Here she says she would not have done it for a husband or a child, which seems to shrink a principle into a preference. The argument is lifted from Herodotus, where the wife of Intaphernes, allowed by Darius to save one condemned relative, chooses her brother because a husband and children can be replaced. There it makes sense, because she is choosing whom to keep alive. Antigone's brother is already dead. Goethe told Eckermann he wished some scholar would prove the lines spurious, and Jebb bracketed them.

annotations.quote: I had not wrought this deed despite the State.
annotations.note: βίᾳ πολιτῶν (_biai politon_, "in defiance of the citizens", l. 907). This is Ismene's phrase from [[s1]], where she said she was not made to act in defiance of the citizens. It is a startling thing for Antigone to say, because in [[s5]] she insisted the citizens agreed with her and were only gagged by fear. Those who reject the passage count this as a further inconsistency. I read it as what the last hundred lines have taught her. The citizens were on stage, and they told her that her own temper destroyed her.

annotations.quote: What is the law I call in aid? ’Tis thus
annotations.note: She calls her reasoning a νόμου (_nomou_, "law", l. 908): in deference to what _nomos_ do I say this? So the _nomos_ she set against Creon's turns out, when spelled out, to be a rule about the irreplaceable. The husband who might have died is imagined with the verb ἐτήκετο (_eteketo_, "was wasting away", l. 906), Niobe's verb, used here of a corpse rotting as her brother's has been. The syntax of the next lines is awkward, and that awkwardness is one of the editors' complaints.

annotations.quote: No second brother can be born for me.
annotations.note: The case for. Aristotle quotes these lines in the Rhetoric as from the Antigone, to show how a speaker should give a reason when a claim sounds incredible, so the passage stood in the text within a century of Sophocles' death. Sophocles and Herodotus were contemporaries and by ancient report acquainted, and a borrowed story is not evidence of a second hand. Most recent editors keep the lines. And as a statement of fact about this house, with father, mother and both brothers dead, the line is simply how alone she is.

annotations.quote: Thus by the law of conscience I was led
annotations.note: 'Conscience' is Storr importing a Christian faculty. The Greek says only that she honoured him above all by such a νόμῳ (_nomoi_, "law", l. 914). My own view is that the passage is Sophocles' and that it tells the truth about her. She never buried a stranger. Her great speech in [[s5]] was made about a brother, and from her first line her loyalty has been to those of the same womb. What embarrasses readers is finding that the heroine of universal law was moved by a particular love. But a twenty-line cut would also heal rather neatly, from 'this my recompense' to 'what ordinance of heaven', so I hold the view without certainty.

annotations.quote: By Creon guilty of a heinous crime.
annotations.note: δεινὰ τολμᾶν (_deina tolman_, "to dare terrible things", l. 915). Both words come from the ode on man in [[s4]], where man is the most _deinon_ of creatures and the one who consorts with wrong for the sake of daring is to be cast out of the city. She puts the judgment in Creon's mouth and the vocabulary fits her exactly. Whether the ode was about her, about him, or about both is a question the play does not let you close.

annotations.quote: A bride unwed, amerced of marriage-song
annotations.note: 'Amerced' means fined, deprived. ἄλεκτρον, ἀνυμέναιον (_alektron, anymenaion_, "without marriage bed, without wedding song", l. 917) repeats the privatives of the lyric in plain speech, and she adds the rearing of a child, the only place she says she wanted one. That gives the replaceable-husband argument a sting people overlook. The woman who has just reasoned that husbands and children can be had again is counting them among what she has lost, a few lines later. That is not coldness. It is someone pricing what she paid.

annotations.quote: By friends deserted to a living grave.
annotations.note: ἔρημος πρὸς φίλων (_eremos pros philon_, "deserted by friends", l. 919) takes up the very word Creon used a moment ago when he ordered her left alone and deserted. And she goes living to the κατασκαφάς (_kataskaphas_, "dug-out chambers", l. 920) of the dead, the noun of the adjective that opened the speech. The disputed passage ends by closing the ring with the speech's first line, which is neat workmanship for an interpolator.

annotations.quote: What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed?
annotations.note: δαιμόνων δίκην (_daimonon diken_, "justice of the gods", l. 921). The Chorus told her she had crashed against the pedestal of Justice, and this is her reply, delayed by sixty lines. She asks it as a real question. In [[s5]] she knew what the gods' justice required. Now the gods have let her be led away, and she asks which of their laws she can have broken.

annotations.quote: Hereafter can I look to any god
annotations.note: Why should she still look to the gods, and which of them can she call as ξυμμάχων (_xymmachon_, "allies", l. 923)? The word is military: someone who fights at your side. No god does. This is the loneliest moment in the play and Sophocles does not soften it. The vindication comes, through Teiresias in [[s11]], but only after she has left the stage, and she dies without knowing she was right.

annotations.quote: Alas, my piety is impious deemed.
annotations.note: The Greek is harsher than 'deemed': by being pious, εὐσεβοῦσʼ (_eusebousa_), she has acquired δυσσέβειαν (_dyssebeian_, "impiety", l. 924), and the verb ἐκτησάμην (_ektesamen_) means got as a possession. Compare the 'sinless sinner' of [[s1]], her boast that she would commit a holy crime. Then she owned the crime and gloried in the holiness. Now the paradox is turned inside out and spoken without defiance: she has only the verdict.

annotations.quote: I shall be taught by suffering my sin;
annotations.note: If this is καλά (_kala_, "fine, right", l. 925) in the gods' eyes, then παθόντες (_pathontes_, "having suffered", l. 926) she would come to acknowledge, ξυγγνοῖμεν (_xyngnoimen_), that she has erred. It is the old idea of learning through suffering, and it is her one conditional admission that she might be wrong. Set it beside Creon, who in [[s13]] says he has learned, too late. She entertains the possibility before she is forced to. He never did.

annotations.quote: No worse ills than the wrongs they do to me.
annotations.note: It sounds like moderation and it is a curse: may they suffer no more than they are doing to me ἐκδίκως (_ekdikos_, "outside justice", l. 928). The verb for their error, ἁμαρτάνουσι (_hamartanousi_, l. 927), is the one Creon's judgment applied to her at l. 914. What they are doing to her is burying a living person among the dead, cut off from everyone she loves. Measure for measure, that is what Creon gets: by the end of [[s13]] the messenger calls him a breathing corpse. The prayer is granted exactly.

annotations.quote: Drives like a gale the maiden still.
annotations.note: The same ψυχῆς ῥιπαὶ (_psyches rhipai_, "gusts of the soul", l. 930) of the same ἀνέμων (_anemon_, "winds", l. 929) still hold her. That is the elders' whole response to forty lines of reasoning, doubt and prayer. They heard the curse at the end and nothing else. The storm comes from their own ode in [[s6]], where the ruin of the house was a swell driven by Thracian winds, and the north wind himself appears in the song they sing next.

annotations.quote: Shall smart full sore for their delay.
annotations.note: Creon's last words in her presence are a threat to the guards for βραδυτῆτος (_bradytetos_, "slowness", l. 932). He has not answered one thing she said, and in the whole scene he never speaks to her, only about her. His impatience is worth marking, because haste is his fault throughout: he is in a hurry to be rid of her now, and at the end of [[s11]] he will be in a hurry to undo it, and will get the order of his errands wrong.

annotations.quote: Brings death most near.
annotations.note: The manuscripts give this cry to Antigone and I see no reason to move it, though some editors have assigned it to the Chorus. If it is hers, it is the only moment in the play where the fact of death reaches her as fear, with no argument round it. It lasts two lines.

annotations.quote: I have no comfort. What he saith,
