annotations.note: The speaker is disputed. Storr gives the couplet to the Chorus, and many editors give it to Creon: I offer you no encouragement to hope the sentence will not be carried out. The verb παραμυθοῦμαι (_paramythoumai_, "I console, I encourage", l. 935) suits either. In Creon's mouth it is a last turn of the knife. In the elders' mouths it is an honest confession that they have nothing left to say, and after the consolations of this scene I find that the more telling reading.

annotations.quote: My fatherland, city of Thebes divine,
annotations.note: She began the scene by addressing the citizens and ends by addressing the city itself, ἄστυ πατρῷον (_asty patroion_, "town of my fathers", l. 937), and the θεοὶ προγενεῖς (_theoi progeneis_, "ancestral gods", l. 938). The Theban royal house descends from gods, so these are literally her forebears. The girl who was told she was mortal and no Niobe goes out claiming the gods as family. It is also her answer to the notion that she is the city's enemy.

annotations.quote: Look, puissant lords of Thebes, on me;
annotations.note: She calls the elders κοιρανίδαι (_koiranidai_, "princes, ruling men", l. 940) of Thebes. It is a pointed title for men who have ruled nothing in this scene. If they are lords, then what is being done is being done by their leave. Just before it she says ἄγομαι (_agomai_) one last time and adds that she delays no longer, which takes Creon's taunt about slowness and makes the going her own act.

annotations.quote: The last of all your royal house ye see.
annotations.note: μούνην λοιπήν (_mounen loipen_, "the only one left", l. 941). Ismene is alive, inside the palace, a few yards away. Antigone told her in [[s5]] that she had chosen to live, and here she strikes her from the family for good. It is the harshest thing in the part. It is also in keeping with the argument about the brother: she counts as kin those to whom the debt is owed, and Ismene declined the debt.

annotations.quote: Martyred by men of sin, undone.
annotations.note: 'Martyred' and 'sin' are Storr's Christian colouring. The Greek is barer and angrier: οἷα πρὸς οἵων ἀνδρῶν (_hoia pros hoion andron_, "what things, from what sort of men", l. 942) I suffer. Hear ἀνδρῶν. Creon has said again and again that he will not be beaten by a woman, and her parting description of her judges is that they are men, and of what kind.

annotations.quote: Such meed my piety hath won.
annotations.note: 'Meed' means reward. Her last words in the play are τὴν εὐσεβίαν σεβίσασα (_ten eusebian sebisasa_, "for having revered reverence", l. 943), the noun and its own verb. The Chorus allowed her 'a kind of piety'. She leaves claiming the thing itself, twice in three words. What has it earned her? On stage, nothing: no sign from the gods, no mourner, no word from Creon. The play then spends its remaining third proving her right about the burial, and none of it reaches her. She does not appear again alive.

links.why: Read the unwritten-laws speech again beside this one; the same woman, with the same act behind her, and none of the certainty.
'How sweet to die' and 'What right has he to keep me from my own?' are both answered here, the first by her fear and the second by the brother argument.
The sign from the gods that she asks for and does not get is delivered to Creon by Teiresias.
She predicts she will go unwept, and in the final scene nobody on stage speaks her name.

s10.essay:
Antigone has been led off, and the elders sing to her back. What they offer is precedent: three stories of people shut away. Danae, locked in a bronze chamber by her father; Lycurgus, the Thracian king who mocked Dionysus and was penned in rock; and a third, told so obliquely that a first-time reader may not see it is a story at all, about two boys blinded by a stepmother on the wild coast of Thrace, and their mother, a daughter of the North Wind.

I find this the hardest ode to read, and I do not think that is only Storr. The elders seem not to know what they mean. Danae was innocent, and Zeus came to her in her cell; is that comfort? Lycurgus was a ruler punished for insulting a god; that is a portrait of Creon, not of the girl they are addressing. The third story is plain atrocity inside a family, with a weaving tool for a weapon. The only thread they draw themselves is that birth protects no one. 'Strange are the ways of Fate.'

So the ode is consolation from men who have no position. They twice call her 'my child,' tenderly, now that she cannot hear them and tenderness costs nothing. Meanwhile the stage is filling with the play's vocabulary of sight: a lightless cell, 'sightless orbits.' The next person through the door is a blind man.

annotations.quote: Like to thee that maiden bright,
annotations.note: Antigone has just been led off and Creon, on the usual view, is still on stage, so the ode is sung over her absence and in front of her judge. The elders offer three stories of people of high birth who were shut up in stone or bronze. Ask of each what the prisoner shares with Antigone and what not. The first word is ἔτλα (_etla_, "she endured", l. 944): the lesson offered is endurance. The ode never says whether she was right.

annotations.quote: Danae, in her brass-bound tower,
annotations.note: Danae's father Acrisius shut her away because of a prophecy that her son would kill him. The Greek has χαλκοδέτοις αὐλαῖς (_chalkodetois aulais_, "bronze-bound halls", l. 945), a chamber rather than Storr's fairy-tale tower. What she gave up is the οὐράνιον φῶς (_ouranion phos_, "light of heaven", l. 944), the sunlight Antigone has just taken leave of. The likeness is close: a king's daughter, innocent, entombed by her own kin to prevent a marriage.

annotations.quote: For a cell, her bridal bower.
annotations.note: τυμβήρει θαλάμῳ (_tymberei thalamoi_, "a tomb-like chamber", l. 946). _Thalamos_ is the word for a bride's room, and it is the Chorus's own word for where Antigone was going at the end of [[s8]]. So the elders have absorbed her equation of tomb and bridal chamber and hand it back as myth. But here is the difference they do not state. Danae's tomb really did become a marriage chamber and she came out of it with a son. Antigone's is a bridal chamber only in metaphor, until Haemon dies in it.

annotations.quote: And yet she sprang of royal line,
annotations.note: τίμιος (_timios_, "honoured", l. 947) in her birth. This is the thread the elders use to tie the three stories together: none of these prisoners was saved by rank. It is a consoling moral only on the surface. A minute ago Antigone called on her ancestral gods and her royal blood, and the ode answers that blood has never helped anyone. The verb for Danae's confinement is κατεζεύχθη (_katezeuchthe_, "she was yoked down", l. 946), and the yoke will return for Lycurgus.

annotations.quote: My child, like thine,
annotations.note: The Greek doubles the address: ὦ παῖ παῖ (_o pai pai_, "child, child", l. 947). They called her child to her face only once, the _teknon_ of [[s9]], and they say it three times in this ode, now that she is out of hearing. The tenderness is real and it costs them nothing. That, I think, is the measure of this Chorus.

annotations.quote: Of Zeus descending in a golden shower.
annotations.note: Zeus reached Danae as a rain of gold and she bore Perseus. The Greek has her ταμιεύεσκε (_tamieueske_, "kept in store, was steward of", l. 950) the seed of Zeus that was χρυσορύτους (_chrysorytous_, "gold-flowing"), a housekeeper's verb, as if she were a treasury. So a god came to Danae in her prison. None comes to Antigone, who asked in [[s9]] which god she could still look to. The example, told to comfort, measures exactly what she has not been given.

annotations.quote: Strange are the ways of Fate, her power
annotations.note: Storr's 'strange' is δεινά (_deina_, "terrible, formidable", l. 951), the adjective that opened the ode on man in [[s4]]. There, nothing was more _deinon_ than man. Here the power that is _deina_ is μοιριδία (_moiridia_, "of fate, allotted"), with an indefinite _tis_: some power of destiny. The elders have reversed their own earlier song, and the reversal is the main thing this ode has to say.

annotations.quote: Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower;
annotations.note: The list is ὄλβος (_olbos_, "prosperity", l. 952), Ἄρης (_Ares_, war), πύργος (_pyrgos_, "a towered wall"), and black ships beaten by the sea. Set it beside [[s4]]: ships crossing the grey sea and the building of cities were man's proudest works there, and the only thing he could not escape was Hades. Now ships and city walls head the list of what cannot escape fate. Who in this play has wealth, an army and a walled city? Not Antigone.

annotations.quote: Thus Dryas’ child, the rash Edonian King,
annotations.note: Lycurgus, king of the Edonians in Thrace, tried to drive out Dionysus and his women. Storr's 'rash' is ὀξύχολος (_oxycholos_, "quick to anger", l. 955). The second example is a king, a man and guilty. It does not fit Antigone well, and it fits Creon very well: a sharp-tempered ruler who sets himself against a god and against inspired women. Did the elders intend that, with Creon listening? I think Sophocles did, and that the Chorus slides into it without quite knowing.

annotations.quote: For words of high disdain
annotations.note: κερτομίοις ὀργαῖς (_kertomiois orgais_, "jeering fits of temper", l. 956). ὀργαῖς is the word the elders fixed on Antigone when they said her self-willed _orge_ destroyed her, so verbally Lycurgus is tied to her. But jeering is not her manner, and it is Creon's: he taunted the Guard, Ismene, Haemon and Antigone herself, and in [[s11]] he will taunt a prophet. The stanza hangs between the two of them, and I do not think that is carelessness.

annotations.quote: Did Bacchus to a rocky dungeon bring,
annotations.note: πετρώδει (_petrodei_, "rocky", l. 957) and δεσμῷ (_desmoi_, "bond, prison"): the rock chamber is the outward link to Antigone's sentence. The verb is ζεύχθη (_zeuchthe_, "he was yoked", l. 955), the same root as Danae's. Creon complained in [[s3]] of citizens who would not keep their necks under the yoke. The yoke in this ode belongs to fate and to Dionysus, who is a god of Thebes and whom the Chorus will summon in [[s12]] to come and heal the city.

annotations.quote: To cool the madness of a fevered brain.
annotations.note: The image is of something dripping away: the δεινὸν (_deinon_, "terrible", l. 958) and ἀνθηρόν (_antheron_, "blooming, exuberant", l. 960) force of his μανίας (_manias_, "madness", l. 958) trickles off, ἀποστάζει (_apostazei_). It is _deinos_ again, of a human fury that is drained by confinement. Imprisonment cures Lycurgus. Antigone is not held long enough to be cured of anything, and the Chorus said only minutes ago that the same winds still drive her.

annotations.quote: ’Twas madness gibes against a god to fling.
annotations.note: ἐπέγνω (_epegno_, "he came to know", l. 960). Lycurgus learned, in his prison, what he had done. That is the thing Antigone in [[s9]] said she would do if the gods judged against her, and the thing Creon does at the end, too late. The participle is ψαύων (_psauon_, "touching, laying hold of", l. 961): he touched the god with jeering tongues. Antigone used the same verb when she told the elders they had touched her sorest wound. Within minutes Creon will be scoffing at Zeus's eagles to Teiresias's face.

annotations.quote: For once he fain had quenched the Maenad’s fire;
annotations.note: He tried to stop the ἐνθέους γυναῖκας (_entheous gynaikas_, "women with the god in them", l. 962) and the Bacchic fire, and provoked the Μούσας (_Mousas_, "Muses", l. 965). A king suppressing women who act for a god: the application to Creon is hard to miss, and it uses the play's charged word _gyne_. Notice also what kind of offence it is. Lycurgus sinned against worship, song and celebration. Creon forbade a lament and has just sneered at songs and wailing.

annotations.quote: By the Iron Rocks that guard the double main,
annotations.note: The third story moves to the far north-east edge of the Greek world: the Dark Rocks at the mouth of the Bosporus, and Salmydessus on the Thracian coast, which the Greek calls ἄξενος (_axenos_, "hostile to strangers", l. 967). The savagery of the setting is deliberate. So is the obscurity: the ode never names Phineus's wife or the stepmother, and Sophocles' audience, who knew the tale, are left to supply it. We have to piece it together.

annotations.quote: There on his borders Ares witnessed
annotations.note: Ares is ἀγχίπτολις (_anchiptolis_, "neighbour to the city", l. 970), a god who lives next door and watches. He does not intervene. Polis-compounds in this play usually carry weight (_hypsipolis_ and _apolis_ in [[s4]]), and here the god nearest the city is the god of violence, a spectator at a crime inside a household. That is a fair picture of what the gods have been in Thebes so far today.

annotations.quote: The vengeance by a jealous step-dame ta’en
annotations.note: King Phineus had two sons by Cleopatra, put her aside and took a second wife, who blinded the boys. Storr's 'jealous step-dame' is ἀγρίας δάμαρτος (_agrias damartos_, "a savage wife", l. 973). The wound is ἀρατὸν ἕλκος (_araton helkos_, "an accursed wound", l. 972), close kin to the word Antigone used when she called herself accursed in [[s9]]. Some versions say Cleopatra was imprisoned, which would complete the pattern, but the ode does not say so, and its interest has shifted from the prisoner to mutilated children.

annotations.quote: The gore that trickled from a spindle red,
annotations.note: κερκίδων (_kerkidon_, "shuttles", l. 976): the weapon is a weaving tool, the emblem of women's work indoors, in bloodied hands. A household instrument turned on the household's own children is this family tragedy in small. It also looks ahead. The play's last death is a wife's, inside the house, with a blade at the altar, cursing her husband for their sons.

annotations.quote: The sightless orbits of her step-sons twain.
annotations.note: The eye-sockets are ἀλαστόροισιν (_alastoroisin_, l. 974), a word from _alastor_, the avenging spirit: the blinded eyes cry out for vengeance. Why end an ode for Antigone with blinded boys? One reason is on its way down the road. The next figure to enter, on a boy's arm, is the blind Teiresias, and his first words are about two seeing with the eyes of one. Blindness that sees, and sight that does not, is where the play goes next.

annotations.quote: Wasting away they mourned their piteous doom,
annotations.note: τακόμενοι (_takomenoi_, "wasting, melting", l. 977) is Niobe's verb from [[s9]], the one Antigone chose for her own likeness. The elders refused her that comparison when she made it, and now they give its key word to the sons of Cleopatra. The boys do what she did throughout the kommos: they weep for themselves because no one else will.

annotations.quote: The blasted issue of their mother’s womb.
annotations.note: Storr's 'blasted issue' flattens a pointed phrase: ἀνύμφευτον γονάν (_anympheuton gonan_, "a birth from an unbridal marriage", l. 980), meaning their mother's marriage was a disaster. It is the vocabulary of Antigone's lament, unwed and without wedding song, and of her cry over her own mother's marriage bed. Children ruined by the marriage that made them describes her as well as it describes them.

annotations.quote: To great Erecththeus’ race;
annotations.note: 'Erecththeus' is a misprint for Erechtheus. Cleopatra's mother was Oreithyia, daughter of the Athenian king Erechtheus, whom the north wind Boreas carried off, so she is of the Ἐρεχθεϊδᾶν (_Erechtheidan_, "the sons of Erechtheus", l. 982), which is a poetic name for the Athenians themselves. For the audience this is the one prisoner in the ode who is their own. Athens honoured Boreas with a cult after the storms that wrecked the Persian fleet.

annotations.quote: Swift as his horses o’er the hills she sped;
annotations.note: After two stanzas of dark the ode opens for a moment into pure speed: the daughter of Boreas, Βορεὰς (_Boreas_, l. 985), reared in far-off caves among her father's storms, ἅμιππος (_hamippos_, "keeping pace with horses") over the steep hills. She is a creature of open air, which makes what happened to her the sharpest contrast in the ode. The cave and the storm wind also gather up the imagery fastened on Antigone, the rock chamber and the gusts of the soul.

annotations.quote: A child of gods; yet she, my child, like thee,
annotations.note: θεῶν παῖς (_theon pais_, "child of gods", l. 986), and then ὦ παῖ (_o pai_, "child", l. 987) to Antigone: the same noun for the goddess's daughter and the condemned girl. In [[s9]] the elders told her she was mortal and Niobe divine, and refused the comparison. Now they make one like it themselves. The address has softened from the 'self-willed' of the kommos, and the whole moral, such as it is, is here: even the granddaughter of a god was overtaken.

annotations.quote: That knows not death nor age—she too was vanquished.
annotations.note: The Μοῖραι μακραίωνες (_Moirai makraiones_, "the long-lived Fates", l. 987) bore down on her too. So what do the three have in common with Antigone? High birth, a prison, and a power no one resists. And what not? Danae was visited by a god and released. Lycurgus was guilty and came to know it. Cleopatra's story is about a cruel marriage, where Antigone has none at all. None of them is said to die in the prison, and none chose her fate, where Antigone, _autonomos_, chose hers. By calling it all destiny the ode avoids naming the one person present who could still open the tomb. Teiresias, entering now, names him.

links.why: The ode's blinded boys and dark cells hand over directly to the blind prophet who sees what Creon cannot.
Antigone chose her own mythical likeness, Niobe, and the elders rejected it; these are the ones they prefer.

s11.essay:
Teiresias comes on led by a boy, 'two wayfarers as one, / Having betwixt us eyes for one,' and for a few lines he and Creon are old colleagues. Creon has always taken his advice; the prophet has helped him steer the city. It matters that Creon has a record of listening. What we are about to watch is not a man who cannot hear, but a man who has stopped hearing today.

The report is horrible and precise. The birds are screaming and tearing one another. The sacrifice will not burn; the fat slides off the thigh bones and the gall bursts. And the cause is physical: the birds and dogs have been feeding on Polyneices and have carried scraps of him to every altar in Thebes. The exhibit Creon ordered in [[s3]] has become the city's pollution. Then Teiresias offers him a way out that costs nothing but pride: 'To err is common / To all men,' and the only fool is the obstinate one.

Creon answers as he answered the Guard. Bribery. Prophets are a money-getting tribe. And then he says the most reckless thing in the play: he will not allow the burial even if Zeus's own eagles carry the carrion up to the god's throne, because 'no human soilure can assail the gods.' As theology that is almost enlightened. In his mouth it is a clever idea put to work for a grudge, and he is saying it to the one man who knows what the gods have just refused.

So Teiresias stops advising and prophesies, and he names the offence more exactly than anyone has: Creon has put a living soul below the earth and kept a dead one above it. Both belong elsewhere. This is Antigone's point about jurisdiction from [[s5]], now made with authority. The price will be a child of his own.

What follows takes about ten lines. The elders, who have not ventured a firm opinion all day, say they have never known this prophet wrong, and Creon folds: 'To yield is grievous.' I find the speed convincing. He was never a monster. He was a man afraid of looking weak, and a larger fear has arrived. Note the order of the elders' instructions, the maiden first and then the tomb, and keep it for [[s13]].

annotations.quote: Princes of Thebes, two wayfarers as one,
annotations.note: He greets Θήβης ἄνακτες (_Thebes anaktes_, "lords of Thebes", l. 988) in the plural: the elders and Creon together, where everyone else today has addressed Creon alone. The road he has walked is κοινὴν ὁδὸν (_koinen hodon_, "a shared road"). Keep the word _koinos_ in mind; in thirty lines he will say that error too is common to all men.

annotations.quote: Having betwixt us eyes for one, we are here.
annotations.note: The Greek uses the dual, ἐξ ἑνὸς βλέποντε (_ex henos bleponte_, "the pair of us seeing from one", l. 989), a grammatical form reserved for two things that make a pair. Sophocles used it in the prologue for the two sisters and the two brothers, and every one of those pairs has been broken. The blind man who sees truly is an old device, and Sophocles gave it to this same prophet again in the Oedipus. What matters here is that Teiresias knows he needs a guide and says so in his first sentence. Creon does not know it yet.

annotations.quote: Why tidings, old Teiresias?
annotations.note: 'Why' is a misprint for 'What'. The Greek asks what is νέον (_neon_, "new", l. 991), a word that in tragedy usually smells of trouble. Notice that the seer arrives unsummoned. In the Oedipus he has to be sent for twice; here he comes of his own accord, which tells you how bad the signs are.

annotations.quote: And when thou hearest thou must heed the seer.
annotations.note: "I will teach, and you obey": πιθοῦ (_pithou_, l. 992) is the imperative of the verb that means both "be persuaded" and "obey". Creon has spent the play demanding this of others and refusing it himself, most recently with Haemon in [[s7]]. Hold on to the word, because at l. 1099 he will finally say it back in the first person.

annotations.quote: Thus far I ne’er have disobeyed thy rede.
annotations.note: 'Rede' is counsel, but the Greek is more inward: he has never stood apart from the seer's φρενός (_phrenos_, "mind", l. 993). The line gives Creon a past in which he was a ruler who took advice, and it shows how far he has travelled since morning. It also sets a trap for him. If he has always followed this mind before, on what ground will he refuse it now?

annotations.quote: So hast thou steered the ship of State aright.
annotations.note: The ship of state was Creon's own figure in his inaugural speech in [[s3]], and "straight" was his favourite word there. Teiresias hands both back to him, but in the imperfect tense: ἐναυκλήρεις πόλιν (_enauklereis polin_, l. 994) is "you were captaining the city". Storr's perfect, 'hast steered', lets the good course run up to the present. The Greek leaves it in the past.

annotations.quote: I know it, and I gladly own my debt.
annotations.note: Literally, "I can testify from experience to benefits": ὀνήσιμα (_onesima_, "profitable things", l. 995). So Creon himself opens the scene's ledger of profit, and in an innocent sense: the seer's advice has paid. Within forty lines the same idea will come back as an accusation of bribery.

annotations.quote: The razor edge of peril.
annotations.note: The first word of the Greek line is the command φρόνει (_phronei_, "think", l. 996), the verb the whole play has been circling and will end on. Then ἐπὶ ξυροῦ τύχης (_epi xyrou tyches_), "on the razor of fortune", a Homeric phrase for the moment when things can still fall either way. That is the point of it. Teiresias is not announcing a doom; he is saying that Creon is balanced and can still step off on the right side.

annotations.quote: Thy words inspire a dread presentiment.
annotations.note: "I shudder at your mouth": φρίσσω (_phrisso_, l. 997) is the physical word, hair standing up. The man who has feared nothing all day is afraid before he has heard a single fact. I would mark this for later, when his collapse seems too quick. The fear is here from the start, and the bluster that follows is laid over it.

annotations.quote: Sitting upon my throne of augury,
annotations.note: The παλαιὸν θᾶκον ὀρνιθοσκόπον (_palaion thakon ornithoskopon_, "ancient bird-watching seat", l. 999) was a real place; Pausanias, centuries later, was still shown Teiresias' observatory at Thebes. He calls it a λιμήν (_limen_, "harbour") for every bird, a calm word chosen to be violated in the next line. Note the method of the speech: two separate techniques of divination, birds and then fire, are tried in turn and both fail.

annotations.quote: A jargon strange of twitterings, hoots, and screams;
annotations.note: Storr turns into an aviary what the Greek puts in two savage words. The birds scream in a frenzy, οἴστρῳ (_oistroi_, the gadfly's sting, l. 1002), and their cry is βεβαρβαρωμένῳ (_bebarbaromenoi_), "barbarized", turned into a foreign language. Bird-cry is the tongue a seer reads. He is saying that the language between gods and men has become gibberish.

annotations.quote: So knew I that each bird at the other tare
annotations.note: ἔγνων (_egnon_, "I knew", l. 1004): the blind man knows by ear what the sighted would have had to see. And what he hears is creatures of one kind tearing each other with their claws, which is the story of the two brothers played again in the air. In the entry song in [[s2]] Polyneices was the eagle screaming over Thebes; now the birds that fed on him have caught his war.

annotations.quote: I straight essayed the sacrifice by fire
annotations.note: The second test, made because he was afraid: δείσας (_deisas_, "in fear", l. 1005), where Storr has the milder 'Perturbed in soul'. ἐμπύρων (_empyron_) is the technical term for reading omens in the way an offering burns. A good prophet checks one method against another before he troubles a king.

annotations.quote: On blazing altars, but the God of Fire
annotations.note: Ἥφαιστος οὐκ ἔλαμπεν (_Hephaistos ouk elampen_, "Hephaestus did not shine", l. 1007). The altars are παμφλέκτοισιν (_pamphlektoisin_, "fully kindled"), so there is nothing wrong with the fire. It is the offering that will not take. The god's name stands for the flame, and the refusal is therefore a god's refusal.

annotations.quote: And sputtered in the ashes a foul ooze;
annotations.note: Greek sacrifice was meant to send clean fat-smoke up to the gods; this one only weeps. The phrase is μυδῶσα κηκὶς (_mydosa kekis_, "a dank ooze", l. 1008), and the participle is the very word (_mydon_) the Guard used in [[s5]] for the rotting body of Polyneices. The altar is doing what the corpse is doing. Storr does not spare us and should not: the play insists that the offence is a bodily fact and no point of etiquette.

annotations.quote: Melted and fell and left the thigh bones bare.
annotations.note: In a proper sacrifice the thigh bones are wrapped in fat, καλυπτῆς (_kalyptes_, "covering", l. 1011), and burn inside it; that wrapped bundle is the gods' share. Here the covering slides off and the bones ἐξέκειντο (_exekeinto_), "lay exposed". It is the vocabulary of a body laid out, and the Chorus will use its cousin of Polyneices at l. 1101. The failed offering is a small model of the crime: something that ought to be covered lies bare.

annotations.quote: Such are the signs, taught by this lad, I read—
annotations.note: ἐμάνθανον (_emanthanon_, "I was learning", l. 1012): the oldest and wisest man in Thebes learns from a child and is not ashamed to say so. Set that against Creon's sneer to Haemon in [[s7]], that men of his age are not to be schooled by a boy. The scene is built to show what Creon could not do.

annotations.quote: As I guide others, so the boy guides me—
annotations.note: ἡγεμών (_hegemon_, "leader, guide", l. 1014) is a word of command, and Teiresias gives it to the boy. Authority in his account is a chain in which everyone who leads is also led. Creon's account in [[s7]] had a single link: the man the city appoints must be obeyed in small things and great, just and unjust.

annotations.quote: The frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb.
annotations.note: ἀσήμων ὀργίων (_asemon orgion_, "rites that give no sign", l. 1013). Nine lines earlier the whirr of wings was "not without meaning", οὐκ ἄσημος (_ouk asemos_, l. 1004); the birds meant something, and what they meant is that the rites now mean nothing. A tutor's question: has Teiresias received a message from the gods? Strictly, no. He has received the absence of one, and reasons from that.

annotations.quote: O King, thy willful temper ails the State,
annotations.note: The Greek is blunter and has no 'O King': "it is from your mind that the city is sick", νοσεῖ πόλις (_nosei polis_, l. 1015), with ἐκ φρενὸς (_ek phrenos_) naming the organ. The _phren_ that Creon said at l. 993 he had never departed from is now set against his own. Disease is the scene's master image from here on: Teiresias will tell Creon he is full of it at l. 1052, and the Chorus will sing of it in [[s12]].

annotations.quote: By what has filled the maw of dogs and crows,
annotations.note: Be exact about what is polluted. It is the βωμοὶ (_bomoi_, altars) and ἐσχάραι (_escharai_, hearths), and παντελεῖς (_panteleis_), all of them without exception (l. 1016). They are "full" of βορᾶς (_boras_, "carrion-meat", l. 1017), scraps of the dead man carried there by birds and dogs. Creon's edict promised exactly this feeding in [[s3]]; he did not think about where the animals would go afterwards. The pollution is public and material: the places where the city talks to its gods are fouled.

annotations.quote: The flesh of Oedipus’ unburied son.
annotations.note: Teiresias will not say 'traitor' and does not even use the name. The dead man is δυσμόρου (_dysmorou_, "ill-fated", l. 1018), "the fallen son of Oedipus"; 'unburied' is Storr's addition. To the prophet he is an unlucky member of an unlucky house, which is how Antigone saw him. Creon's political category has simply dropped out of the description.

annotations.quote: Therefore no birds trill out a happy note,
annotations.note: εὐσήμους (_eusemous_, "of good sign", l. 1021), the third _sema_ word in twenty lines. The traffic between Thebes and the gods is blocked in both directions: prayers and thigh-smoke do not go up (ll. 1019-20), and signs do not come down. The cause is stated physically. The birds have eaten the fat of a slain man's blood, so the instruments of prophecy are themselves contaminated.

annotations.quote: O ponder this, my son. To err is common
annotations.note: τέκνον, φρόνησον (_teknon, phroneson_, "child, think", l. 1023). The king is called child, and told for the second time to use his mind. Then the generous move: error is κοινόν (_koinon_, "common", l. 1024) to all, the same word as the shared road of his entrance. Teiresias is making it as easy as he can for Creon to back down without disgrace, and Haemon tried the same door in [[s7]].

annotations.quote: The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise.
annotations.note: Medical language again: the man who ἀκῆται (_aketai_, "heals", l. 1027) the harm and does not stay ἀκίνητος (_akinetos_, "immovable"). Such a man is no longer ἄβουλος (_aboulos_, "ill-counselled") or ἄνολβος (_anolbos_, "unblest"); Storr's 'wastrel' for the second is a strange choice, since the word concerns fortune and not thrift. This is the doctrine of the play in a sentence: the fault is ordinary, and what ruins a man is refusing the remedy while there is time.

annotations.quote: No fool, the saw goes, like the obstinate fool.
annotations.note: No proverb is announced in the Greek. The line is a verdict: αὐθαδία (_authadia_, "self-will", literally pleasing oneself, l. 1028) ὀφλισκάνει (_ophliskanei_), "is convicted of", stupidity, the stupidity being _skaiotes_, left-handed clumsiness. The verb is a law-court term for losing a case. The man who has acted as judge all day hears the language of sentence turned on himself.

annotations.quote: Let death disarm thy vengeance. O forbear
annotations.note: Storr dissolves the key word. The Greek says εἶκε τῷ θανόντι (_eike toi thanonti_, "yield to the dead man", l. 1029), and yielding is what Haemon begged for with his bending trees and slackened sail in [[s7]]. The same verb returns at l. 1096 when Creon breaks. Then κέντει (_kentei_, "stab, goad"): do not go on stabbing one who has perished.

annotations.quote: By slaying twice the slain? I mean thee well;
annotations.note: ἐπικτανεῖν (_epiktanein_, "to kill over again", l. 1030), and he asks what ἀλκὴ (_alke_, "prowess") there is in it. This is the plainest objection to the edict, and it has taken until now for anyone to voice it: the man is already dead. The appeal is to Creon's soldierly pride, since _alke_ is a warrior's virtue and there is none in fighting a corpse.

annotations.quote: Counsel’s most welcome if I promise gain.
annotations.note: The last word of the speech is the fatal one: κέρδος (_kerdos_, "gain", l. 1032). Teiresias means it honestly, that it is pleasant to learn from a good adviser when the advice profits you. But _kerdos_ has been Creon's obsession since he accused the guards of taking bribes in [[s3]], and he hears only the sense he always hears. I think Sophocles makes the seer hand him the word so that we can watch what he does with it.

annotations.quote: Like anchors at a target; yea, ye set
annotations.note: 'Anchors' is a slip in this printing for 'archers': τοξόται σκοποῦ (_toxotai skopou_, "archers at a mark", l. 1033). Who are the 'all'? Antigone, Ismene, Haemon, the muttering city, and now the seer; in Creon's mind they have merged into one conspiracy. Teiresias takes up the image at the end of the scene and tells him that these arrows will not miss.

annotations.quote: Your soothsayer on me. Peddlers are ye all
annotations.note: Two commercial verbs carry the Greek: ἐξημπόλημαι κἀμπεφόρτισμαι (_exempolemai kampephortismai_, l. 1036), "I have been sold off and loaded as cargo", and by the whole tribe of seers. Creon has one theory of opposition and it is always the same: somebody has been paid. He applied it to the guards in [[s3]], and now applies it to the one man in Thebes whose record he has just vouched for.

annotations.quote: Go to, and make your profit where ye will,
annotations.note: The imperative is the verb of _kerdos_ itself (_kerdainete_, "make your gains"), followed by ἐμπολᾶτε (_empolate_, "trade away", l. 1037). Within six lines of the seer's honest use of the word, Creon has turned it into a sneer. Ask what the seer could possibly gain by Polyneices' burial. Creon never says, because the charge is a reflex and has no content.

annotations.quote: Silver of Sardis change for gold of Ind;
annotations.note: Not silver. The Greek is ἤλεκτρον (_elektron_, l. 1038), electrum, the pale natural alloy of gold and silver that came from the river at Sardis and made Lydia rich, paired with Indian χρυσόν (_chryson_, "gold", l. 1039). The geography belongs to Sophocles' own century more than to heroic Thebes. Creon reaches for the far ends of the world to say that no price would be enough, which shows how large the imagined bribe has grown.

annotations.quote: Ye will not purchase this man’s burial,
annotations.note: 'Purchase' is Storr keeping the trade metaphor going. The Greek is flat: "you shall not hide that man in a grave", τάφῳ (_taphoi_) and οὐχὶ κρύψετε (_ouchi krypsete_, l. 1039). Even now he will not name Polyneices; he is 'that one'. This is the edict's last restatement, and it is addressed to a prophet who has just told him the gods reject it.

annotations.quote: Not though the winged ministers of Zeus
annotations.note: The blasphemy. Storr's 'winged ministers' is polite; the Greek says the αἰετοὶ (_aietoi_, "eagles", l. 1040) of Zeus might snatch the body as βορὰν (_boran_, "carrion", the seer's word from l. 1017) and carry it ἐς Διὸς θρόνους (_es Dios thronous_, "to the thrones of Zeus", l. 1041). He has taken the report of fouled altars and raised it to the highest altar there is. Earlier he only slighted Zeus of the household when he condemned his niece; now he pictures rotting flesh on the god's seat and says he would not care.

annotations.quote: Not e’en in awe of prodigy so dire
annotations.note: Storr's 'prodigy' hides the word that matters: μίασμα (_miasma_, "pollution", l. 1042). Creon says he would not flinch from this as a pollution and so allow the burial. He names the thing precisely and refuses to fear it. Yet at the end of [[s7]] he was careful to leave food in Antigone's cave so that the city should escape exactly this stain. He believes in pollution when the belief costs him nothing.

annotations.quote: No human soilure can assail the gods;
annotations.note: 'Soilure' is defilement: θεοὺς μιαίνειν (_theous miainein_, "to pollute gods", l. 1044) is beyond human strength. The thought would be respectable in a philosopher, and it sounds like the enlightened talk of Sophocles' own day. But it answers something Teiresias never said. He did not claim the gods were stained. He said the altars were, and that the gods had stopped listening. Creon uses a sound piece of theology as permission to go on fouling their altars.

annotations.quote: Of craft and cunning when it tries to gloss
annotations.note: The clever who fall are πολλὰ δεινοὶ (_polla deinoi_, "formidable in many things", l. 1046), the adjective of the great ode in [[s4]], where man was the most _deinos_ of all creatures and his cleverness could carry him to ruin as easily as to greatness. Creon means the seer. The sentence describes Creon: a very able man about to take a shameful fall for speaking ugly things well.

annotations.quote: Foul treachery with fair words for filthy gain.
annotations.note: His speech ends where the seer's did, on τοῦ κέρδους χάριν (_tou kerdous charin_, "for the sake of gain", l. 1047). Two speeches, the same last word, opposite meanings: one man offers profit, the other can only hear corruption. Storr's 'filthy' is his own; the Greek puts the shame in the words spoken and leaves the gain bare.

annotations.quote: Alas! doth any know and lay to heart—
annotations.note: Teiresias begins a sentence and Creon cuts across it; the question is completed two lines later. Sophocles splits one thought over the line-for-line exchange so that we hear the interruption. The verb φράζεται (_phrazetai_, "considers", l. 1048a) asks whether anyone thinks things through, and the man opposite proves the answer by not letting him finish.

annotations.quote: Is this the prelude to some hackneyed saw?
annotations.note: πάγκοινον (_pankoinon_, "common to everyone", l. 1049): Creon sneers that a platitude is coming. He is right, and the platitude is true, and the play will end with the Chorus reciting it over him. The word is another _koinos_ compound, and it returns in the hymn of [[s12]] for the folds of Eleusis that receive all comers.

annotations.quote: How far good counsel is the best of goods?
annotations.note: εὐβουλία (_euboulia_, "good counsel", l. 1050) is ranked best of κτημάτων (_ktematon_, "possessions"). Since Creon will talk of nothing but property, the seer puts wisdom in the terms of property. The word comes back at l. 1098, when the Chorus tells Creon it is the one thing he now needs to get.

annotations.quote: True, as unwisdom is the worst of ills.
annotations.note: Creon caps the maxim correctly: μὴ φρονεῖν (_me phronein_, "not thinking straight", l. 1051) is the greatest harm. He can recite the moral of his own tragedy and has no idea it applies to him. The Chorus' closing lines in [[s13]] say exactly this, that good sense is the chief part of happiness.

annotations.quote: Thou art infected with that ill thyself.
annotations.note: νόσου πλήρης (_nosou pleres_, "full of that disease", l. 1052). The adjective is the one used of the altars at l. 1017, πλήρεις (_plereis_), full of carrion. The altars are full of the corpse and the king is full of the sickness; the two conditions are one, and the city's illness has been traced to a single patient.

annotations.quote: I will not bandy insults with thee, seer.
annotations.note: A flicker of the old respect. He still calls him 'the seer' and says he does not want to answer abuse with abuse. It lasts one line, and Teiresias will not let him keep the pose.

annotations.quote: And yet thou say’st my prophesies are frauds.
annotations.note: The seer points out that the insult has already been delivered: to say he prophesies ψευδῆ (_pseude_, "falsehoods", l. 1054) is the worst thing one can say of a prophet. The Chorus will answer this word directly at l. 1094, where they testify that he has never once spoken a falsehood to the city.

annotations.quote: Prophets are all a money-getting tribe.
annotations.note: φιλάργυρον γένος (_philargyron genos_, "a silver-loving breed", l. 1055). The Greek audience knew venal diviners, and the gibe had a real target in their world. It has none here, and Sophocles has taken care that we know it, since Creon admitted at l. 995 that this prophet's advice had always served him. Oedipus will make the same charge against the same man in the later play, and be just as wrong.

annotations.quote: And kings are all a lucre-loving race.
annotations.note: Teiresias returns the compound with interest: αἰσχροκέρδειαν (_aischrokerdeian_, "shameful gain", l. 1056), and he says it of τυράννων (_tyrannon_), which Storr softens to 'kings'. So _kerdos_ finally lands on Creon. What is his shameful profit, given that no money is involved? I take it to be winning: he would rather keep his victory over a dead man and a girl than keep the city clean.

annotations.quote: Dost know at whom thou glancest, me thy lord?
annotations.note: He pulls rank, as he did with Haemon and the Guard. The word is ταγοὺς (_tagous_, "commanders", l. 1057), a military title, in a lofty plural. When Creon runs out of argument he always reaches for the fact of his office.

annotations.quote: Lord of the State and savior, thanks to me.
annotations.note: ἐξ ἐμοῦ (_ex emou_, "through me", l. 1058) you hold this city, σώσας (_sosas_, "having saved it"). This is the debt acknowledged at l. 995, now called in. The play does not say what the earlier counsel was. Eurydice's dying reproach about Megareus in [[s13]] suggests it cost Creon a son, in which case the prophet who is about to take his second son once required his first.

annotations.quote: Skilled prophet art thou, but to wrong inclined.
annotations.note: A remarkable concession in mid-quarrel: σοφὸς σὺ μάντις (_sophos su mantis_, "you are a skilled seer", l. 1059). Creon never doubts the art, only the man's honesty. That is why he collapses so quickly once the prophecy is spoken. He has already granted that this prophet knows.

annotations.quote: The mystery deep hidden in my breast.
annotations.note: τἀκίνητα (_takineta_, "the things that should not be moved", l. 1060). At l. 1027 the seer warned against being ἀκίνητος (_akinetos_), immovable. Because Creon would not move, what ought to have stayed unmoved is now stirred up. Note what this implies about the first speech: Teiresias came with a diagnosis and a cure and was holding the worst in reserve.

annotations.quote: Say on, but see it be not said for gain.
annotations.note: κίνει (_kinei_, "move it, then", l. 1061): Creon orders the prophecy himself, with one more jab about κέρδεσιν (_kerdesin_, "profits"). Here is the question the scene leaves us with. Would the doom have been spoken, or even fixed, if he had yielded at l. 1032? The seer's talk of a cure implies it was still avoidable then. The prophecy that follows has no 'unless' in it.

annotations.quote: Such thou, methinks, till now hast judged my words.
annotations.note: Storr guesses at a difficult line. The Greek (l. 1062) is closer to "So indeed I think I shall speak, τὸ σὸν μέρος (_to son meros_), as far as you are concerned". That is, you say 'not for gain', and you are right: what I am about to tell you will bring no gain to you. It is a grim joke on Creon's word, and Storr's version misses it.

annotations.quote: Be sure thou wilt not traffic on my wits.
annotations.note: "Know that you will not trade in τὴν ἐμὴν φρένα (_ten emen phrena_, "my mind")" (l. 1063). His last word before the prophecy is the commercial metaphor again, and its object is the very _phren_ the seer diagnosed at l. 1015 as the source of the city's sickness. He is defending the diseased organ as though it were his treasure.

annotations.quote: Know then for sure, the coursers of the sun
annotations.note: κάτισθι (_katisthi_, "know it well", l. 1064) throws back Creon's "be sure" from the line before; the seer answers a command to know with a stronger one. The Greek has no horses, only τρόχους ἁμιλλητῆρας ἡλίου (_trochous hamilleteras heliou_, "the racing wheels of the sun"). Not many circuits, he says. In the event the sun does not complete one.

annotations.quote: Thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins
annotations.note: σπλάγχνων (_splanchnon_, l. 1066) is "inward parts, guts", and Storr's 'loins' makes it decorous. These are also the parts a sacrificer handles and a seer inspects. After a speech about an offering the gods would not accept, Creon is told that one will be taken from his own body. The Greek adds "one"; as [[s13]] will show, the count is low.

annotations.quote: In quittance of thy murder, life for life;
annotations.note: The terms of the prophecy, and Storr blurs them. The Greek is νέκυν νεκρῶν ἀμοιβὸν (_nekyn nekron amoibon_, "a corpse in exchange for corpses", l. 1067), with ἀντιδοὺς (_antidous_, "paying over in return"). There is no 'murder' in the line and no 'life'. One dead body is owed for dead bodies in the plural, which counts the living Antigone as already a corpse. And the idiom is that of payment. Creon wanted to talk about buying and selling, and this is the bill.

annotations.quote: For that thou hast entombed a living soul,
annotations.note: ψυχήν (_psychen_, "a life", l. 1069) has been lodged in a tomb ἀτίμως (_atimos_, "without honour"). The verb κατῴκισας (_katoikisas_) is the one used for settling people in a new home, as a founder settles colonists. Creon has made a household in a grave, and the phrase picks up Antigone's own bitter address to her tomb as a bridal chamber and dwelling in [[s9]].

annotations.quote: And sent below a denizen of earth,
annotations.note: The indictment in five words: τῶν ἄνω βαλὼν κάτω (_ton ano balon kato_, "having thrown below one of those above", l. 1068). A 'denizen of earth' is someone who belongs up here among the living. The sentence then balances it with its mirror: he keeps up here one who belongs below. Notice that Antigone comes first. The seer's first speech was all about the corpse; the charge of burying the living is new, and it stands at the head of the sentence.

annotations.quote: A corpse unlaved, unwept, unsepulchered.
annotations.note: Three negatives in a row: ἄμοιρον, ἀκτέριστον, ἀνόσιον (_amoiron, akteriston, anosion_, l. 1071). Storr keeps the hammering and changes the sense. The words are "without his portion", "without funeral rites", "unhallowed"; there is no washing or weeping in them, and 'unwept' is borrowed from Antigone's own triplets earlier in the play. The first is the important one. The dead man has been denied his share, and the gods below theirs, since the line says he belongs to them.

annotations.quote: Herein thou hast no part, nor e’en the gods
annotations.note: An argument about jurisdiction. In the dead neither Creon nor the gods above have any share, μέτεστιν (_metestin_, l. 1072); the upper gods βιάζονται (_biazontai_, "are being forced", l. 1073) by him. That is an astonishing thing to say: Creon is doing violence to the Olympians by leaving on their ground what is not theirs. This is why I resist the tidy scheme, usually credited to Hegel, of two equal rights colliding. The prophet does not weigh state against family. He says a boundary in the order of things has been crossed, twice.

annotations.quote: For this the avenging spirits of Heaven and Hell
annotations.note: The Ἐρινύες (_Erinyes_, l. 1075) are named, of Hades and of the gods together, so both worlds send them; Storr's 'Hell' brings in a Christian place the Greek does not know. They are ὑστεροφθόροι (_hysterophthoroi_, "destroying late", l. 1074) and they λοχῶσιν (_lochosin_, "lie in ambush"). The Chorus sang of a Fury in the mind in [[s6]] as the thing that ruins this family. Now Furies wait for Creon, who is of the family only by marriage and thought himself outside its curse.

annotations.quote: What these have suffered thou shalt suffer too.
annotations.note: Literally, he is to be caught "in these same" κακοῖς (_kakois_, "evils", l. 1076). Storr's 'these' wavers between the victims and the gods. I read it as exact retribution in kind. He put the living among the dead, and he will end as what the Messenger in [[s13]] calls a breathing corpse; he kept the dead from their own, and he will stand holding his own dead.

annotations.quote: And now, consider whether bought by gold
annotations.note: κατηργυρωμένος (_katergyromenos_, "silvered over", l. 1077), plated with silver like a cheap object made to look precious. It is the seer's last reply to the charge of bribery, and it is contemptuous. He does not argue the point. He says: wait a little, and judge by what you hear in your house.

annotations.quote: Of men and women through thy desolate halls;
annotations.note: ἀνδρῶν γυναικῶν (_andron gynaikon_, "of men, of women", l. 1079), set side by side without a conjunction, and their κωκύματα (_kokymata_, "shrieks of mourning"). Creon has built his position on the difference between these two words: no woman shall rule him, better to fall to a man. The prophecy levels them in one sound. The cry is the kind Antigone raised over her brother's body in [[s5]], and it will come from his own doors. 'Desolate' is Storr's; the Greek says only "your house".

annotations.quote: And all thy neighbor States are leagues to avenge
annotations.note: 'Leagues' is a slip for 'leagued'. The cities are stirred up ἐχθραὶ (_echthrai_, "in enmity", l. 1080): Creon's whole policy rested on sorting friend from enemy, and it has made him enemies abroad. These four lines widen the crime to all the Argive dead left on the field, the story Euripides tells in his Suppliants. They sit oddly in a play that has spoken of one corpse only, and some editors have suspected them. If they stand, they show the edict as policy, applied to a whole army.

annotations.quote: I’ the maw of wolf or hound, or winged bird
annotations.note: The verb Storr passes over is the bitter one: the dogs καθήγνισαν (_kathegnisan_, "consecrated", l. 1081) the torn remains. It is the proper word for performing funeral rites. The only burial these men received was in the bellies of animals, and Teiresias says so in the vocabulary of the ritual they were refused.

annotations.quote: That flying homewards taints their city’s air.
annotations.note: The bird carries an unholy ὀσμὴν (_osmen_, "smell", l. 1083) to a city that is ἑστιοῦχον (_hestiouchon_, "possessing the hearth"). So what happened to the altars and hearths of Thebes at l. 1016 is happening in every city that lost men here. Pollution in this play does not stay where it is put. It travels on wings, and the image of the gorged bird ties the end of the prophecy back to the birds that opened the first speech.

annotations.quote: These are the shafts, that like a bowman I
annotations.note: τοξότης (_toxotes_, "archer", l. 1084) answers Creon's complaint at l. 1033 that everyone shoots at him: very well, here are τοξεύματα (_toxeumata_, "arrows"), and sure ones. Notice that he admits to anger, θυμῷ (_thymoi_, l. 1085), and says "for you hurt me". A prophet who is stung and strikes back is an uncomfortable figure. I think Sophocles wants us uneasy about how much of the doom was drawn out by the quarrel.

annotations.quote: On younger men, and learn to curb his tongue
annotations.note: Let him vent his temper on νεωτέρους (_neoterous_, "younger men", l. 1088). The audience has just watched him do it to Haemon. The closing line (l. 1090) asks for a better νοῦν (_noun_, "mind") than the φρενῶν (_phrenon_, "wits") he now carries, so the seer's exit, like his entrance and his diagnosis, is about Creon's thinking. He leaves as he came, led by the boy, and Creon has said nothing.

annotations.quote: My liege, that man hath gone, foretelling woe.
annotations.note: δεινὰ θεσπίσας (_deina thespisas_, "having prophesied terrible things", l. 1091). The word _deinos_, which the ode in [[s4]] made so double-edged, has only its dark side left by this point in the play. There is a silence to imagine before this line: Creon alone with the elders, and they are the ones who speak first.

annotations.quote: The prophet’s warning to the State to fail.
annotations.note: Never has he uttered a ψεῦδος (_pseudos_, "falsehood", l. 1094) to the city, which is a direct reply to Creon's charge at l. 1054. This is the moment the Chorus finally commits itself. They have hinted, hedged, and deferred all day; they once wondered aloud whether the burial was the gods' work and were silenced. Now they speak as the collective memory of Thebes, grey-haired men who have watched this prophet for a lifetime.

annotations.quote: I know it too, and it perplexes me.
annotations.note: The turn, eleven lines after the seer's exit: ἔγνωκα (_egnoka_, "I have recognised it", l. 1095) and ταράσσομαι φρένας (_tarassomai phrenas_, "I am shaken in my mind"). Ask what did it. Not argument: Haemon gave him better arguments and he threatened to kill the girl in front of him. What moves him is fear, and the authority of a prophet whose skill he conceded at l. 1059. I think the speed is the point. A will this rigid breaks all at once.

annotations.quote: To yield is grievous, but the obstinate soul
annotations.note: εἰκαθεῖν (_eikathein_, "to yield", l. 1096), the verb of Haemon's trees and the seer's "yield to the dead", is at last in Creon's mouth, and he calls it δεινόν (_deinon_, "terrible"). He uses the same adjective for the alternative in the next line. That is his predicament exactly: two terrible things, and he has only now noticed the second.

annotations.quote: That fights with Fate, is smitten grievously.
annotations.note: There is no 'Fate' in the Greek. What he fears is to resist and strike his spirit against ἄτῃ (_atei_, l. 1097), _ate_, the ruinous delusion the Chorus sang of in [[s6]] as the thing a god sends on the man he means to destroy. Creon has heard that ode's lesson and names his danger correctly. He names it too late, which is how _ate_ works.

annotations.quote: Son of Menoeceus, list to good advice.
annotations.note: εὐβουλίας (_euboulias_, l. 1098), the 'best of possessions' from l. 1050, and the Chorus says he must "get hold of" it, as of something he does not have. They address him by his father's name and as παῖ, 'child'. For the third time in the scene the king is spoken to as a son who needs teaching.

annotations.quote: What should I do. Advise me. I will heed.
annotations.note: The speaker label in this printing says CHORUS, but the line is Creon's. Its last word is πείσομαι (_peisomai_, "I will obey", l. 1099), the answer, a hundred lines late, to the seer's opening πιθοῦ at l. 992. It is the first time all day that he has asked anyone what to do. The man who told his son that the ruler must be obeyed in everything now takes orders from the elders he summoned to be an audience.

annotations.quote: Go, free the maiden from her rocky cell;
annotations.note: The order is fixed by the grammar: κόρην (_koren_, "the girl", l. 1100) with the particle that means 'first', the tomb with the one that means 'and then'. The living first, then the dead; it is the obvious order, since a corpse can wait and a girl in a cave cannot. It is also the order of the seer's indictment at l. 1068. Watch what Creon does when he reaches the plain.

annotations.quote: And for the unburied outlaw build a tomb.
annotations.note: 'Outlaw' is Storr's. The Chorus says only τῷ προκειμένῳ (_toi prokeimenoi_, "for him who lies exposed", l. 1101), the ordinary word for a body laid out before burial. No traitor, no enemy, no name. The political description of Polyneices, which the elders accepted in [[s3]], has gone from their speech as it went from the seer's.

annotations.quote: Is that your counsel? You would have me yield?
annotations.note: παρεικαθεῖν (_pareikathein_, "to give way", l. 1102). He promised one line ago to obey, and his first response to the advice is to query it. I hear disbelief more than resistance: he cannot quite credit that these deferential old men are telling him to surrender. Each such line costs time, and time is now the only thing that matters.

annotations.quote: Is swift to overtake the impenitent.
annotations.note: Storr's 'impenitent' is Christian colouring. The Greek is κακόφρονας (_kakophronas_, "the wrong-thinking", l. 1104), another _phronein_ compound: the gods' harms, βλάβαι (_blabai_), are ποδώκεις (_podokeis_, "swift-footed") and cut off those who think badly. The warning about speed is right and already out of date. Antigone has been in the cave since before the last ode.

annotations.quote: My heart’s resolve; but Fate is ill to fight.
annotations.note: He stands out of his own heart, ἐξίσταμαι (_existamai_, l. 1105), and the reason he gives is ἀνάγκῃ (_anankei_, "necessity", l. 1106), against which one must not fight. Storr again writes 'Fate'. Mark what the yielding is and is not. He does not say he was wrong, or that Antigone was right, or that the dead have claims. He says he is compelled. Recognition of the fault comes only in [[s13]], over the bodies.

annotations.quote: Go, trust not others. Do it quick thyself.
annotations.note: The elders have noticed how Creon rules: through guards, through proclamations, through other men's hands. Everything he has ordered today was carried out by someone else. Now he must go in person, and the Messenger's report will show him on his knees at the mouth of the cave.

annotations.quote: My henchmen! Get ye axes! Speed away
annotations.note: He shouts for servants "present and absent", which is the speech of a man who has lost his composure. Why ἀξίνας (_axinas_, "axes", l. 1109)? The cave was sealed with stones, and an axe is no tool for that. They are presumably for cutting wood, and the Messenger will speak of fresh-cut boughs on Polyneices' pyre. So even as he gives the order, his mind is on the burial.

annotations.quote: To yonder eminence! I too will go,
annotations.note: ἐπόψιον τόπον (_epopsion topon_, "the place in full view", l. 1110) is the high ground where the body lies; the Guard's men sat on the hilltops there in [[s5]]. He sends his men to the corpse. The destination he names first is the second item in the Chorus' instructions.

annotations.quote: ’Twas I that bound, I too will set her free.
annotations.note: ἔδησα (_edesa_, "I bound") and ἐκλύσομαι (_eklysomai_, "I will release"), with παρὼν (_paron_, "being there in person", l. 1112). This is what he says he will do, and it matches the Chorus' order. What he does, as [[s13]] reports, is go first to Polyneices, wash and burn and bury him with full rites, and only then turn to the cave, where he is minutes too late. Whether the reversal kills her is a real question. I think it is in character: he sees to the city's pollution and the gods' claim before the person. And he has always supposed that what he tied he could untie.

annotations.quote: Almost I am persuaded it is best
annotations.note: Storr softens the verb. Creon says δέδοικα (_dedoika_, "I am afraid", l. 1113) that it may be best. Fear governs the sentence; he has not been persuaded of anything. That is the measure of his change at this point, and it is why the scene leaves me uneasy. He has given up his position, but nothing suggests he has understood why it was wrong.

annotations.quote: To keep through life the law ordained of old.
annotations.note: τοὺς καθεστῶτας νόμους (_tous kathestotas nomous_, "the established laws", l. 1113). His first speech in [[s3]] made _nomos_ mean his own proclamation; Antigone answered in [[s5]] with the unwritten ordinances that no one can date. He now concedes her ground in her vocabulary, without naming her. The Greek says to keep them until one's life ends, and his exit line therefore finishes on the word for ending a life.

links.why: Creon met the Guard's news with the same charge of bribery; the habit is the same and this time the witness cannot be frightened.
This is the divine verdict Antigone asked for on her way to the tomb and did not live to hear.
The prophecy of 'life for life' is paid within the hour, and the order in which Creon carries out the elders' advice decides it.

s12.essay:
Creon has run off shouting for axes, and the elders, alone and suddenly hopeful, do what they did at dawn: they call on Bacchus. This is a dance-song, a summons to the city's own god, born of a Theban mother, to come and heal. They chase him over the map, from Italy to Eleusis, Parnassus and its Castalian spring, the vine-covered slopes of Nysa, and bring every stanza home to Thebes, 'thine own.'

It is a beautiful ode and a cruel placement. Sophocles liked to set a burst of joy just before the worst news, and he does it here with complete assurance. The audience knows what a prophet's 'life for life' means. The elders have talked themselves into believing that because the king has changed his mind the story has changed its ending. The Greek asks the god to come 'with cleansing foot'; Storr has only 'Save us, O save!' The next figure to enter is a messenger.

The 'plague' they sing of is the pollution Teiresias described, the sickness of a city whose altars are fouled. And the god they pray to is not a safe one. His followers are a 'maddened rout' who dance all night. Thebes has spent the day learning what happens when a ruler tries to manage the things that belong to the gods, and it ends the day calling on the least manageable god it has.

Slips in this printing: 'All hall' is 'All hail,' and 'thy swift was wending' should be 'thy swift way wending.'

annotations.quote: Thou by many names adored,
annotations.note: πολυώνυμε (_polyonyme_, "you of many names", l. 1115) is the proper opening of a Greek prayer: name the god fully, list his haunts, then ask him to come. The ode keeps to that form, two stanzas of places and then the request. Why do the elders sing hope here? Because from where they stand the problem is solved. The king has yielded, the prophet's cure is being applied, and all that is left is to ask the city's own god to finish the cleansing. The audience can count the minutes Creon has lost and knows better.

annotations.quote: Child of Zeus the God of thunder,
annotations.note: Zeus is βαρυβρεμέτα (_barybremeta_, "deep-thundering", l. 1116), and the epithet is chosen with care, since it was that thunder which killed the god's mother. Storr has reversed the Greek order, where the mortal bride comes first and Zeus second. The elders begin from the Theban side of the god's parentage because their claim on him runs through it.

annotations.quote: Of a Theban bride the wonder,
annotations.note: Καδμείας νύμφας ἄγαλμα (_Kadmeias nymphas agalma_, "glory of the Cadmean bride", l. 1115). An _agalma_ is a thing one delights in and also a precious object offered to a god. The bride is Semele, daughter of Cadmus. Three women in this play are brides in a bad sense: Semele consumed by her bridegroom, Antigone married to her tomb, and Eurydice, who is about to come out of the palace doors.

annotations.quote: Fair Italia’s guardian lord;
annotations.note: Ἰταλίαν (_Italian_, l. 1118) is the Greek south of Italy, vine country, where Athens was helping to found the colony of Thurii at about the time this play is usually dated. Some editors have wanted to read an Attic place-name here, on the ground that Italy is a long way to go in a Theban hymn. I would keep it. The catalogue is meant to sweep from the far west home to Thebes.

annotations.quote: Of the Eleusinian Queen
annotations.note: Δῃοῦς (_Deious_, "of Deo", l. 1120) is Demeter, and her κόλποις (_kolpois_, "folds, bosom") are the sheltered plain of Eleusis, which Storr makes into glades. They are παγκοίνοις (_pankoinois_, "common to all", l. 1119) because the Mysteries took anyone who came. It is the word Creon used at l. 1049 to sneer at a commonplace. Eleusis matters for another reason: its rites concerned what happens to the dead. The god invoked to heal Thebes has one foot in the world below, where the offence was committed.

annotations.quote: Where the Dragon’s teeth were sown,
annotations.note: The σπορᾷ (_sporai_, "sowing", l. 1125) of the savage δράκοντος (_drakontos_, "serpent"): Cadmus sowed the teeth and armed men grew, who at once killed one another. Thebes begins in kin-slaughter, and the play began the morning after two brothers repeated it. In [[s2]] the dragon stood for the city that beat off the Argive eagle. Here it is simply part of the address, the ground the god is asked to walk on.

annotations.quote: Thebes, O Bacchus, is thine own.
annotations.note: He is Βακχεῦ Βακχᾶν (_Baccheu Bacchan_, "Bacchus of the Bacchants", l. 1120) and dwells in Thebes their ματρόπολιν (_matropolin_, "mother-city", l. 1121). Dionysus was born of a Theban princess, which makes him family, and the elders are calling in a relative. It is the second time they have done so. The entry song in [[s2]] ended with Bacchus invited to lead the victory dances through the night, and that night has not yet come.

annotations.quote: Thee on the two-crested rock
annotations.note: The διλόφου πέτρας (_dilophou petras_, "twin-peaked rock", l. 1126) is Parnassus above Delphi, which Dionysus was held to occupy in the winter months when Apollo was away. What sees him there is λιγνύς (_lignys_, l. 1127), the smoky flare of torches. Flame and smoke going up from a mountain to a god: after the seer's account of altars that would not burn, the picture is of a sacrifice that works.

annotations.quote: Where Corisian maidens flock,
annotations.note: Storr's 'Corisian' should be Corycian: Κωρύκιαι (_Korykiai_, l. 1127), the nymphs of the great cave high on Parnassus, here called Bacchic. A cave full of dancing girls who honour a god is an uncomfortable thing to sing while a girl hangs in another cave not far from the city. I doubt the elders hear it. I am sure Sophocles did.

annotations.quote: By Nysa’s bastion ivy-clad,
annotations.note: Νυσαίων ὀρέων (_Nysaion oreon_, "the Nysaean hills", l. 1131). Nysa was the mountain where the infant god was nursed, and every region that grew vines claimed one; the strait mentioned later suggests the Euboean Nysa is meant, just across the water from Boeotia. Ivy and grape-clusters are his plants. The slopes "send" him, so the god is pictured already on his way.

annotations.quote: And through our streets we Thebans shout,
annotations.note: Storr gives the shouting to the Thebans. In the Greek the cries are "immortal" and the god is the one acting: he is watching over the ἀγυιάς (_agyias_, "streets", l. 1135) of Thebes, the verb being the one from which we get 'overseer'. He is addressed by the same title at l. 1147. The elders want inspection, a god who walks the streets and sees what is wrong in them.

annotations.quote: Oh, as thou lov’st this city best of all,
annotations.note: ὑπερτάταν πόλεων (_hypertatan poleon_, "highest of cities", l. 1137) in his honour. The great ode in [[s4]] said the man who keeps the laws of the land and the justice of the gods stands high in his city, and the reckless man has none. The Chorus still thinks of Thebes as the city that stands high. Their ground for asking is the god's partiality, which is how Greek prayer works: you have favoured us before, do so now.

annotations.quote: To thee, and to thy Mother levin-stricken,
annotations.note: 'Levin' is an old word for lightning: ματρὶ σὺν κεραυνίᾳ (_matri syn kerauniai_, "with your thunder-struck mother", l. 1138). Semele asked to see Zeus as he is and was burned up by the sight. Even the city's patron comes out of a story about a mortal woman destroyed by contact with the divine. The elders mean it as an honour. In this play, on this day, it reads as a warning about what divine attention costs.

annotations.quote: Thou see’st with what a plague our townsfolk sicken.
annotations.note: No epidemic has been mentioned anywhere. The νόσου (_nosou_, "disease", l. 1141) is the seer's word from l. 1015 and l. 1052, and the Chorus has taken over his diagnosis entire: the πάνδαμος πόλις (_pandamos polis_, "the city with all its people") is gripped by it. They call it βιαίας (_biaias_, "violent", l. 1140), which recalls the seer's charge that the gods themselves were being forced. One man's order has made everyone unclean. What they do not say is whose mind the sickness came from.

annotations.quote: Thy ready help we crave,
annotations.note: The Greek is much more precise than Storr's general plea. He is asked to come καθαρσίῳ ποδὶ (_katharsioi podi_, "with cleansing foot", l. 1142), which is to say dancing, and to purify. This is the irony of the whole ode. A healing is prayed for and the next person through the entrance is the Messenger. The cleansing does come, and it takes the form of three deaths and a king emptied out. The play does not tell us whether to call that the god's answer or his silence.

annotations.quote: Or o’er the roaring straits thy swift was wending,
annotations.note: The printing is garbled; read 'thy swift way wending'. The strait is στονόεντα πορθμόν (_stonoenta porthmon_, l. 1145), and the adjective means "groaning, full of moans" more than 'roaring'. It is the Euripus between Euboea and the mainland. In a hymn of joy the god's road home is given the epithet of lamentation, a few lines before the house fills with the wailing Teiresias foretold.

annotations.quote: Save us, O save!
annotations.note: Storr's cry is not in the Greek, which asks only that the god μολεῖν (_molein_, "come", l. 1142). Sophocles does this more than once: he places a song of excited hope directly before the catastrophe, in the Ajax, the Oedipus and the Women of Trachis as well as here. It is a deliberate use of the Chorus' limited view. They are decent, pious, and one step behind events, and their joy raises the height from which the next scene falls.

annotations.quote: Brightest of all the orbs that breathe forth light,
annotations.note: Storr makes the god a star. The Greek makes him the chorus-leader of the stars, those ἄστρων (_astron_, l. 1146) that are πῦρ πνειόντων (_pyr pneionton_, "breathing fire"). The whole night sky is imagined as a dancing chorus with Dionysus at its head. A chorus of old men in the god's own theatre is asking the leader of a greater chorus to come and take over the dance.

annotations.quote: Authentic son of Zeus, immortal king,
annotations.note: After the titles comes the one verb the hymn has been working towards: _prophanethi_, "appear", show yourself. Greek hymns often end by asking for an epiphany, and tragedies sometimes grant one, with a god on the roof in the last scene. This play does not. No god appears in Antigone at any point, and everything divine is reported, inferred, or read from signs.

annotations.quote: Leader of all the voices of the night,
annotations.note: νυχίων (_nychion_, "of the night", l. 1146) and φθεγμάτων ἐπίσκοπε (_phthegmaton episkope_, "overseer of voices", l. 1147). It is a strange and lovely title, and a reminder of how long this one day has run since two sisters met before sunrise. The night voices the elders mean are the cries of the god's worshippers. The voices this night will actually hold are the ones the seer promised at l. 1079, men and women wailing in Creon's house.

annotations.quote: Come, and thy train of Thyiads with thee bring,
annotations.note: The Θυίαισιν (_Thyiaisin_, l. 1151) are the women who ran on Parnassus for Dionysus, and they are called his περιπόλοις (_peripolois_, "attendants", l. 1150). Storr's later 'Thy handmaids we' is his own; the elders do not claim to be the god's women. Still, it is notable that a play so anxious about women out of doors and out of control ends its last ode by asking for a troop of them.

annotations.quote: Thy maddened rout
annotations.note: μαινόμεναι (_mainomenai_, "raving", l. 1151). Madness has been a term of abuse all day, thrown at Antigone by Creon and at Creon by nearly everyone. In [[s2]] the attacker who came against Thebes with fire was described as raging like a bacchant. Here the same frenzy is holy and wished for. The ode does not reconcile the two, and I do not think it can. Dionysus is the god in whom destruction and blessing have one face.

annotations.quote: Who dance before thee all night long, and shout,
annotations.note: πάννυχοι χορεύουσι (_pannychoi choreuousin_, "they dance all night", l. 1151) repeats the all-night dances the elders proposed at dawn in [[s2]]; the play's two great hymns to Bacchus frame the day. The last words are τὸν ταμίαν Ἴακχον (_ton tamian Iakchon_, l. 1152). Iacchus is his Eleusinian name, the cry of the initiates' procession, and _tamias_ is a steward, one who gives out portions. The dance never happens. The name is still in the air when a man walks on and begins to speak of a fortune overturned.

links.why: The entrance song ended with the same god and the same wish to dance, just before Creon came on to announce the edict.
The prayer to be saved is answered at once by the messenger's first words.

s13.essay:
The Messenger begins with a moral before he gives any news, and it is a better one than the play's last lines. Creon had everything, a saved city, a throne, sons, and 'a life / Without life’s joys I count a living death.' That is the sentence Creon passed on Antigone, now passed on him by a servant.

Then Eurydice comes out. We have not seen her before and did not know to expect her. She asks for the story as one 'not unacquaint with misery,' hears all of it, and leaves without a syllable. The elders and the Messenger stand discussing what her silence might mean. I think it the finest stroke of stagecraft in the play: a dozen lines, an exit, and everyone on stage and off knows.

The narrative itself turns on an order of events. The elders told Creon to free the girl and then build the tomb. He does it the other way round. He goes first to the plain, prays, washes what is left of Polyneices, burns it, and heaps 'a mighty mound.' Only then does he go to the cave. I do not think this is carelessness. He is doing the pious thing thoroughly, at last, and the thoroughness kills her. She, for her part, has not waited either. She has hanged herself with her own linen, as her mother did. Haemon is holding her. He looks at his father, spits, draws, lunges, misses, and turns the sword on himself, 'wroth with himself.' The quarrel of [[s7]] ends there without another word between them.

Creon returns carrying the body and says what he could not say all day: 'The fault was mine, mine only.' I believe him, and so do the elders, who answer with the driest line in the play: 'Too late thou seemest to perceive the truth.' The second blow follows at once. Eurydice has died at the altar, cursing him. He begs for death and the elders refuse him even the prayer. He has to go on living, 'a cipher, less than nothing.'

In all this nobody mentions Antigone. Creon mourns his son and his wife and never speaks her name. She said she would go unwept, and the play that is called after her lets that happen. Its closing verse, that wisdom comes to the old through punishment, seems to me small for what we have seen, and I suspect it is meant to be. These elders always did arrive at wisdom a scene behind.

annotations.quote: Of Cadmus and Amphion. No man’s life
annotations.note: The Messenger addresses the elders as neighbours of two founding houses: Cadmus who sowed the city and Amphion who walled it. Both houses ended badly, Amphion's with Niobe's children, whom Antigone took as her own emblem in [[s9]]. The address is a small history of Theban ruin before a new chapter of it is read out.

annotations.quote: As of one tenor would I praise or blame,
annotations.note: This is the old maxim that no life can be judged while it is still running, here spoken by a servant. Notice that he refuses blame as well as praise. He is about to report a catastrophe caused by his master, and his first move is to decline the role of judge; the judging will be left to the Chorus and, in the end, to Creon himself.

annotations.quote: For Fortune with a constant ebb and rise
annotations.note: Storr gives a tide; the Greek gives a pair of scales and a building. τύχη (_tyche_, "chance, fortune") is named twice in l. 1158: it ὀρθοῖ (_orthoi_, "sets upright") and it καταρρέπει (_katarrhepei_, "makes the pan sink"). The first verb belongs to Creon's own vocabulary. In [[s3]] he said the gods had set the city upright again and that he would keep it sailing straight. The Messenger now hands that work to luck.

annotations.quote: And none can read a mortal’s horoscope.
annotations.note: There is no horoscope in Sophocles. The word is μάντις (_mantis_, "prophet, seer", l. 1160): no one is a prophet of what is settled for mortals. This is said a few minutes after Teiresias left the stage having prophesied exactly this. The word comes back twice more in the next sixty lines, and each time it corrects the Messenger.

annotations.quote: Was enviable. He had saved this land
annotations.note: ζηλωτός (_zelotos_, "enviable", l. 1161) and then σώσας (_sosas_, "having saved") the land from ἐχθρῶν (_echthron_, "enemies", l. 1162). An ordinary Theban grants Creon the whole of his own case: there was a war, there were enemies, he saved the city. I think this matters for how we judge the edict. The play does not want us to think the sorting of friend from enemy was a tyrant's fantasy; it was true, and it was not enough.

annotations.quote: A monarch’s powers and ruled the state supreme,
annotations.note: _pantele monarchian_ ("complete sole rule", l. 1163), and the verb for his ruling is _euthyne_ ("he steered straight", l. 1164): the ship of state once more. Haemon told him in [[s7]] that a city belonging to one man is no city, and that he would rule a desert well. The Messenger's summary of the good days already contains the fault.

annotations.quote: Now all is gone and wasted, for a life
annotations.note: The test the Messenger applies is _hedonas_ ("pleasures", l. 1165): when a man has lost those, he is not alive. A tutor should ask whether that is a servant's shallow philosophy or the play's. I think it is closer to the play than it looks. Creon warned his son not to lose his wits for pleasure in a woman, and treated every tie of affection as something a ruler could afford to cut. The Messenger says that what he cut was the life.

annotations.quote: Without life’s joys I count a living death.
annotations.note: ἔμψυχον (_empsychon_, "with breath in it") and νεκρόν (_nekron_, "corpse"), both in l. 1167: a breathing corpse. The play's central image changes owners here. Antigone was to be the living dead, shut in rock; Teiresias charged Creon with lodging a living soul in a grave. It is Creon who ends that way, in a palace, and he will say so himself at the end.

annotations.quote: The pomp and circumstance of kings; but if
annotations.note: Storr borrows Othello's phrase. The Greek is plainer and sharper: live with a _tyrannon_ (l. 1169) bearing, a tyrant's outward show.
